## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlfleetstack{15}{20}{45}{100}{20}{30}{10}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why does scale transform hardware failure from rare exception to routine condition that systems must absorb continuously?_

A single accelerator can run for years between hardware failures. A thousand accelerators turn that same component risk into failures every couple of days, and ten thousand see failures every few hours, while shared power and network faults can interrupt many workers at once. Individual devices need not become less reliable for the fleet to experience failures routinely. A program on one machine can often stop and restart when a component fails; a distributed training job must also recover agreement among surviving workers about which progress remains valid. Restarting quickly is of little value if the restored state silently changes the computation. Preserving more state reduces the work at risk, but consumes storage bandwidth and memory while the job is healthy. Waiting longer between saves reduces that overhead while increasing the progress a failure can erase. Serving imposes a different consequence: users may abandon a request before recovery completes, and replacing a worker may leave the request's context unavailable. A response that arrives on time can still be unacceptable if recovery has discarded information needed to produce it. Engineers must therefore bound lost work and recovery delay while preserving the validity of training and the usefulness of service. The goal is continued useful execution despite repeated failures, with the costs and limits of recovery made explicit. In C³ terms, fault tolerance spends compute and communication on coordination so that component failures do not routinely become failures of the entire workload.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::
::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate mean time between fleet failures from component rates and estimate interruption frequency for large training clusters
- Classify hardware, software, and silent-data-corruption failures by detectability, blast radius, and recovery path
- Select checkpoint intervals that balance write overhead against acceptable lost work and recovery delay
- Design distributed checkpointing and elastic recovery plans for multi-terabyte model state across GPU fleets
- Evaluate fault injection and observability evidence to validate detection, isolation, and recovery behavior
- Design serving redundancy, failover, and state-recovery policies under latency budgets and partial failures
- Select graceful degradation strategies that preserve useful service when models, features, regions, or capacity fail

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fault-tolerance-reliability-rates
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FLEET RELIABILITY RATES — PERSISTENT (single source of truth)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: PERSISTENT. Per-GPU and fleet failure rates derived from canonical
# │          MTTF/fleet constants. Consumed by the failure-rate footnote
# │          [^fn-fits-failure-rate] and the Fallacies and Pitfalls section
# │          (@sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-fallacies-pitfalls-74b8).
# │
# │ Goal: Derive lambda, FIT, and fleet failure cadence from one constant set so
# │       every quoted reliability number is traceable and cannot drift.
# │ Show: GPU FIT, lambda_hour, fleet FIT total, fleet failure rate, hours between.
# │ How:  lambda = 1/MTTF; FIT = 10^9/MTTF; fleet rate = N/MTTF; interval = 1/rate.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_math, fmt_time, sci_latex

class FleetReliabilityRates:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    fleet_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    lambda_gpu = 1 / gpu_mttf_h  # per-GPU failure rate (per hour)
    gpu_fit = BILLION / gpu_mttf_h  # failures per 10^9 device-hours
    fleet_fit_total = fleet_gpus * gpu_fit  # aggregate FITs across the fleet
    fleet_rate_per_h = fleet_gpus / gpu_mttf_h  # fleet failures per hour
    hours_between = 1 / fleet_rate_per_h  # mean hours between fleet failures

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(gpu_fit * gpu_mttf_h - BILLION) < 1, "FIT definition: FIT x MTTF must equal 10^9")
    check(abs(hours_between * fleet_rate_per_h - 1) < 1e-9, "interval must be reciprocal of fleet rate")
    check(0 < fleet_rate_per_h < fleet_gpus, "fleet failure rate must be positive and below the GPU count")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    _fleet_tex = fmt(fleet_gpus, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _mttf_tex = fmt(gpu_mttf_h, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _fit_tex = fmt(gpu_fit, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    gpu_mttf_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    gpu_mttf_prose_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    fleet_gpus_str = fmt_count(fleet_gpus, label="GPU")
    fleet_fit_str = fmt(fleet_fit_total, precision=0)
    hours_between_str = fmt_time(hours_between, "hour", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    gpu_mttf_sym_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True)  # margin caption
    gpu_mttf_attr_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word", attributive=True)
    gpu_fit_str = fmt(gpu_fit, precision=0)
    node_gpus_str = fmt(Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node, precision=0)  # series-system example
    hours_between_sym_str = fmt_time(hours_between, "hour", precision=0)  # margin caption
    fit_eq_math = fmt_math(rf"\text{{FIT}} = {_fit_tex}")
    lambda_eq_math = fmt_math(rf"\lambda_{{\text{{hour}}}} = {sci_latex(lambda_gpu, precision=1)}")
    fleet_rate_eq_math = fmt_math(f"{_fleet_tex}/{_mttf_tex} = {fmt(fleet_rate_per_h, precision=1, commas=False)}")
```

## Failure Analysis at Scale {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-analysis-scale-6b4b}

::: {.content-visible when-format="html:js"}
<span id="sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-analysis-scale-6b4b"></span>
:::

Imagine a 10,000-GPU cluster midway through a three-month training run for a new foundation model. The communication layer has done its job, and thousands of devices exchange gradients through AllReduce, AllGather, and AllToAll as if they were one machine. Then the arithmetic of scale catches up. A GPU fails every few hours, and if the system cannot absorb that ordinary physical event, synchronized training halts and millions of dollars of compute sit idle. **Fault tolerance**\index{Fault Tolerance!definition} is the system property that lets distributed execution continue making useful progress when components fail, degrade, or disappear. In the Fleet Stack of @fig-fleet-stack, fault tolerance occupies the Reliability & Control row of the Distribution band, where it protects the progress that parallelism and communication produce. The challenges span the full failure spectrum, from transient bit flips through intermittent aging-related errors to permanent component failures. @Fig-fault-tolerance-failure-spectrum arranges these failure modes along a persistence continuum from faults that clear spontaneously to those requiring physical replacement, mapping each mode to its operational response: immediate retry or rollback for transient events, node draining and stress-testing for intermittent recurrence, and hardware substitution for permanent failures. The analysis that follows first establishes how often failures arrive at scale, and @tbl-fault_types later ties each class to the evidence that exposes it. Gray failures (subtle component degradations that produce no explicit crash) and silent data corruption (SDC) add a second axis of difficulty, pairing low detection rates with a high blast radius.

::: {#fig-fault-tolerance-failure-spectrum fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The ML failure spectrum**: Hardware faults ordered by how long they persist. A transient fault leaves nothing to repair, an intermittent fault returns under the load that exposed it, and a permanent fault repeats on every retry. Persistence decides the fleet response, from retry through quarantine to replacement, and fault tolerance engineering must handle all three to keep a fleet making progress." fig-alt="An arrow labeled fault persistence runs from clears on its own to lasts until repaired above three cards: transient, intermittent, and permanent. Each card gives how the fault behaves, a typical cause, and the fleet response, from correct or retry, through drain and stress-test, to replace and restore a checkpoint from before the fault."}
![](images/svg/failure-spectrum.svg)

:::

That fragility is the direct consequence of successful synchronization. Distributed training systems achieve massive throughput by coordinating thousands of devices, and collective communication creates dependencies among the participating ranks. One stalled device can therefore stop progress in its synchronous training group, even while unrelated jobs continue elsewhere in the fleet. Fault-tolerant ML systems preserve progress by detecting failure, checkpointing recoverable state, restarting or elastically reshaping jobs, and treating hardware churn as normal execution rather than an exceptional path. That reliability envelope covers both halves of the fleet's work. Training needs recovery that preserves weeks of accumulated progress, while serving needs redundancy, failover, and graceful degradation that preserve a latency contract, and both draw their spare capacity from a shared fleet pool.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How the scheduler holds spare capacity for failed jobs and prepositions replacement nodes while a missed heartbeat is confirmed is developed in @sec-fleet-orchestration-failure-rates.
:::

The recovery target here is trustworthy execution: preserving valid training progress and restoring a service after its infrastructure or software fails. A restored model can still make poor predictions on changed inputs even when every component executes correctly. Evaluating that behavioral robustness requires a separate contract for model quality under distribution shifts and adversarial inputs, developed in @sec-robust-ai. The distinction lets us use model-quality signals to diagnose a fault without treating every quality regression as evidence of failed hardware.

The transition from small-scale experimentation to large-scale production changes the relationship between systems and failures. A researcher training a model on a single GPU can go years without a hardware failure. That same workload on a 1,000-GPU cluster sees GPU-only failures every couple of days, and a production cluster fails more often once PCIe, power, storage, and network domains enter the failure budget. This shift from *rare exception* to *routine occurrence* demands different engineering approaches. The mathematical analysis that follows makes this transition precise and quantitative.

::: {.column-margin}
```{=latex}
\vspace*{6mm}
```
![](images/svg/fault_tolerance_mtbf_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Time ladder showing system mean time between failures collapsing as fleet size grows: 1 GPU at 50,000 hours, 1,000 GPUs at 50 hours, 10,000 GPUs at 5 hours."}

*System mean time between failures (MTBF) collapses as the fleet grows: `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_sym_str` to `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.hours_between_sym_str`.*
:::

Because failures cannot be eliminated at this scale, fault-tolerant systems verify completion rather than assume it, treat failure as a normal code path, exercise recovery continuously, and account for partial failures that naive error handling may not anticipate. These techniques draw on decades of distributed systems research, but ML workloads change the economics. Training checkpoints are large but can be sized from the model and optimizer state, while some optimization algorithms tolerate bounded numerical perturbations without requiring bitwise replay. That tolerance must be established for the training method; stochasticity does not make arbitrary corruption or inconsistent recovery safe. A recovery design can exploit approximate execution only while preserving its declared convergence and quality requirements.

### The mathematics of inevitable failure {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-mathematics-inevitable-failure-93ef}

System reliability engineering provides the foundational framework for understanding failure at scale [@birolini2017]. Individual components exhibit failure rates characterized by the failure rate parameter $\lambda$,[^fn-fits-failure-rate] measured in failures per unit time. For a single component with constant failure rate $\lambda$, the probability of surviving without failure until time $t$ follows an exponential distribution,[^fn-poisson-failure-rate] as in @eq-single-component-reliability:

[^fn-poisson-failure-rate]: **Poisson process**\index{Poisson process!failure modeling}: A statistical model for events occurring independently at a constant average rate. In this model, event counts follow a Poisson distribution and waiting times follow an exponential distribution, giving the survival function $R_{\text{single}}(t) = e^{-\lambda t}$. With independent identical component hazards, the probability of at least one failure in a 10,000-component cluster is $1 - e^{-N \lambda t}$. The aggregate hazard $N\lambda$ scales linearly with component count; the failure probability is nonlinear in both $N$ and $t$, approaching $N\lambda t$ only when that product is small.

[^fn-fits-failure-rate]: **Failure rate ($\lambda$)**\index{Failure rate!FITs}: Expressed in FITs (Failures In Time), where 1 FIT equals one failure per billion device-hours. A data center GPU with a `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_attr_str` MTBF has `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fit_eq_math`, corresponding to `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.lambda_eq_math` failures/hour. That seems negligible for one device but becomes dominant at fleet scale: a cluster with `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_gpus_str` accumulates `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_fit_str` FITs from GPUs alone, translating to an expected GPU failure every `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.hours_between_str`.

$$ R_{\text{single}}(t) = e^{-\lambda t} $$ {#eq-single-component-reliability}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The independence, exponential-lifetime, and Poisson results this failure arithmetic rests on are developed in @sec-appdx-reliability-foundations-probability-tools.
:::

MTBF\index{MTBF!system failure rate}\index{MTBF!component vs. system} for this component equals $1/\lambda$. In this book's convention, mean time to failure (MTTF)\index{MTTF!per-component failure rate}\index{MTTF!vs. MTBF}\index{Mean time to failure|see{MTTF}} names a single component's expected time to its first failure while MTBF names the repairable system's expected operating time between successive failures, excluding recovery downtime. Under the constant-rate exponential model used here the two coincide numerically, and the fault-tolerance model uses MTTF for per-component constants and MTBF for composed system rates. Data center GPUs often use planning MTBF values in the tens of thousands of hours, with field behavior depending on operating conditions, cooling effectiveness, manufacturing variation, and workload stress.[^fn-gpu-mtbf-reliability] @Sec-appdx-reliability-foundations-component-rates catalogs the reference per-component FIT and MTTF values (GPU, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), network interface card (NIC), power supply, PCIe switch, optical cable, ToR switch) that anchor these $\lambda$ and FIT figures, so a reader can substitute the constant for any device and reproduce the rates used throughout the fault-tolerance analysis.

[^fn-gpu-mtbf-reliability]: **GPU MTBF variation**\index{GPU!MTBF variation}\index{MTBF!GPU field variation}: This chapter uses `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_prose_str` as a planning constant for current data center GPUs (A100 and H100 class), not as a guarantee for every deployed GPU. Published fleet studies from Google TPUv4 pods and Meta GPU clusters report that field reliability depends on topology, cooling, workload, and operational practice [@zu2024tpuv4; @kokolis2025; @dubey2024llama]. The planning constant therefore anchors the arithmetic, while operators should substitute measured fleet rates when they have them.

When multiple independent components operate in a system where any single failure causes system failure, @eq-system-reliability-product formalizes how system reliability becomes the product of individual component reliabilities:

$$ \ReliabilityFunctionSystem = \prod_{i=1}^{N} R_i(t) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} e^{-\lambda_i t} $$ {#eq-system-reliability-product}

For $N$ identical components with individual failure rate $\lambda$, @eq-system-reliability-n-components gives the identical-component simplification:

$$ \ReliabilityFunctionSystem = e^{-N\lambda t} $$ {#eq-system-reliability-n-components}

The system failure rate becomes $N\lambda$, and @eq-system-mtbf expresses how the system MTBF scales inversely with component count. This inverse scaling explains why per-device reliability that looks excellent in isolation erodes at cluster scale:

$$ \MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}} = \frac{1}{N\lambda} = \frac{\MeanTimeToFailure_{\text{component}}}{N} $$ {#eq-system-mtbf}

The consequence is a gap between failure cadence and job length. At `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_gpus_str`, the GPU-only calculation gives an expected interval of `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.hours_between_str`, so a training run measured in weeks accumulates dozens of expected failures and one measured in months accumulates hundreds. These are planning averages, not a schedule of incidents; a shorter job can finish without failure even when its expected failure count exceeds one. Once the expected time between failures falls below the length of the job, fault tolerance becomes part of the execution budget for long-running fleet work.

Scale and reliability diverge sharply across training generations. By pairing accelerator counts (left axis, log scale) with modeled system MTBF (opposing right axis), @fig-cluster-scaling-trend tracks how training fleets expanded by four orders of magnitude from 2012 (AlexNet on two GPUs) to 2024 (Llama 3 on over 16,000 GPUs). Applying the same per-device planning rate across those sizes compresses system MTBF from tens of thousands of hours to under ten hours. The opposing axis illustrates the scaling model rather than a history of measured failure rates, showing why recovery becomes an active scheduling constraint.

::: {#fig-cluster-scaling-trend fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The rise of fleet-scale training**: Accelerator count for state-of-the-art training runs from 2012 to 2024, with system mean time between failures on the opposing axis. Cluster size rises about four orders of magnitude and system MTBF falls correspondingly, which is what turns fault tolerance from a reliability feature into a scheduling constraint." fig-alt="Log-scale chart of training cluster accelerator count from 2012 to 2024 with a second axis for system mean time between failures. Accelerator count rises about four orders of magnitude while system MTBF falls correspondingly."}

### The Young-Daly checkpoint interval {#sec-fault-tolerance-young-daly}

Every training recovery path in this chapter ultimately falls back on a saved copy of training state, so the first question is what that copy must contain.

::: {#dfn-fault-tolerance-checkpointing .callout-definition title="Checkpointing"}

***Checkpointing***\index{Checkpointing!definition} is the periodic serialization of the complete training state (parameters, optimizer state, data loader position, and random state) to persistent storage at a recorded training step.

1.  **Significance**: It minimizes lost work after a system failure by trading checkpoint I/O against rework. Writing too often wastes accelerator time on storage traffic; writing too rarely risks replaying many completed steps after a failure. The Young-Daly interval\index{Young-Daly formula!square-root trade-off} developed in this section chooses the cadence that balances write cost against expected lost work.
2.  **Distinction**: A resumable checkpoint captures a consistent execution state, including optimizer state, random-number generator state, data position, and learning rate schedules. It can use full or incremental storage; bitwise replay additionally requires compatible deterministic execution.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that checkpointing is "just writing to disk." For large models it is a storage-system stress test, because the simultaneous write from thousands of GPUs can trigger a checkpoint storm that saturates the entire network fabric $(\Bandwidth)$.

:::

A checkpoint is useful only if it resumes the recorded step consistently. In distributed training, every shard must belong to the same recoverable state; a collection of files from different steps does not preserve progress. For the interval model, assume that writing a checkpoint completes durably before it becomes available for recovery and that a failure discards the work performed since the last completed checkpoint.

When failures are expected during a job, the key engineering decision is how often to write that state, because every save costs I/O time and every unsaved step is work a failure can erase. The Young-Daly formula\index{Young-Daly formula!optimal interval}\index{Daly formula|see{Young-Daly formula}}[^fn-young-daly-formula] (principle \ref{pri-young-daly}, applied in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-interval-failure-analysis-c28d) gives a first-order estimate of that balance through a square-root rule:

$$ \OptimalCheckpointIntervalCkpt = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}}} $$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: young-daly-checkpoint-state
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESUMABLE CHECKPOINT STATE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-young-daly, the T_write paragraph below.
# │
# │ Goal: Size a resumable mixed-precision Adam checkpoint for a 70B model and
# │       for the 175B running example from one bytes-per-parameter anchor.
# │ Show: 14 bytes per parameter; ~1 TB (70B) and >2 TB (175B).
# │ How:  params x ReferenceStats.MixedPrecisionAdam.CheckpointBytesPerParameter.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, ReferenceStats
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt

class YoungDalyCheckpointState:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    ckpt_bpp = ReferenceStats.MixedPrecisionAdam.CheckpointBytesPerParameter
    params_70b = Models.Language.Llama3_70B.parameters
    params_175b = Models.Language.GPT3.parameters

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    ckpt_70b_tb = (params_70b * ckpt_bpp).to(TB).magnitude
    ckpt_175b_tb = (params_175b * ckpt_bpp).to(TB).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(0.9 < ckpt_70b_tb < 1.0, "70B checkpoint must 'approach a terabyte'")
    check(ckpt_175b_tb > 2.0, "175B checkpoint must 'exceed two terabytes'")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    ckpt_bpp_str = fmt(ckpt_bpp.magnitude, precision=0)
```

$\CheckpointWriteTime$ in distributed ML training is not the time to flush a small process state; it includes transferring model weights and optimizer state to durable storage. The reference format here stores BF16 weights, separate FP32 master weights, and two FP32 moment tensors per parameter for Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam). A single resumable checkpoint for a 70B-parameter model therefore approaches a terabyte at `{python} YoungDalyCheckpointState.ckpt_bpp_str` bytes per parameter; for the later 175B-parameter running example, it exceeds two terabytes. Reducing $\CheckpointWriteTime$ requires a smaller payload or higher sustained write bandwidth, and $\CheckpointWriteTime$ itself is the central constraint that determines how tightly the checkpoint interval can be set before I/O overhead displaces productive training compute.

To see the balance, consider an interval between saves. Doubling that interval approximately halves the checkpoint writes per unit of training, but a failure then loses twice as much work on average. Under the constant-rate, rare-failure approximation, failure occurs approximately uniformly within an interval, so the average lost work is half the interval. When write time is small relative to the interval, the wasted fraction from saving and replaying work is approximately the sum below. Detection, allocation, and restoration time require a separate recovery budget.

$$ W(\CheckpointIntervalCkpt) \approx \frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointIntervalCkpt} + \frac{\CheckpointIntervalCkpt}{2 \cdot \MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}}} $$

Setting the first derivative to zero ($\frac{dW}{d\CheckpointIntervalCkpt} = -\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointIntervalCkpt^2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot \MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}}} = 0$) directly yields the square-root minimum $\OptimalCheckpointIntervalCkpt = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}}}$. In @fig-checkpoint-tradeoff, this balance forms a U-shaped convex curve for the chapter's 10,000-GPU cluster running a 175B-parameter model: write overhead (dashed blue) falls hyperbolically while expected rework (dashed red) climbs linearly, reaching a minimum near $\OptimalCheckpointIntervalCkpt \approx 14$ minutes. The modeled saving-and-rework loss there is 5.9 percent, before adding recovery downtime. Its scaling consequence is the one to carry forward. As clusters grow, system MTBF drops, so the optimal interval shrinks, demanding higher-bandwidth storage to keep $\CheckpointWriteTime$ small before the "checkpoint tax" consumes the cluster's compute capacity. Because the relationship is a square root, halving MTBF tightens the interval by only $\sqrt{2}\approx 1.4\times$, so doubling cluster size does not demand doubling checkpoint I/O bandwidth when checkpoint size and the other assumptions stay fixed. The chapter applies the formula to its own cluster once the system MTBF is in hand.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The per-tier storage bandwidths that bound how quickly a checkpoint can be written are established in @sec-storage-hierarchy.
:::

[^fn-young-daly-formula]: **Young-Daly formula**\index{Young-Daly formula!history}: @young1974 derived the first-order optimal checkpoint interval, and @daly2006 independently refined it with tighter second-order bounds.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: checkpoint-tradeoff-inputs
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHECKPOINT TRADE-OFF INPUTS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-checkpoint-tradeoff and its caption.
# │
# │ Goal: Feed the U-curve the same two inputs the Young-Daly notebook uses
# │       later, so the plotted optimum and the worked interval agree.
# │ Show: T_write ~24.5 s (175B, 14 B/param, registry write bandwidth);
# │       full-system MTBF ~3.87 h (GPU + PCIe + shared NIC, 10,000 GPUs);
# │       tau_opt ~13.8 min.
# │ How:  Same series-rate composition as the worked MTBF cascade (redundant
# │       PSUs add no term); tau_opt = sqrt(2 * T_write * MTBF_system).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Models, Systems
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_time

class CheckpointTradeoffInputs:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(Models.Language.GPT3.parameters)  # 14 B/param
    write_bw = float(Systems.Reliability.Recovery.checkpoint_write_bw_gbs) * (GB / second)
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    gpus_per_node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    pcie_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.PcieSwitch.mttf_hours)
    nic_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Nic.mttf_hours)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_write_h = (ckpt_bytes / write_bw).to(hour).magnitude
    rate_per_gpu = 1 / gpu_mttf_h + 1 / pcie_mttf_h + (1 / gpus_per_node) / nic_mttf_h
    mtbf_h = 1 / (n_gpus * rate_per_gpu)
    tau_opt_h = math.sqrt(2 * t_write_h * mtbf_h)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(22 < t_write_h * 3600 < 27, "175B checkpoint write should be ~24.5 s")
    check(3.5 < mtbf_h < 4.2, "full-system MTBF should match the worked cascade (~3.87 h)")
    check(12 < tau_opt_h * 60 < 15, "tau_opt should match the Young-Daly notebook (~13.8 min)")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_write_s_str = fmt_time(t_write_h * 3600, "second", precision=1, commas=False)
    mtbf_h_str = fmt_time(mtbf_h, "hour", precision=1, commas=False)
    tau_opt_min_str = fmt_time(round(tau_opt_h * 60), "minute", precision=0, commas=False)
    n_gpus_str = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0)
```

::: {#fig-checkpoint-tradeoff fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The checkpoint trade-off**: Checkpoint save overhead (dashed blue) falls as the interval lengthens, while expected rework after a failure (dashed red) rises; their sum (solid) is minimized at the Young-Daly interval. The curves use this chapter's 175B running example on its `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster, with a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.t_write_s_str` checkpoint write and a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.mtbf_h_str` full-system MTBF, which put the optimum near `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_min_str`. The minimum is shallow, so an interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while a far shorter or far longer one costs a great deal." fig-alt="Three curves against checkpoint interval in minutes: checkpoint overhead decreasing, rework cost increasing linearly, and total wasted time with a shallow minimum marked near 14 minutes."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHECKPOINT TRADE-OFF (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-checkpoint-tradeoff.
# │
# │ Goal: Plot save overhead, expected rework, and their sum vs. interval for
# │       the chapter's 175B / 10,000-GPU example; mark tau_opt.
# │ Show: Three curves; optimum annotation near 14 min.
# │ How:  Inputs from CheckpointTradeoffInputs (no literals); book_style.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.5))

t_write = CheckpointTradeoffInputs.t_write_h
mtbf = CheckpointTradeoffInputs.mtbf_h
tau_opt = CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_h

tau = np.linspace(tau_opt / 6, tau_opt * 4, 300)
over_ckpt = t_write / tau
over_rework = tau / (2 * mtbf)
total_waste = over_ckpt + over_rework
waste_opt = t_write / tau_opt + tau_opt / (2 * mtbf)

ax.plot(tau * 60, over_ckpt * 100, label='Checkpoint overhead ($T_{\\mathrm{write}}/T_{\\mathrm{ckpt}}$)', color=COLORS['BlueLine'], linestyle='--')
ax.plot(
    tau * 60,
    over_rework * 100,
    label='Expected rework ($T_{\\mathrm{ckpt}}/(2\\,\\mathrm{MTBF}_{\\mathrm{system}})$)',
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
    linestyle='--',
)
ax.plot(tau * 60, total_waste * 100, label='Total wasted time', color=COLORS['primary'], linewidth=2.5)

ax.scatter([tau_opt * 60], [waste_opt * 100], color=COLORS['primary'], s=40, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f'$T^*_{{\\mathrm{{ckpt}}}} \\approx {tau_opt * 60:.0f}$ min, {waste_opt * 100:.1f}% wasted',
    xy=(tau_opt * 60, waste_opt * 100),
    xytext=(tau_opt * 60 + 12, waste_opt * 100 + 7),
    ha='left',
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=COLORS['primary'], shrinkB=4, lw=0.75),
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.25', facecolor='white', edgecolor='#CBD5E1', lw=0.6, alpha=0.95),
)

ax.set_xlabel('Checkpoint interval $T_{\\mathrm{ckpt}}$ (minutes)')
ax.set_ylabel('Share of wall time wasted (%)')
ax.set_xlim(0, tau_opt * 4 * 60)
ax.set_yticks([0, 5, 10, 15, 20])
ax.set_ylim(0, 20)

ax.legend(loc='upper right', frameon=True, facecolor='white', edgecolor='#CBD5E1', framealpha=0.95)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

A quick availability calculation shows the same scaling pressure from another angle.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lego-nines-reliability
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class NinesReliability:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    availability_pct = 99.99
    single_gpu_success = availability_pct / 100

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    downtime_min_year = (1 - single_gpu_success) * HOURS_PER_YEAR * MINUTES_PER_HOUR
    cluster_prob = single_gpu_success**n_gpus
    fleet_mtbf = FleetReliabilityRates.hours_between * hour
    fast_mttr = 5 * minute
    slow_mttr = 30 * minute
    fast_availability = (fleet_mtbf / (fleet_mtbf + fast_mttr)).to("").magnitude
    slow_availability = (fleet_mtbf / (fleet_mtbf + slow_mttr)).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < cluster_prob < 1, "Probability must be in (0,1)")
    check(cluster_prob < 0.5, "Cluster survival must be low at scale")
    check(0 < slow_availability < fast_availability < 1, "Faster repair must improve availability")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0)
    availability_str = fmt_percent(availability_pct / 100, precision=2, commas=False, style='prose')
    downtime_min_str = fmt_time(downtime_min_year, 'minute', precision=1, commas=False, style='word')
    survival_str = fmt(single_gpu_success, precision=4, commas=False)
    cluster_prob_str = fmt(cluster_prob, precision=2, commas=False)
    cluster_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(cluster_prob * 100) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    fleet_mtbf_str = fmt_time(fleet_mtbf, hour, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    fast_mttr_str = fmt_time(fast_mttr, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    slow_mttr_str = fmt_time(slow_mttr, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    fast_availability_str = fmt_percent(fast_availability, precision=2, commas=False, style="prose")
    slow_availability_str = fmt_percent(slow_availability, precision=2, commas=False, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-fault-tolerance-9s-reliability .callout-notebook title="The 9s of reliability"}

**Problem**: A cluster of `{python} NinesReliability.n_gpus_str` GPUs runs with each GPU at `{python} NinesReliability.availability_str` availability (only `{python} NinesReliability.downtime_min_str` of downtime per year). Assuming independent up/down states, what is the probability that the entire cluster is up at the same instant?

**Math**:

1.  Single GPU availability probability $(R_{\text{GPU}})$: A GPU with `{python} NinesReliability.availability_str` availability has an all-up probability $R_{\text{GPU}} =$ `{python} NinesReliability.survival_str` at a randomly chosen instant.
2.  Cluster availability probability $(R_{\text{cluster}})$: $R_{\text{cluster}} = (R_{\text{GPU}})^{N}$.
3.  **Result**: $(R_{\text{GPU}})^{N} \approx$ `{python} NinesReliability.cluster_prob_str`.

**Systems insight**: Even with `{python} NinesReliability.availability_str` reliable hardware, a `{python} NinesReliability.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster has only a `{python} NinesReliability.cluster_pct_str` chance that every GPU is simultaneously available. Hardware reliability alone is insufficient; software must handle failures automatically.

:::

::: {#psp-fault-tolerance-scale-transforms-failure .callout-perspective title="Scale transforms failure"}

A cluster of `{python} NinesReliability.n_gpus_str` GPUs turns a per-GPU MTBF of `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_prose_str` into a system MTBF of `{python} NinesReliability.fleet_mtbf_str`. For a repairable system, steady-state availability\index{Availability!MTBF and MTTR} is $A = \MeanTimeBetweenFailures/(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures+\MeanTimeToRepair)$, where mean time to recovery (MTTR)\index{MTTR!availability impact}\index{MTTR!recovery interval}\index{Mean time to recovery|see{MTTR}} is the recovery interval. Cutting MTTR from `{python} NinesReliability.slow_mttr_str` to `{python} NinesReliability.fast_mttr_str` raises availability from `{python} NinesReliability.slow_availability_str` to `{python} NinesReliability.fast_availability_str`. This stationary two-state model assumes unconstrained repair capacity and complete outage; correlated incidents, repair contention, and degraded operation require direct measurement [@birolini2017]. Systems must engineer recovery, not merely improve components.

:::

### Quantitative reliability analysis {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-quantitative-analysis}

The GPU-only calculation in the opening reliability example supplies the scale intuition; a real training system then composes GPUs, HBM, links, power supplies, storage paths, and redundancy into one failure budget. With MTBF and the FIT rate already defined ($\text{FIT} = 10^9/\MeanTimeBetweenFailures$, so a `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_attr_str` GPU contributes `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_fit_str` FIT), the new question is how component rates compose. The composition rule depends on the redundancy structure and the independence assumptions. For series systems\index{Reliability!series system}\index{Series system!reliability calculation} (for example, a node where all `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.node_gpus_str` GPUs must work), failure of any component fails the whole. With independent constant-rate failures, reliabilities multiply and rates add:
$$\ReliabilityFunctionSystem = \prod_{i=1}^{N} R_i(t), \qquad \MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}} = \frac{1}{\sum \lambda_i}$$
which is why the system failure rate grows linearly with component count while system MTBF falls in inverse proportion. For parallel systems\index{Reliability!parallel system}\index{Parallel system!redundancy calculation} providing redundancy, suppose that any surviving component can satisfy the required service. With independent failures and no repair during the observation interval, the system survives until every component has failed:
$$\ReliabilityFunctionSystem = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - R_i(t))$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ UNPROTECTED-HBM SOFT-ERROR BUDGET (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Goal: Show why unprotected HBM at cluster scale corrupts memory every tens of seconds.
# │ How: 250 FIT/Mbit x (1,024 x H100 HBM) megabits -> aggregate FIT -> mean time to first error.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_memory_capacity, fmt_time

class HbmSerBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ser_fit_per_mbit = Systems.Reliability.Hbm.soft_error_fit_per_mbit
    cluster_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # Archetype A reference cluster
    hbm_per_gpu = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.capacity
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    total_mbit = (cluster_gpus * hbm_per_gpu).to(bit).magnitude / 1e6
    aggregate_fit = float(ser_fit_per_mbit) * total_mbit
    failures_per_hour = aggregate_fit / BILLION  # FIT = failures per 1e9 device-hours
    time_to_error_s = SEC_PER_HOUR / failures_per_hour
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(10 <= time_to_error_s <= 60, "Illustrative raw-error interval should be tens of seconds")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    fit_per_mbit_str = fmt(ser_fit_per_mbit, precision=0, commas=False)
    time_to_error_str = fmt_time(round(time_to_error_s), 'second', precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    cluster_gpus_str = fmt(cluster_gpus, precision=0, commas=True)
    hbm_per_gpu_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(hbm_per_gpu, unit=GiB, precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#lhs-fault-tolerance-archetype-a-gpt-4-llama-3-memory-soft-error .callout-lighthouse title="Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): Memory soft-error scale"}

Composition makes the distinction between raw faults and job interruptions essential. As an illustrative raw-bit-error budget, assume `{python} HbmSerBudget.fit_per_mbit_str` FIT per megabit across `{python} HbmSerBudget.cluster_gpus_str` GPUs with `{python} HbmSerBudget.hbm_per_gpu_gb_str` each, the size of the Archetype A reference cluster. The resulting interval between raw memory errors is roughly `{python} HbmSerBudget.time_to_error_str`. This is not a measured job-failure interval. Error-correcting code (ECC) protection can correct covered error patterns before they affect computation, while detected uncorrectable errors and escaped corruption require different recovery paths. At that raw rate, unprotected memory in the reference cluster would corrupt training state many times per hour, so ECC is a precondition for large-scale training rather than an option. A fleet reliability budget therefore needs the residual job-interrupting and silent-corruption rates under its actual protection scheme; raw bit-error rates alone cannot establish whether memory, logic, or interconnect dominates.

:::

These per-component FIT figures describe a raw soft-error budget, which differs from the `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_attr_str` device MTTF used in the worked cascade that follows. A device-level interruption rate includes the effects of its protection mechanisms and the failure modes assigned to that device boundary. The cascade treats its GPU, PCIe, power, and network contributions as separate categories; a measured whole-node rate that already includes those paths cannot be added to them again. The raw-bit calculation motivates memory protection, while the interruption model sets the checkpoint interval.

### Cluster MTBF calculation {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-worked-example-cluster-mtbf-calculation-9255}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fault-tolerance-mtbf-cascade
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLUSTER MTBF CASCADE — WORKED EXAMPLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-worked-example-cluster-
# │          mtbf-calculation-9255. Drives the Steps 1-3 display equations and the
# │          closing narrative (every 3.9 h, 6.2/day, ~43/week).
# │
# │ Goal: Reproduce the worked MTBF cascade from canonical MTTF/fleet constants so
# │       every quoted rate is traceable and cannot drift.
# │ Scope: chapter-anchor — checkpoint analysis reuses the worked cluster MTBF.
# │ Show: lambda per subsystem, total, system rate, cluster MTBF, failure cadence.
# │ How:  lambda = 1/MTTF; network shared across the node's GPUs; power enters only
# │       through series (non-redundant) PSUs, 0 for the DGX H100's 4+2 supply;
# │       system = N*total. Narrative cadence follows the displayed rate (0.2583)
# │       for self-consistency.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_rate, fmt_time

class FailureCascadeExample:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    fleet_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    gpu_mttf = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    pcie_mttf = float(Systems.Reliability.PcieSwitch.mttf_hours)
    psu_mttf = float(Systems.Reliability.Psu.mttf_hours)
    nic_mttf = float(Systems.Reliability.Nic.mttf_hours)
    gpus_per_node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node
    series_psus = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.series_psus  # 0: 4+2 redundant supplies
    psus_per_node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.psus_per_node
    psu_redundancy = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.psu_redundancy
    psus_required = psus_per_node - psu_redundancy
    ref_gpus = Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference.system.total_accelerators

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    l_gpu = 1 / gpu_mttf
    l_pcie = 1 / pcie_mttf
    l_power = (series_psus / gpus_per_node) / psu_mttf  # 0 for the DGX H100's 4+2 supply
    l_net = (1 / gpus_per_node) / nic_mttf
    l_total = l_gpu + l_pcie + l_power + l_net
    l_system = fleet_gpus * l_total
    l_system_disp = round(l_system, 4)  # rate as displayed (0.2583)
    mtbf_h = 1 / l_system_disp  # narrative follows the displayed rate
    per_day = 24 * l_system_disp
    per_week = 24 * 7 * l_system_disp
    weekly_failures = round(per_week)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(0 < l_gpu < 1, "per-GPU failure rate must be a small positive value")
    check(l_power == 0, "DGX H100 PSUs are 4+2 redundant: no single-PSU term in the series sum")
    check(2.0 < mtbf_h < 5.0, "10k-GPU cluster MTBF should be a few hours")
    check(per_week > per_day > 1, "weekly failures must exceed daily, both above one")
    check(9 < fleet_gpus / ref_gpus < 11, "prose says 'roughly ten times' the reference cluster")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    fleet_gpus_str = fmt(fleet_gpus, precision=0)
    ref_gpus_str = fmt(ref_gpus, precision=0)
    gpu_mttf_hours_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    pcie_mttf_hours_str = fmt_time(pcie_mttf, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    psu_mttf_hours_str = fmt_time(psu_mttf, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    nic_mttf_hours_str = fmt_time(nic_mttf, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    gpus_per_node_str = fmt(gpus_per_node, precision=0)
    psus_per_node_str = fmt(psus_per_node, precision=0)
    psus_required_str = fmt(psus_required, precision=0)
    psu_redundancy_str = fmt(psu_redundancy, precision=0)
    _gpu_d = fmt(gpu_mttf, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _pcie_d = fmt(pcie_mttf, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _psu_d = fmt(psu_mttf, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _nic_d = fmt(nic_mttf, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _fleet_d = fleet_gpus_str.replace(",", "{,}")
    _npn = gpus_per_node_str
    lambda_gpu_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \lambda_{{\text{{GPU}}}} = \frac{{1}}{{{_gpu_d}}} = {l_gpu*1e5:.1f} \times 10^{{-5}} \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    lambda_pcie_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \lambda_{{\text{{PCIe}}}} = \frac{{1}}{{{_pcie_d}}} = {l_pcie*1e5:.1f} \times 10^{{-5}} \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    lambda_power_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \lambda_{{\text{{power/GPU}}}} = \frac{{n_{{\text{{psu,series}}}}}}{{{_npn}}} \times \frac{{1}}{{{_psu_d}}} = \frac{{{series_psus}}}{{{_npn}}} \times \frac{{1}}{{{_psu_d}}} = 0 \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    lambda_net_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \lambda_{{\text{{network/GPU}}}} = \frac{{1}}{{{_npn}}} \times \frac{{1}}{{{_nic_d}}} = {l_net*1e5:.3f} \times 10^{{-5}} \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    lambda_total_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \lambda_{{\text{{total/GPU}}}} = ({l_gpu*1e5:.1f} + {l_pcie*1e5:.1f} + {l_net*1e5:.3f}) \times 10^{{-5}} = {l_total*1e5:.3f} \times 10^{{-5}} \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    lambda_system_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \lambda_{{\text{{system}}}} = {_fleet_d} \times {l_total*1e5:.3f} \times 10^{{-5}} = {l_system:.4f} \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    mtbf_eq_math = fmt_display_math(rf" \text{{MTBF}}_{{\text{{system}}}} = \frac{{1}}{{{l_system_disp:.4f}}} = {mtbf_h:.2f} \text{{ hours}} ")
    mtbf_hours_str = fmt_time(mtbf_h, "hour", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    mtbf_hours_2dp_str = fmt_time(mtbf_h, "hour", precision=2, commas=False, style="word")
    failures_per_day_str = fmt_rate(per_day, "failures/day", precision=1, commas=False)
    weekly_failures_str = fmt_count(weekly_failures, precision=0, label="failure")
```

Consider a training cluster designed for large language model development, roughly ten times the `{python} FailureCascadeExample.ref_gpus_str`-GPU Archetype A reference cluster, with the following specifications:

- `{python} FailureCascadeExample.fleet_gpus_str` NVIDIA H100\index{H100!cluster reliability}\index{NVIDIA!H100} GPUs
- Individual GPU MTBF: `{python} FailureCascadeExample.gpu_mttf_hours_str`
- Each GPU connected to host via PCIe (MTBF: `{python} FailureCascadeExample.pcie_mttf_hours_str`)
- Each node contains `{python} FailureCascadeExample.gpus_per_node_str` GPUs fed by `{python} FailureCascadeExample.psus_per_node_str` power supply units (MTBF: `{python} FailureCascadeExample.psu_mttf_hours_str` each) in `{python} FailureCascadeExample.psus_required_str`+`{python} FailureCascadeExample.psu_redundancy_str` redundancy, so the node keeps full performance with any `{python} FailureCascadeExample.psu_redundancy_str` of them failed
- Network infrastructure per node (NIC, cables): MTBF `{python} FailureCascadeExample.nic_mttf_hours_str`

Together, these components define the failure domain used in the rate calculations in this worked example.

#### Failure rate calculation per GPU subsystem {.unnumbered}

Each GPU operates within a failure domain that includes the GPU itself, its PCIe connection, and a proportional share of the node's network infrastructure. Power enters the sum only through supplies whose single failure stops the node, counted as $n_{\text{psu,series}}$ in the power equation. With the node's supplies in redundant sets, no single unit qualifies, so the power term below is zero in this first-order calculation. The approximation omits the residual risk that additional independent failures exhaust redundancy before repair. A fault upstream of the chassis, such as the loss of the circuits feeding it, can also take down the whole node; that risk belongs to the correlated failures treated later in this chapter.

Under the model, the cluster experiences a failure every `{python} FailureCascadeExample.mtbf_hours_str` on average. The expected failure cadence is `{python} FailureCascadeExample.failures_per_day_str`; a training run lasting one week has an expected count of `{python} FailureCascadeExample.weekly_failures_str`. Actual incident times vary, but the expected loss is large enough that recovery must be part of normal execution planning.

The cluster MTBF scaling\index{Cluster!MTBF scaling} in @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling isolates the GPU-only baseline across cluster sizes. The full-system calculation is lower once PCIe and network failure domains are included.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: cluster-mtbf-scaling-table
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLUSTER MTBF SCALING TABLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling — GPU-only MTBF and failures-per-day rows
# │          across seven cluster sizes.
# │
# │ Goal: Compute each row's cluster MTBF and expected failures per day from the
# │       single canonical per-GPU MTTF constant, so the whole table reproduces
# │       the 1/N scaling law and cannot drift from the registry.
# │ Show: Per-row cluster MTBF (hours, plus a days parenthetical for the long-MTBF
# │       rows) and expected failures per day.
# │ How:  cluster_mtbf = MTTF / N; failures_per_day = 24 * N / MTTF.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import day, hour
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_text, fmt_time

def _mtbf_h(v):
    # integer-like rows display as whole hours; fractional rows keep one place
    return fmt_time(round(v) * hour, hour, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")

def _mtbf_cell(v):
    # show the days parenthetical only where the cluster MTBF is at least a day
    hrs = _mtbf_h(v)
    if v >= 24.0:
        days = fmt_time(round(v / 24.0) * day, day, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
        return fmt_text(hrs, " (", days, ")")
    return hrs

def _fpd_cell(v):
    if v < 0.01:
        return fmt(v, precision=3, commas=False)
    if v < 1.0:
        return fmt(v, precision=2, commas=False)
    if float(round(v, 1)).is_integer():
        return fmt_int(int(round(v)))
    return fmt(v, precision=1, commas=False)

class ClusterMtbfScaling:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    sizes = [8, 64, 512, 1000, 4000, 10000, 25000]

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    cluster_mtbf_h = []
    failures_per_day = []
    for _n in sizes:
        cluster_mtbf_h.append(gpu_mttf_h / _n)
        failures_per_day.append(24.0 * _n / gpu_mttf_h)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(cluster_mtbf_h[3] - 50.0) < 1e-9 and abs(cluster_mtbf_h[5] - 5.0) < 1e-9, "1,000-GPU MTBF must be 50h and 10,000-GPU MTBF must be 5h")
    check(abs(failures_per_day[5] - 4.8) < 0.01, "10,000-GPU failure rate must be 4.8 failures/day")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    gpu_mttf_hrs_str = fmt_time(round(gpu_mttf_h) * hour, hour, precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    n0_str, n1_str, n2_str, n3_str, n4_str, n5_str, n6_str = [fmt_int(_n) for _n in sizes]
    mtbf0_str, mtbf1_str, mtbf2_str, mtbf3_str, mtbf4_str, mtbf5_str, mtbf6_str = [_mtbf_cell(_v) for _v in cluster_mtbf_h]
    fpd0_str, fpd1_str, fpd2_str, fpd3_str, fpd4_str, fpd5_str, fpd6_str = [_fpd_cell(_v) for _v in failures_per_day]
```

| `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.n1_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.gpu_mttf_hrs_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.mtbf1_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.fpd1_str` |

: **Cluster MTBF Scaling**: GPU-only mean time between failures falls in inverse proportion to cluster size, transforming failures from rare events to continuous operating conditions at scale. Additional host, power, storage, and network failure domains reduce system-level MTBF further. {#tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: published-failure-rates
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PUBLISHED FAILURE RATES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The Kokolis/Llama 3 paragraph below and @fig-published-failure-rates.
# │
# │ Goal: Pin the published fleet MTTF evidence to Literature so the prose and
# │       the figure quote the same measured and projected values.
# │ Show: 16,384-GPU projected MTTF (1.8 h); Llama 3 405B snapshot of 419
# │       unexpected interruptions over 54 days on 16,384 H100s (~3.1 h MTTF).
# │ How:  Literature.FleetOperations.Kokolis*; Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_*;
# │       Models.Language.Llama3_405B.training_accelerators_ref; MTTF = days*24/count.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature, Models
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_time

class PublishedFailureRates:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    kokolis_16k_mttf_h = float(Literature.FleetOperations.Kokolis16KGpuProjectedMttfHours)
    llama_gpus = Models.Language.Llama3_405B.training_accelerators_ref.magnitude
    llama_interruptions = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_UnexpectedInterruptions)
    llama_days = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_SnapshotDays)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    llama_mttf_h = llama_days * 24 / llama_interruptions

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(float(Literature.FleetOperations.Kokolis16KGpuJobGpus) - llama_gpus) < 1, "Kokolis projection and Llama 3 run must share a job size")
    check(1.5 < kokolis_16k_mttf_h < 2.0 and 2.5 < llama_mttf_h < 3.5, "prose brackets the cadence at 'roughly two to three hours'")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str = fmt_time(kokolis_16k_mttf_h, "hour", precision=1, style="word", attributive=True)
    llama_mttf_attr_str = fmt_time(llama_mttf_h, "hour", precision=1, style="word", attributive=True)
    llama_mttf_str = fmt_time(llama_mttf_h, "hour", precision=1, style="word")
    llama_gpus_str = fmt(llama_gpus, precision=0)
    llama_interruptions_str = fmt(llama_interruptions, precision=0)
    llama_days_str = fmt(llama_days, precision=0)
```

The theoretical $1/N$ scaling in @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling is not merely a textbook exercise. On a log-log scale of MTTF versus accelerator count, @fig-published-failure-rates charts empirical measurements and fitted projections from Meta's production clusters against the theoretical $50{,}000\,\text{h}/N$ dashed line. The @kokolis2025 study of Meta's Research SuperCluster reported measured MTTF values for observed RSC job sizes and projected a `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` MTTF for `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str`-GPU jobs; Meta's Llama 3\index{Llama-3!failure report} training report independently documented `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_interruptions_str` unexpected interruptions across a `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_days_str`-day snapshot on `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str` H100 GPUs, an observed MTTF of about `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_str`. Together, the measured Llama run and Kokolis projection put `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str`-GPU training on a failure cadence of roughly two to three hours, bracketed by the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` projection and the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_attr_str` measurement. This evidence turns the idealized $1/N$ relation into an engineering constraint that determines checkpoint frequency, recovery architecture, and infrastructure investment.
