### Failure taxonomy {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-taxonomy-e78c}

The MTBF calculations in the reliability analysis quantify how often failures occur, which is critical for setting checkpoint intervals and sizing recovery infrastructure. Designing effective fault tolerance also requires understanding what kind of failures occur. Use the vocabulary carefully: a fault is the underlying defect or event, an error is the corrupted state it produces, and a failure is the externally visible behavior the training system must handle [@avizienis2004basic]. A network partition that resolves in seconds demands different handling than a permanent GPU failure. A silent memory corruption that produces incorrect gradients requires different detection mechanisms than a node crash that stops responding entirely.

No single label captures all of these differences. Reliability decisions require three orthogonal axes: persistence (transient, intermittent, or permanent), manifestation (fail-stop, degraded, or value-corrupting), and failure scope (one device, one node, a rack or power domain, or the whole job). A transient fault can therefore manifest as either a detected crash or silent corruption, while a permanent switch failure can remain confined to one rack or partition an entire job. The subsections that follow project this three-axis space onto the failure classes most useful for recovery; they do not define mutually exclusive buckets [@constantinescu2008; @lamport1982byzantine].

#### Transient failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-transient-failures-57b4}

A transient fault clears without physical repair, but the state it corrupts can persist after the disturbance ends. Recovery must therefore retry or validate affected work before relying on that state. Large-scale training systems encounter several forms of temporary disruption. Network packet loss\index{Transient fault!network packet loss} momentarily drops data while transport retransmission succeeds. Memory bit flips\index{Memory!bit flip} can result from cosmic-ray-induced single-event upsets.[^fn-seu-soft-error] Under temperature spikes, thermal throttling\index{Thermal throttling!performance degradation} temporarily reduces compute throughput without halting execution, while software timeouts\index{Software timeout!resource contention} emerge when transient contention delays communication beyond its allotted time.

[^fn-seu-soft-error]: **Single-event upset (SEU)**\index{SEU!error rate}: From particle physics, where "upset" denotes a nondestructive state change. Cosmic rays and alpha particles from chip packaging can flip bits in memory and logic; the observed rate depends on altitude, process technology, packaging materials, shielding, and workload [@ziegler1996; @baumann2005]. ECC memory corrects single-bit errors but cannot handle every multi-bit upset in the same word, leaving a residual silent-corruption risk that compounds across the terabytes of state in large-scale ML training.

Transient faults are particularly difficult to diagnose in ML training when they leave no explicit error signal. A memory bit flip during gradient computation can propagate into later updates if hardware protection and the computation itself do not mask it. Training can then continue with corrupted state. Large-scale SDC studies show escaped corruption, while DRAM field studies show memory errors are common enough that fleet-level monitoring matters [@dixit2021silent; @sridharan2015; @schroeder2009]. In ML training, that same undetected-corruption pattern can surface as degraded gradients, anomalous loss curves, or rollback-worthy checkpoints rather than an explicit crash.

The appropriate response to transient failures depends on detection capability. Errors that trigger explicit exceptions can be handled through bounded retry logic. Silent corruption requires end-to-end validation. Checksums detect changed bytes in storage or transport, cross-rank digests reveal disagreement about a supposedly identical reduced buffer, and statistical or replay checks test whether the computation itself remains plausible. A rank that computes the wrong local gradient and then correctly checksums those wrong bytes passes an ordinary checksum; only independent recomputation, invariants, or model-level evidence can expose that error.

#### Fail-stop failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failstop-failures-5cdd}

Fail-stop failures\index{Fail-stop failure!characteristics}\index{Fail-stop failure!detection and recovery} cause components to cease operation entirely and detectably. The failed component stops responding to requests and is suspected through timeout mechanisms, though a timeout alone cannot distinguish an outright crash from an isolated or delayed host. A GPU hardware failure\index{GPU!hardware failure} renders an individual accelerator unresponsive, while a broader node crash\index{Node!crash} abruptly terminates all training processes on the host. Similarly, a network partition\index{Network partition!fault tolerance} severs communication between a healthy node and the remaining cluster, and a storage failure\index{Storage!failure} prevents workers from writing or reading checkpoint shards.

In synchronous distributed training, a failed participant can stall the job's next update. A conventional AllReduce requires every participating rank to supply its input before the reduction can complete. A single GPU that goes silent, whether from a hardware fault, a process crash, or a network partition, can therefore block the ranks waiting on that result until recovery begins. If all 10,000 GPUs belong to a job whose progress depends on the failed group, the other 9,999 accelerators can be left waiting for the missing contribution. Smaller communication groups limit the immediate dependency, although later training stages can propagate the stall across the job.

A stopped component usually gives a clearer symptom than a component returning plausible but incorrect values. The missing response still leaves uncertainty about whether the component crashed or communication merely slowed. Once recovery starts, the system replaces or restarts the failed participant and restores the most recent valid checkpoint. Minimizing detection and recovery latency must therefore be balanced against false suspicions and the validity of the saved state.

Detection time $T_{\text{detect}}$ typically involves heartbeat mechanisms\index{Heartbeat protocol!liveness signal} where each GPU rank periodically signals liveness to a coordinator. If no heartbeat arrives within the timeout period $\HandoverTimeout$, the coordinator declares failure. Setting $\HandoverTimeout$ requires balancing false positive rate against detection latency. False positives declare healthy workers failed due to transient delays, while slow detection wastes compute during the detection window, a cost that scales linearly with the number of GPUs blocked in the collective.

For a heartbeat interval of $H$ seconds and network-delay standard deviation $\sigma_d$ in seconds, @eq-timeout-calculation defines the timeout heuristic:

$$ \HandoverTimeout = H + k\sigma_d $$ {#eq-timeout-calculation}

Here, $k$ is a dimensionless safety multiplier; values from three to five illustrate a tuning range rather than a guaranteed false positive rate. The heuristic treats the normal heartbeat delivery delay as small relative to the heartbeat interval. A deployment with substantial baseline delay or a heavy delay tail must account for those measurements as well as $\sigma_d$. The practical difficulty is distinguishing a genuinely dead rank from one that is temporarily slow, for example, a GPU lagging because it is writing a large checkpoint to attached storage while the collective is already waiting. Tuning $\HandoverTimeout$ too tightly causes checkpoint writes to trigger false failure declarations; tuning it too loosely extends the window during which other ranks wait for the missing contribution.

#### Byzantine failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-byzantine-failures-8a24}

Where a fail-stop component ceases to participate, a value-corrupting component can keep running while returning incorrect results. Byzantine failures\index{Byzantine failure!classification} allow arbitrary behavior, including inconsistent messages to different participants [@lamport1982byzantine]. ML systems can encounter this broader failure model through silent data corruption\index{Silent data corruption!mechanism} or adversarial corruption. Numerical instability\index{Numerical instability!Byzantine failure} and determinism violations\index{Determinism!violation} also require validation when they break the execution contract, but ordinary rounding differences or intentionally stochastic outputs are not themselves evidence of a faulty worker. The recovery concern is a participant whose accepted contribution can corrupt shared state without a visible crash.

##### The physics of silent corruption {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-physics-silent-corruption-5d5d}

Digital hardware implements *deterministic* operations, but physical fault occurrence requires a *probabilistic* reliability model. Two mechanisms illustrate the distinction. Single-event upsets (SEUs)\index{SEU!mechanism}\index{Single-event upset|see{SEU}}, the particle strikes introduced with transient failures, create fleet exposure that grows with device count and operating time even when the per-device rate is low. Manufacturing variances\index{Manufacturing variance!silicon margin} can leave "marginal" chips that pass initial QA but fail under particular inputs or operating conditions. Voltage and temperature margins matter, including supply disturbances during rapid current changes ($di/dt$). These defects can produce repeatable errors, so a probabilistic fleet model does not imply that every individual fault is random.

Facebook documented a pervasive SDC issue where a hardware fault caused a valid file to be reported as "size zero" during decompression [@dixit2021silent]; the system "worked" without crashing, but data was silently deleted. In ML, the same failure manifests as valid-looking but numerically corrupted gradients. The pipeline trace in @fig-sdc-example follows a single ALU or memory bit flip as it corrupts an individual tensor entry, taints gradient reduction during the backward pass, commits into weights, and finally surfaces as degraded quality at evaluation. The comparative timelines beneath contrast this silent latency with a standard detected error: while a hardware trap halts within milliseconds to restart cleanly from the last checkpoint, silent corruption commits contaminated state into checkpoints over hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a costly rollback.

::: {#fig-sdc-example fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Silent data corruption propagation**: A hardware bit flip moves left to right from one wrong tensor value through the backward pass and the weight update, surfacing only at the final stage as degraded model quality. The two timelines below contrast a detected error, which traps within milliseconds and restarts from the last checkpoint, with silent corruption, which is saved into checkpoints for hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a rollback; the gap between the two is the cost of silence." fig-alt="Five red stage boxes in a row linked by arrows: bit flip in memory or ALU, wrong value in one tensor entry, backward pass taints gradients, weight update commits to weights, quality drops seen at evaluation. Below, two timelines share a time axis marked t equals zero, milliseconds, and hours to days. Detected error: a fault dot, a trap dot, then a green restart from checkpoint box. Silent corruption: a fault dot, a long red dashed box reading corrupt state saved into checkpoints, an alert dot, then a green roll back box."}
![](images/svg/sdc-propagation.svg)

:::

Real-world telemetry from production training fleets confirms that this corruption is routine rather than anomalous. In an invited MLSys 2024 keynote addressing silent data corruption (@fig-sdc-jeffdean), Jeff Dean documented that at modern training scales, hardware bit flips occur regularly and erroneous computations from a single malfunctioning accelerator propagate to infect the global model state [@dean2024mlsys].

::: {#fig-sdc-jeffdean fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Silent data corruption at scale**: Jeff Dean presents on silent data corruption (SDC) at MLSys 2024, arguing that at the scale of large ML training jobs hardware errors occur routinely, and that incorrect computations from one buggy chip can propagate and infect an entire training run. Source: Jeff Dean, MLSys 2024 keynote (Google)." fig-alt="Photograph of Jeff Dean giving a keynote at MLSys 2024. On stage he stands at a podium; a projected slide titled 'Silent Data Corruption errors (SDCs)' explains that ML-scale hardware errors can propagate and infect the entire training system."}

![](./images/jpg/sdc-google-jeff-dean.jpeg)

:::

In the Google training telemetry presented by @dean2024mlsys, @fig-sdc-training-fault identifies an abrupt gradient-norm anomaly as an SDC event. The plot shows the symptom without identifying the damaged bit or circuit. Corrupting a floating-point exponent is one mechanism that can greatly change a tensor value and subsequent updates. Gradient clipping can limit update magnitude, but it does not reconstruct the correct gradient; an anomaly detector must trigger validation or recovery before suspect state is accepted.

::: {#fig-sdc-training-fault fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Gradient norm deviation**: Transient hardware faults, such as silent data corruption (SDC), can disrupt optimization by causing abrupt changes in gradient norms. Google's production examples show SDC anomalies surfacing as visible gradient-norm spikes. Source: [@dean2024mlsys]." fig-alt="Line graph of gradient norm over training time showing smooth baseline with sudden spike anomaly caused by silent data corruption event."}

![](images/jpg/google_sdc_jeff_dean_anomaly.jpg)

:::

Google addresses this vulnerability with system-level mitigation. @Fig-sdc-controller diagrams this three-stage reactive failover protocol: when runtime monitors flag an anomalous gradient and replay implicates a suspect accelerator (G2), the scheduler isolates that device, promotes a standby hot spare (S) into the active ring, and provisions a replacement spare (S') while the suspect unit undergoes hardware diagnostics [@dean2024mlsys]. This protocol shifts the burden of correctness from unverified hardware to system-level auditing.

::: {#fig-sdc-controller fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Hot-spare failover**: An $N+1$ pool of four active GPUs and one standby spare. When loss or gradient sanity checks flag a suspect GPU and replay implicates it, the job drains that device and resumes on the spare from the last known-good state; the device goes to repair and a healthy unit refills the spare slot. Google's data-center examples use this reactive pattern to keep training moving despite hardware faults, in contrast to running every computation on two or three redundant units and comparing results [@dean2024mlsys]. The standing cost is the idle spare." fig-alt="Three panels left to right, each a row of five GPU slots. Panel 1: G0, G1, and G3 active in blue, G2 outlined in red and labeled suspect, and a dashed green spare S. Panel 2: G2 dashed gray and labeled isolated, and S solid blue and labeled active. Panel 3: a new dashed green spare S prime occupies the G2 slot, labeled new spare, with G2 sent to repair."}
![](images/svg/sdc-controller.svg)

:::

This hot spare pattern illustrates one approach to SDC mitigation, but recognizing silent corruption in the first place requires understanding what distinguishes it from benign training noise.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\FloatBarrier
:::

::: {#chk-fault-tolerance-detecting-silent-corruption .callout-checkpoint title="Detecting silent corruption"}

Verify your understanding of Byzantine failures and SDC:

- [ ] **SDC danger**: explain why silent data corruption is more dangerous for ML training than a simple node crash.
- [ ] **Hot spare vs. restart**: compare a hot spare redundancy strategy with traditional checkpoint-restart in terms of recovery latency.
- [ ] **Sanity checker**: identify the metric used as a "sanity checker" to identify potential hardware faults: GPU temperature or gradient norm.
- [ ] **Byzantine scope**: assess the True or False claim that Byzantine failures only occur when a malicious actor intentionally sabotages the training cluster.

:::

Silent-corruption detection is the first defense, but the same logic extends to any Byzantine worker whose output remains syntactically valid. Ordinary data-parallel workers process different batches and need not produce identical local gradients; the required contract is that each contribution correctly represents its assigned computation. A single Byzantine worker can violate that contract and corrupt the averaged gradient, potentially causing training to diverge or converge to a poor solution. @Fig-failure-types contrasts the diagnostic mechanisms: missing heartbeats make the silent worker W2 suspect, while worker W6 remains active and sends incorrect values. Liveness evidence alone cannot establish the validity of those values.

::: {#fig-failure-types fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Fail-stop vs. Byzantine failures**: In the fail-stop model (left), a failed worker simply ceases to send messages, which is easily detected by timeouts. In the Byzantine model (right), a failed worker continues to participate but sends incorrect data (for example, corrupted gradients reported as valid), which can poison the global model state if not detected by redundant validation." fig-alt="Two panels divided by a dashed line. Left, fail-stop: workers W1, W3, and W4 send dashed heartbeat arrows up to a coordinator labeled timeout flags W2; W2 is gray, crossed out in red, labeled crashed, with a dotted line labeled silence. Caption text reads absence of signal is the evidence. Right, Byzantine: workers W5, W7, and W8 send gradient arrows to a coordinator labeled averages all gradients; W6 is outlined in red, labeled looks healthy, and sends a red dashed arrow labeled wrong. Text reads a signal does not prove correctness."}
![](images/svg/failure-types.svg)

:::

Redundant computation supplies one form of evidence against Byzantine failures. Workers repeating a computation from matching inputs, state, and random-number streams can compare results under a stated numerical tolerance. Statistical outlier detection and invariants provide additional evidence without fully repeating the computation. Each method has a coverage limit: agreement can miss shared faults, while a statistical anomaly can arise from legitimate data variation. Detection overhead must therefore be evaluated together with the faults the method can expose.

Byzantine-resilient distributed training algorithms exist but impose significant overhead. Algorithms such as Krum [@blanchard2017machine] and coordinate-wise trimmed mean [@yin2018byzantine] compute aggregates that are robust to a bounded number of Byzantine workers, but they require more communication and computation than simple averaging. The systems consequence is visible here: corrupted gradients can push the optimizer toward an unreliable model state while the training job appears healthy. Reliability therefore has to protect semantic correctness, not only process liveness.[^fn-byzantine-consensus-overhead]

[^fn-byzantine-consensus-overhead]: **Byzantine-resilient ML**\index{Byzantine-resilient ML!algorithmic overhead}\index{Byzantine fault tolerance!ML overhead}: Named after Lamport's 1982 "Byzantine Generals Problem," these algorithms (Krum\index{Byzantine fault tolerance!Krum algorithm}, trimmed mean\index{Byzantine fault tolerance!trimmed mean}, signSGD) tolerate a bounded fraction of corrupted workers, with the exact bound depending on the algorithm and assumptions. The trade-off is concrete: for $N$ workers, Krum requires pairwise distance computations over worker gradients, so overhead grows quadratically with worker count and directly competes with the throughput gains of data parallelism [@blanchard2017machine].

#### Correlated failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-correlated-failures-95e8}

The reliability calculations in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-mathematics-inevitable-failure-93ef assume independent failures. Real systems depart sharply from this assumption by exhibiting correlated failures, where common physical or operational dependencies take down multiple components simultaneously. At the node level, a power fault that exhausts the chassis's redundant supplies\index{Correlated failure!power supply}, such as the loss of the circuits feeding it, takes down every GPU in the chassis. At the cluster level, a top-of-rack network switch failure\index{Correlated failure!network switch} isolates all attached nodes, while a cooling system failure\index{Correlated failure!cooling system} can trigger thermal shutdowns across a row of racks. Beyond physical infrastructure, shared software dependencies create broad blast radii. A software bug\index{Correlated failure!software bug} in an updated CUDA driver can crash processes across nodes when they exercise the affected path, and operator error\index{Correlated failure!operator error} during cluster reconfiguration can render an entire fleet unreachable.

Correlated failures violate the independence assumption underlying @eq-system-reliability-n-components. A model that counts only independent device failures omits shared hazards and their potentially larger blast radius; incident frequency and the number of affected devices must be modeled separately. Correlated failures can also defeat redundancy strategies. Three replicas of a model provide no protection against a shared power failure if all three run on the same power domain.

Defending against correlated failures\index{Correlated failure!failure domain protection} requires understanding failure domains\index{Failure domain!ML infrastructure} and ensuring redundancy spans independent failure domains. @Tbl-failure-domains catalogs common failure domains in ML infrastructure, from single GPUs to entire data center regions, each requiring distinct mitigation strategies. @Fig-failure-domains diagrams these nested containment boundaries, framing how physical disruptions scale upward from individual eight-GPU nodes to multi-rack power and network envelopes.

| **Failure Domain**     |                   **Impact Scope**                  | **Typical Recovery Time** |   **Mitigation Strategy**    |
|:-----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------:|:-------------------------:|:----------------------------:|
| **Single GPU**         |                        1 GPU                        |      Seconds (spare)      | Hot spare, elastic training  |
| **Node (power/OS)**    | `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.node_gpus_str` GPUs |          Minutes          | Checkpoint, node replacement |
| **Rack (ToR switch)**  |                     32--64 GPUs                     |      Minutes to hours     |    Cross-rack redundancy     |
| **Power domain**       |                    100--500 GPUs                    |           Hours           |     Multiple power feeds     |
| **Data Center region** |                       All GPUs                      |       Hours to days       |   Geographic distribution    |
| **Software version**   |               All GPUs running version              |     Minutes (rollback)    |       Staged rollouts        |

: **Failure Domains in ML Infrastructure**: Understanding failure domain boundaries enables placement of redundant components across independent domains, preventing correlated failures from defeating redundancy strategies. {#tbl-failure-domains}

The nesting of failure domains in @tbl-failure-domains has direct consequences for redundancy placement: placing replicas within the same domain provides zero protection against that domain's failure mode.

::: {#fig-failure-domains fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Hierarchy of failure domains**: Failure domains are often nested or overlapping. A GPU failure affects one device. A node failure affects `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.node_gpus_str` GPUs. A rack switch failure affects 32--64 GPUs (each rack is drawn with only two of its four to eight nodes). A power distribution unit (PDU) failure may affect multiple racks. The red rack shows one such correlated failure: a single top-of-rack switch fault removes every GPU it contains, while the neighboring rack is untouched, which is why replicas must span independent domains (for example, different racks or rows)." fig-alt="Nested rectangles: a datacenter labeled blast radius all GPUs contains a power and network domain spanning several racks, which contains two racks, each drawn with two of its eight-GPU nodes. The left rack is outlined in red, labeled ToR switch fails and 32 to 64 GPUs, and all its GPU squares are red; the right rack is labeled unaffected and its GPUs are blue."}
![](images/svg/failure-domains.svg)

:::

This containment hierarchy explains why replica placement must match the fault being tolerated. The highlighted rack in @fig-failure-domains contains nodes that share a top-of-rack (ToR) switch, so that switch's loss can disconnect every attached node from the job. A neighboring rack with a separate switch can remain reachable during that event even if both racks share a power domain. The same placement does not protect against loss of their shared power source. Redundancy must therefore cross the relevant failure boundary, not merely occupy different devices.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Top-of-rack aggregation and the physical rack failure domain are established in @sec-network-fabrics-tor.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tpuv4-war-story-scale
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TPUv4 WAR-STORY SCALE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: War story "The supercomputer that swapped in spare cubes" below.
# │
# │ Goal: Pin the TPUv4 supercomputer's chip count to the registry pod.
# │ Show: 4,096 chips.
# │ How:  Systems.Pods.TPUv4_4096.chips.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt

class TpuV4WarStoryScale:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    pod_chips = Systems.Pods.TPUv4_4096.chips
    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(pod_chips > 1000, "war story describes a multi-thousand-chip pod")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    pod_chips_str = fmt(pod_chips, precision=0)
```

::: {#ws-fault-tolerance-google-tpuv4-routing .callout-war-story title="The supercomputer that swapped in spare cubes (2024)"}

**Context**: Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) v4\index{TPU!v4 supercomputer} machine-learning supercomputer used `{python} TpuV4WarStoryScale.pod_chips_str` TPU chips connected by a custom 3D torus inter-chip interconnect (ICI) fabric, and Google engineers published their operating experience with automatic fault resiliency and hardware recovery [@zu2024tpuv4].

**Mechanism**: At `{python} TpuV4WarStoryScale.pod_chips_str`-chip scale, machine and link failures could remove participants or paths required by a job's configured communication topology.

**Impact**: Losing a required participant can interrupt the synchronous job across the slice. Losing a link instead raises a routing question: whether the remaining fabric can still provide the required communication paths.

**Fix**: Google used optical circuit switches (OCS) to assemble replacement slices from spare healthy TPU cubes for machine outages, together with fault-tolerant routing for supported OCS outage patterns. The response depended on which resource failed.

**Systems lesson**: Fault tolerance is a topology-management problem. In tightly coupled accelerator fleets, recovery must preserve the communication graph, not merely replace an individual component; otherwise one local hardware fault can become a cluster-wide training interruption.

:::

### The bathtub curve and hardware lifecycle {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-bathtub-curve-hardware-lifecycle-7d8a}

The failure taxonomy classifies failure types and domains, answering what kind of failures occur. Equally critical for fault tolerance design is determining *when* over an accelerator's operating lifespan those failures strike. @Fig-bathtub-curve plots the hazard function $\lambda(t)$ across component lifecycles on a logarithmic scale, partitioning operational longevity into three distinct reliability regimes:

The first phase, infant mortality\index{Bathtub curve!infant mortality}, exhibits elevated failure rates from manufacturing defects, improper installation, and early-life failure of marginal components. This phase typically lasts days to weeks for electronic components. Burn-in testing[^fn-burnin-screening-hardware] operates components under stress conditions before deployment to precipitate infant mortality failures before production use.

[^fn-burnin-screening-hardware]: **Burn-in testing**\index{Burn-in testing!reliability screening}: A controlled screening procedure stresses components before deployment to expose early-life defects. Temperature, voltage, duration, and acceptance criteria depend on the component and its qualified test procedure; a generic semiconductor screening recipe is not an operating specification for an assembled accelerator. Screening reduces the defective population entering service but does not certify every later workload or fault mode.

After surviving infant mortality, components enter the useful-life\index{Bathtub curve!useful life} phase, where they exhibit relatively constant failure rates under the standard reliability-engineering model [@birolini2017; @klutke2003]. This phase represents the longest portion of component lifetime and is the period where the exponential reliability model in @eq-single-component-reliability applies most accurately. For data center GPUs, the useful-life window is an operational planning concept shaped by refresh cycles, cooling, utilization, and observed fleet health rather than a fixed physical duration.

As components age, they enter the wear-out\index{Bathtub curve!wear-out} phase, where failure rates increase due to accumulated wear. For GPUs, wear mechanisms include electromigration[^fn-electromigration-silicon-wearout] in circuits, thermal cycling stress on solder joints, and degradation of thermal interface materials. The onset of wear-out depends heavily on operating conditions; components operated at high temperatures or with frequent thermal cycling enter wear-out earlier.

[^fn-electromigration-silicon-wearout]: **Electromigration**\index{Electromigration!wear-out mechanism}: Gradual displacement of metal atoms in conductors by electron momentum transfer, first characterized in early electromigration studies and later modeled in Black's reliability equation [@black1969electromigration]. Mean time to failure decreases with higher current density and higher temperature, so sustained high-power accelerator workloads make thermal management a direct determinant of fleet lifespan.

The practical implication for ML systems is that fleet-wide failure rates can depend on age distribution. Under the bathtub model, a new cohort passes through elevated early-life risk, a relatively stable period, and eventual wear-out. Screening, operating conditions, and replacement policy determine how much of that pattern appears in field data. Mixed-age fleets combine cohorts at different stages, so their aggregate hazard need not follow the curve of a single cohort.

::: {#fig-bathtub-curve fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The bathtub curve**: Hardware failure rates $\lambda(t)$ vary over time. (1) Infant mortality: high failure rate initially due to manufacturing defects. (2) Useful life: constant, low failure rate where random failures dominate. (3) Wear-out: increasing failure rate as components age. Burn-in testing aims to filter out infant mortality failures before deployment." fig-alt="Line graph of failure rate vs. component age showing bathtub shape. Three phases: infant mortality with high decreasing rate, useful life with constant low rate, and wear-out with increasing rate. Vertical dashed line marks burn-in period."}


:::

These three hazard regimes in @fig-bathtub-curve translate directly into admission control and maintenance policies. Before assigning new or repaired nodes to a long training run, operators use matrix-multiply, memory, and communication stress tests to expose marginal components. During service, temperature trends, error counts, and performance degradation help identify devices for scheduled replacement. Screening moves failures out of expensive production runs. An infant-mortality failure caught during a few hours of stress testing costs only idle time, while the same failure weeks into a pretraining run forces a checkpoint rollback, which is why operators often route fresh or repaired nodes to short jobs first. Monitoring then checks whether the constant-rate model remains appropriate as the fleet ages.

### Model-type diversity in failure impact {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-modeltype-diversity-failure-impact-8ec0}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: LLM failure-impact prose below (@tbl-failure-impact-by-model).
# │ Goal: Format GPT-3 checkpoint size for the 175B running example.
# │ Note: resumable checkpoint = 14 B/param (bf16 weights, fp32 master
# │       weights, fp32 Adam moments; no gradients or activations).
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, ReferenceStats
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_memory, fmt_text

class FaultToleranceIntroRecap:
    m = Models.Language.GPT3
    ckpt_bpp = ReferenceStats.MixedPrecisionAdam.CheckpointBytesPerParameter
    gpt3_ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(m.parameters)  # 14 B/param default
    gpus_example = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators * 2.5  # scenario assumption: 25,000-GPU run
    rate = Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.GpuTrainingUtilityScenarioPerHour.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude
    daily_cost = gpus_example * rate * 24
    vit_ckpt = ReferenceStats.CheckpointArchetypes.MediumVisionTransformerCheckpointSize
    recsys_table = ReferenceStats.RecommenderAtScaleProfile.EmbeddingTableSize
    check(
        abs((gpt3_ckpt_bytes / (m.parameters * ckpt_bpp)).to("").magnitude - 1) < 1e-9, "calc_checkpoint_size must use the registry 14 B/param anchor"
    )
    check(2.3e12 < gpt3_ckpt_bytes.to(byte).magnitude < 2.6e12, "175B resumable checkpoint must be about 2.45 TB")
    check(1.0 < vit_ckpt.to(GB).magnitude < 2.0, "ViT-Large checkpoint row is a single-digit-GB 'middle ground'")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ckpt_bpp_str = fmt(ckpt_bpp.magnitude, precision=0)
    gpt3_ckpt_tb_str = fmt_memory(gpt3_ckpt_bytes, unit=TB, precision=2, commas=False)
    gpus_example_str = fmt(gpus_example, precision=0, commas=True)
    rate_str = fmt_usd(rate, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
    daily_cost_str = fmt_usd(daily_cost, scale="M", precision=1, commas=False)
    vit_ckpt_str = fmt_memory(vit_ckpt, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    recsys_table_str = fmt_text(fmt_memory(recsys_table, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False), "+")
```

While the mathematics of failure rates apply universally, the failure impact by model type differs dramatically. The impact of losing an hour of training depends on what that training costs, how much state must be recovered, and how long recovery takes. @Tbl-failure-impact-by-model quantifies these factors across model architectures, revealing orders-of-magnitude variation from large language models (LLMs) incurring millions of dollars in wasted compute to vision models losing modest amounts of progress.

| **Model Type**                  | **Typical Training Duration** |                        **Checkpoint Size**                        |      **State Sensitivity**      |                              **Failure Cost**                             |
|:--------------------------------|:-----------------------------:|:-----------------------------------------------------------------:|:-------------------------------:|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------:|
| **Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3)** |           2--4 weeks          |    `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.gpt3_ckpt_tb_str` (175B)    |  High (position in data order)  | `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.daily_cost_str` compute per 24 hr loss |
| **Vision (ViT-Large)**          |           1--3 days           |          `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.vit_ckpt_str`         |   Medium (augmentation state)   |                           \$10--50K per day loss                          |
| **Archetype B (DLRM at Scale)** |           Continuous          | `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.recsys_table_str` (embeddings) | Very High (embedding freshness) |                          Revenue impact per hour                          |
| **Speech (Whisper-scale)**      |           3--7 days           |                              5--10 GB                             |              Medium             |                          \$50--200K per day loss                          |
| **Scientific (AlphaFold)**      |         Days to weeks         |                             10--50 GB                             |     High (exploration state)    |                               Research delay                              |

: **Failure Impact by Model Type**: The cost of training failures varies dramatically by model type, driven by training duration, checkpoint overhead, and the value of accumulated training state. These differences demand model-specific fault tolerance strategies. {#tbl-failure-impact-by-model}

Large language model training illustrates how a costly allocation magnifies each hour of lost progress. For example, a large training run consuming `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.gpus_example_str` GPUs at approximately `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.rate_str` incurs `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.daily_cost_str` in compute costs per day. A failure that loses 24 hours of training progress costs `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.daily_cost_str` in wasted compute plus schedule delay. The checkpoint overhead is correspondingly large. The reference resumable checkpoint stores `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.ckpt_bpp_str` bytes per parameter (BF16 weights, FP32 master weights, and the two FP32 Adam moments, but no gradients or activations), so a 70B-class model approaches a terabyte and the 175B-parameter running example reaches `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.gpt3_ckpt_tb_str`.

Recommendation systems such as Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) present a different challenge when training updates models continuously rather than episodically. For a workload whose useful signals change rapidly, delayed embedding updates can reduce recommendation quality even if serving remains available. A failure that loses recent updates therefore has a freshness cost as well as a replay cost. The recovery budget must reflect the workload's measured sensitivity to stale state.[^fn-recsys-model-freshness]

[^fn-recsys-model-freshness]: **RecSys freshness**\index{Recommendation system!freshness fault tolerance}: Freshness makes recovery delay part of the model-quality budget. Its importance depends on how quickly useful user and item signals change and how strongly predictions depend on them. Comparing quality at different state ages establishes the permitted staleness; that measured limit determines how much checkpoint and replication overhead is justified.

Vision models illustrate how a smaller state budget can permit more frequent saves on the same storage path. The vision transformer (ViT)-Large example has a checkpoint of about `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.vit_ckpt_str`, smaller than the large language and embedding-heavy examples here; actual overhead still depends on sustained write bandwidth and training step time. Recovery must preserve optimizer and schedule state as well as weights. Reproducible data processing also requires the augmentation configuration, random-number generator state, and data position, rather than only the initial shuffling seed.

Scientific workflows can require state beyond the model and optimizer. An iterative molecular-search pipeline, for example, must retain which configurations have been evaluated if those results determine its next candidates. A training pipeline that samples scientific datasets must preserve the sampling state needed by its own recovery contract. The governing question is which prior decisions affect future work; the checkpoint boundary must include that state wherever it resides.

### Economic framework for fault tolerance investment {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-economic-framework-fault-tolerance-investment-e032}

Fault tolerance mechanisms consume resources: storage for checkpoints, bandwidth for checkpoint writes, compute cycles for redundant calculations, and engineering time for implementation and maintenance. Rational investment in fault tolerance requires quantifying both the cost of failures and the cost of prevention.

Failure costs include wasted compute, schedule delay, opportunity cost, and engineering time. Wasted compute measures GPU-hours expended on training steps that must be repeated. Schedule delay captures how extended time to a trained model impacts business timelines. Opportunity cost recognizes that compute consumed by recovery cannot be used for other training. Engineering cost accounts for time spent debugging failures and manually recovering.

Prevention costs include storage, throughput overhead, recovery infrastructure, and complexity. Storage cost scales with model size and checkpoint frequency. Checkpoint writes consume memory bandwidth and may stall training. Recovery infrastructure requires spare capacity and automated recovery systems. Fault tolerant systems are harder to develop and debug.

Optimal investment in fault tolerance balances these costs. For small-scale training on a few GPUs where failures are rare, minimal fault tolerance may be cost-optimal. Infrequent checkpoints and manual recovery suffice. For large-scale training on thousands of GPUs where failures occur multiple times daily, extensive fault tolerance provides positive return on investment. Frequent checkpoints, automatic recovery, and elastic training become essential. @Fig-checkpoint-tradeoff charts this economic balance: checkpoint write overhead declines hyperbolically as the interval widens, while expected rework scales linearly, producing a convex total-waste curve whose shallow minimum identifies the cost-optimal interval where marginal save overhead matches marginal rework risk.

@Eq-ft-total-cost presents a simplified economic model for expected cost per training run:

$$ C_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{compute}} + \mathbb{E}[N_{\text{failures}}] \times C_{\text{per-failure}} + C_{\text{ft}} $$ {#eq-ft-total-cost}

where $C_{\text{compute}}$ is the base compute cost, $\mathbb{E}[N_{\text{failures}}]$ is the expected number of failures during training, $C_{\text{per-failure}}$ is the cost per failure, and $C_{\text{ft}}$ is the cost of fault tolerance mechanisms. The cost per failure includes wasted compute plus overhead.

@Eq-ft-investment-criterion formalizes when fault tolerance investment is justified:

$$ \frac{\partial C_{\text{ft}}}{\partial x} < -\frac{\partial (\mathbb{E}[N_{\text{failures}}] \times C_{\text{per-failure}})}{\partial x} $$ {#eq-ft-investment-criterion}

where $x$ represents investment in fault tolerance mechanisms and the base compute cost is held fixed. The negative derivative on the right is the marginal reduction in expected failure cost. Additional protection reduces total expected cost while this reduction exceeds its marginal cost; an interior optimum equates the two when the cost functions have a suitable minimum.

Three foundational principles guide every design decision in this domain.

::: {#psp-fault-tolerance-three-rules-failure-at-scale .callout-perspective title="Three rules of failure at scale"}

1. *At scale, failures are continuous, not exceptional.* A 10,000-GPU cluster experiences failures every few hours. Systems must be designed expecting failure as normal operation.
2. *Checkpoint intervals have an optimum.* The Young-Daly formula, $\OptimalCheckpointIntervalCkpt = \sqrt{2 \times \CheckpointWriteTime \times \MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}}}$, provides quantitative guidance for checkpoint frequency under its stated assumptions. @Sec-fault-tolerance-young-daly derives it.
3. *Training and serving have fundamentally different fault tolerance requirements.* A long training job can budget minutes for recovery while preserving accumulated progress; an interactive serving request may have only milliseconds left before its deadline. Those budgets motivate checkpoint recovery for training and ready alternate capacity for serving.

:::

Rule 3 sets the order of what follows, with training recovery first and serving resilience later. Both depend on knowing how the physical faults behind these failures look once they reach a fleet.

## Hardware Faults at Fleet Scale {#sec-fault-tolerance-hardware-fault-taxonomy}

A cosmic ray that flips one bit in a GPU's high-bandwidth memory and a solder joint that cracks under thermal cycling are physical events, but the recovery system never observes them directly. It observes symptoms: a gradient spike with no process crash, a rank that disappears from the collective, or a node that fails only after it heats under sustained load. The failure taxonomy of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-taxonomy-e78c already classifies such events by persistence, manifestation, and scope. For hardware, persistence carries most of the operational weight because it decides whether the fleet should retry, quarantine, or replace a component, while manifestation decides whether the fleet notices the fault at all.

ML workloads raise the stakes of each fault. A training step performs trillions of arithmetic operations on state that persists into later steps, so a wrong value can survive beyond the computation that produced it. The damage depends on the affected value and its later use. Under the IEEE 754 format,[^fn-ieee754-fp-vulnerability] a sign-bit flip inverts a weight, while an exponent-bit flip can move a small gradient by many orders of magnitude. Fault-injection studies show that network resilience varies with model, layer, and bit position, so a few faults in vulnerable locations can cost disproportionate accuracy [@reagen2018]. A valid-looking corrupted value can enter learned state without triggering the process failure that would otherwise initiate recovery.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How an FP16 exponent-bit flip rescales a value by $2^{16}$ and can saturate an attention softmax is developed in @sec-appdx-reliability-sdc-perturbation.
:::

[^fn-ieee754-fp-vulnerability]: **IEEE 754**\index{IEEE 754!bit-flip vulnerability}: The IEEE 754 floating-point standard defines the binary32 format with 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits [@ieee_754_2019]. The bit layout creates an asymmetric vulnerability for ML: a sign-bit flip inverts a weight entirely ($0.5 \to -0.5$), while an exponent-bit flip can shift magnitude by orders of magnitude, so resilience mechanisms often prioritize the most sensitive bit positions rather than treating all bits as equally important.

Fleet scale turns these rare device events into routine operating conditions. Smaller geometries and lower operating voltages can reduce the charge needed to disturb a stored value [@baumann2005], and fleet studies at Google and Meta found that a small but persistent population of processors, on the order of a few per several thousand machines, computes wrong results without raising any error [@hochschild2021; @dixit2021silent]. Studies of accelerator training fleets reach the same conclusion: rare hardware faults appear often enough that software-level detection and recovery become part of the training system design [@he2023]. ML system architects must therefore treat hardware as an unreliable substrate\index{Hardware!unreliable substrate} and budget for end-to-end integrity checks, replayed computation on high-value paths, and periodic consistency checks as system requirements rather than high-performance computing specialties.

### Fault persistence and the fleet response {#sec-ft-fault-persistence-response}

Each persistence class from the taxonomy maps to a different fleet action. A transient fault\index{Transient fault!fleet response} leaves no lasting defect from that event. A single-event upset, a voltage droop on an unstable power path [@reddi2013], a timing violation, or a soft error in combinational logic [@mukherjee2005] can corrupt a tensor, packet, or instruction. Detection and correction can prevent propagation; affected state may otherwise require rollback. During training, an undetected error in weights or gradients can compromise convergence and contaminate subsequent checkpoints [@he2023]. During stateless inference, an activation error can remain confined to one request [@mahmoud2020]. If that activation enters retained state such as a KV cache, later outputs can also depend on it.

A permanent fault\index{Permanent fault!fleet response} announces itself through repeatability. The same accelerator, memory cell, or link fails again after retry, often at the same address or in the same workload phase. Manufacturing defects and wear-out mechanisms such as electromigration and oxide breakdown produce this signature, and the stuck-at fault, in which a signal remains fixed at 0 or 1 regardless of input, is its standard abstract model [@seong2010]. Repeatability helps locate the defect but does not make the result trustworthy. A permanent datapath fault keeps producing wrong gradients until the device is drained from the cluster [@he2023], and rerunning the computation on the same device reproduces the error instead of exposing it. The fleet must stop trusting the component, quarantine it, and restore from a checkpoint that predates its first bad write.

Intermittent faults\index{Intermittent fault!fleet response} create the most operational ambiguity because they produce evidence and then disappear. A node may pass a reboot test, rejoin the fleet, and fail again only when the next job drives the package into the same thermal, voltage, or communication regime. Cracked solder joints, aging packages, and contamination between contacts create these load-dependent conditions [@constantinescu2008; @rashid2015], and reduced voltage margins cause timing errors that are hard to reproduce [@zhang2018thundervolt]. Sporadic errors of this kind can accumulate across iterations and degrade convergence without any explicit failure [@rashid2015]. An intermittent node should therefore remain suspect until evidence clears it. The fleet drains it from long jobs, correlates its error logs, and readmits it only after it passes stress tests under the load that exposed the fault; otherwise one marginal component can make validation and recovery untrustworthy for every job that lands on it. @Tbl-fault_types summarizes the three responses.

| **Persistence**  | **Fleet signature**                                       | **Detection evidence**                                         | **Fleet response**                                                |
|:-----------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Transient**    | One-time wrong value or lost message; retry succeeds      | Corrected-error counters, checksum mismatches, gradient spikes | Correct or retry; roll back if durable state was contaminated     |
| **Intermittent** | Recurring errors under specific load, heat, or voltage    | Correlated error logs and repeated anomalies on one node       | Drain and quarantine; readmit only after screening under load     |
| **Permanent**    | Reproducible failure at the same device, address, or link | Failed self-test or replay mismatch on the same device         | Replace the component; restore from a checkpoint before the fault |

: **Hardware Fault Persistence and Fleet Response**: The persistence class of a hardware fault determines the evidence that exposes it and the action the fleet takes. Manifestation is a separate axis: any of the three classes can surface as a crash or as silent corruption [@constantinescu2008]. {#tbl-fault_types}

### Fleet-scale detection and mitigation {#sec-ft-hardware-fault-detection-mitigation-8f7f}

Fault rates drive fleet decisions through compounding. The analysis in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-mathematics-inevitable-failure-93ef shows how per-device failure rates become fleet interruption rates, and memory errors compound in the same way. Field studies of DRAM in large data centers found errors frequent enough that error-correcting memory, background scrubbing, and error-rate monitoring are standard fleet practice rather than optional hardening [@schroeder2009; @sridharan2015]. Protection consumes some capacity and bandwidth for check bits and scrubbing, but that cost is small compared with a corrupted multi-week run.

Detection works in layers with different coverage and cost. At the hardware layer, error-correcting codes\index{ECC!error detection and correction}\index{Error correction code|see{ECC}}[^fn-hamming-ecc-memory] [@hamming1950] correct and detect the memory-error patterns covered by the implemented code, and link-level CRCs[^fn-crc-packet-validation] check corruption in transit. These protections operate within their enabled storage and transport boundaries; they do not validate an incorrect arithmetic result merely because its bytes arrive intact. Before deployment, built-in self-test and burn-in screening expose manufacturing defects and permanent faults [@bushnell2002]. During service, operators periodically pull nodes from production and run known-answer stress tests on arithmetic, memory, and interconnect, because defective processors often fail only on particular instruction mixes, data patterns, or operating points [@hochschild2021; @dixit2021silent].

[^fn-hamming-ecc-memory]: **Hamming codes (1950)**\index{Hamming code!ECC origin}: Richard Hamming developed error-correcting codes at Bell Labs. A Hamming code uses parity checks to locate a single-bit error with $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ check-bit overhead; adding an overall parity bit yields the extended single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting form. Memory ECC implementations vary in code and coverage, so the system must account for both corrected errors and residual faults outside that coverage.

[^fn-crc-packet-validation]: **CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check)**\index{CRC!gradient validation}: Polynomial checksum family introduced by @peterson1961. CRC coverage depends on the polynomial, frame length, and error model; it is best understood as a low-cost detection layer rather than a universal guarantee. In distributed ML training, checksums or hashes can validate gradient payloads exchanged during collectives; without a verification layer, a corrupted gradient packet can silently poison the parameter update for every worker in the collective.

The software layer draws its cheapest evidence from metrics the training loop already emits. Statistical checks on loss, gradient norms, and activations flag silent drift [@chandola2009], missed heartbeats identify suspected failures [@kawazoe_aguilera1997], and watchdog timers catch tasks that stall without crashing [@pont2002using]. A node that stays alive but runs slowly or erratically is a gray failure; it can degrade progress while still meeting a liveness timeout, so @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distinguishing-stragglers-failures-285d treats it through straggler detection. Redundant computation adds stronger evidence on selected paths, either periodically or in response to an anomaly, by replaying a step on another device or comparing independently computed results. Its frequency depends on the residual corruption risk, the value of the protected state, and the cost of detecting an error late.

::: {#chk-fault-tolerance-classifying-hardware-faults .callout-checkpoint title="Classifying a hardware fault"}

Verify your understanding of the transient, permanent, and intermittent fault categories and the fault, error, failure progression:

- [ ] **Transient fault**: classify a GPU that produces a wrong result once after a cosmic-ray strike and then computes correctly for the rest of the run, and justify why detection and rollback to a known-good checkpoint, not node replacement, match that fault.
- [ ] **Intermittent vs. permanent**: distinguish an intermittent fault from a permanent one when both can produce a stuck-at value, including the diagnostic signal that separates them.
- [ ] **Fault-error-failure chain**: trace a single bit flip through the fault, error, failure chain, identifying where error correction codes and checkpoint-restart each intervene.
- [ ] **Silent corruption**: explain why silent corruption sits apart from the other fault manifestations even when its underlying fault is an ordinary transient bit flip.

:::

## Check-and-Verify Defenses Against Silent Data Corruption {#sec-ft-sdc-verification}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_fault_tolerance_margin_001.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One red curve over training steps that rises and flattens toward a dashed certainty line, with a dot marking 63 percent: cumulative silent-corruption probability approaches certainty over a long run."}

*Silent data corruption accumulates until it becomes routine.*
:::

As clusters scale to 100,000+ GPUs, even a small per-GPU SDC rate accumulates across repeated collective operations. A single collective is not certain to contain an SDC event: under the illustrative rate used in the analysis that follows, the per-step probability remains small while the cumulative probability grows over a long training run. Standard AllReduce reduces the supplied contributions; it does not establish that an *alive* worker computed a *correct* gradient. The fleet therefore needs validation appropriate to its fault model in addition to liveness checks.

Check-and-verify methods\index{Silent data corruption!detection methods} test data-path invariants, subject to the boundary drawn for transient failures in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-transient-failures-57b4. Digests test byte integrity and agreement within their error-detection limits; they cannot establish that the original computation was correct. Independent computation, an algorithmic invariant, or replay tests that additional claim under a declared fault model. A quick estimate shows how much exposure those checks must cover.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: sdc-prob-calc
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class SDCCollective:
    """The risk of silent corruption in global collectives."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators * 10
    p_sdc_per_gpu_hr = Systems.Reliability.SdcRatePerGpuHr  # illustrative generic SDC-rate assumption
    training_step_s = 2  # scenario assumption: illustrative step time
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    _sdc_exp = round(math.log10(float(p_sdc_per_gpu_hr)))
    exposure_gpu_hr = n_gpus * (training_step_s / SEC_PER_HOUR)  # aggregate GPU-hours per step
    p_step_sdc = 1 - (1 - p_sdc_per_gpu_hr) ** exposure_gpu_hr
    expected_steps = 1 / p_step_sdc
    expected_hours = expected_steps * training_step_s / SEC_PER_HOUR
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(p_step_sdc > 0.00005, f"Prob {p_step_sdc:.6f} unexpected")
    check(abs(exposure_gpu_hr - 55.56) < 0.1, f"Expected ~55.6 GPU-hours exposure, got {exposure_gpu_hr:.2f}")
    check(abs(float(p_sdc_per_gpu_hr) / 10**_sdc_exp - 1) < 1e-9, "SDC rate must be an exact power of ten to render as 10^k")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    prob_str = fmt_percent(p_step_sdc, precision=4, commas=False, style='prose')
    n_gpus_str = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0, commas=True)
    n_gpus_k_str = fmt_text(fmt_int(n_gpus // 1000), "k")
    training_step_s_str = fmt_time(training_step_s, unit="second", precision=0, commas=False)
    training_step_attr_str = fmt_time(training_step_s, unit="second", precision=0, style="word", attributive=True)
    sdc_rate_math = fmt_math(rf"10^{{{_sdc_exp}}}")
    steps_between_str = fmt_count(round(expected_steps), commas=True, label="step")
    hours_between_str = fmt_time(round(expected_hours), "hour", precision=0, style="word")
    _n_tex = n_gpus_str.replace(",", "{,}")
    exposure_eq_math = fmt_math(rf"{_n_tex} \times ({training_step_s}/{SEC_PER_HOUR}) \approx {fmt_int(round(exposure_gpu_hr))}")
```

::: {#nbk-fault-tolerance-napkin-math-sdc-certainty .callout-notebook title="SDC risk accumulation"}

**Problem**: Under an illustrative generic SDC-rate assumption, calculate the probability that at least one GPU in a `{python} SDCCollective.n_gpus_str`-GPU fleet experiences an SDC event during a single `{python} SDCCollective.training_step_s_str` training step.

1. **Fleet size**: `{python} SDCCollective.n_gpus_str` accelerators.
2. **Individual risk**: `{python} SDCCollective.sdc_rate_math` per GPU-hour (an illustrative generic SDC-rate assumption).
3. **The exposure**: In a `{python} SDCCollective.training_step_attr_str` window, the fleet has `{python} SDCCollective.exposure_eq_math` "GPU-hours" of exposure.
4. **The probability**: $\Pr(\text{at least one SDC}) \approx$ `{python} SDCCollective.prob_str`.

**Systems insight**: Under this illustrative constant-rate assumption, a `{python} SDCCollective.n_gpus_k_str`-GPU fleet expects one SDC event every `{python} SDCCollective.steps_between_str` (roughly every `{python} SDCCollective.hours_between_str`), even though the per-step probability is only `{python} SDCCollective.prob_str`. A CRC or hash can protect each shard or reduced buffer against corruption in transit or storage, while a redundant reduction can test the arithmetic path independently. Robustness moves from being a *restart* problem to a *verification* problem only when the verification covers the failure mechanism being claimed.

:::

Full replication protects a broader computation path at a correspondingly high resource cost. Dual modular redundancy\index{DMR!fleet contrast} runs every computation twice and compares the results, and triple modular redundancy\index{TMR!fleet contrast} runs it three times and takes a majority vote, paying 100 and 200 percent hardware overhead to detect or mask a fault within a single control deadline [@sheaffer2007; @arifeen2020]. These guarantees depend on the replicas avoiding a shared fault. That price can be justified when one wrong output can endanger a vehicle and the replicated hardware is a small computer. For fleet training, duplicating every step of a run on `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_gpus_str` doubles the compute devoted to those steps, before comparison and coordination costs. When corruption is rare and rollback can recover valid state, selective redundancy can protect useful progress at lower cost. Screening removes suspect devices, statistical checks run continuously, standby pools absorb drained nodes along the hot-spare promotion sequence of @fig-sdc-controller, and periodic or triggered recomputation checks selected execution paths.

These checks reduce the risk of an unreliable substrate, but they do not protect against faults that the software stack introduces itself, bugs that look like valid computation while corrupting the ML pipeline.

## Software Faults {#sec-ft-software-faults}

A team spends three months testing an LLM against complex prompt-level failure cases, only to realize that its preprocessing script kept only the last 512 tokens of each input, silently discarding the system prompt on long requests. The example exposes an ordinary source of ML failure that algorithmic testing can miss. A logic error in a data loader or prompt assembler can preserve valid tensor shapes while changing the computation's meaning, allowing the pipeline to continue without a crash.

Software faults require a different recovery lens from hardware failures. Hardware faults enter from silicon, electrons, and physical wear; software faults enter through design choices, dependency versions, and pipeline glue. The fault-tolerance problem shifts from replacing a failed component to identifying which valid-looking transformation corrupted data, gradients, or predictions, and every boundary between framework, library, runtime, and distributed system is a place where such a transformation can hide.

### Software fault properties and propagation {#sec-ft-software-fault-properties}

Software faults in ML frameworks range from logic errors to resource leaks, concurrency bugs, and integration failures, and they propagate across system boundaries. A tensor leaked on every iteration lets a correctly sized job drift toward the device memory limit over hundreds of steps and then fail with an out-of-memory error, which makes root-cause attribution difficult without per-layer memory profiling. Race conditions in asynchronous updates can lose or overwrite parameter updates, and deadlocks[^fn-deadlock-pipeline-stall] leave workers waiting on messages that never arrive. Some of these faults appear only under high load, on particular hardware, or with a specific pairing of a high-level library and a low-level numerical library such as cuDNN, so root-cause analysis must treat the model code, the runtime, and its dependencies as one versioned artifact.

[^fn-deadlock-pipeline-stall]: **Pipeline deadlock**\index{Deadlock!pipeline parallelism}: In pipelined training, a deadlock can form when stage 1 waits for a free buffer to send activations to stage 2 while stage 2 waits for stage 1 to accept its backward gradients. Neither stage can proceed, and because every other stage depends on them, the whole job stalls with no error raised, which a collective timeout eventually converts into a detectable failure.

### Software fault detection and prevention {#sec-ft-software-fault-detection-prevention}

Because many software faults leave the pipeline running while corrupting gradients, reliability evidence must establish which invariant failed and which recovery action is now safe. Several tests verify recovery guarantees that later sections build in full. A restore drill checks a manifest, the record that names every checkpoint shard and the training step they share. A membership test kills or partitions a worker and checks what happens to its ownership. In an epoch-and-lease design, a membership epoch identifies the group's current incarnation and is unrelated to a training epoch over the dataset; a lease grants ownership for a bounded period unless renewed. Lease expiration lets the coordinator replace an owner, but the storage or update service must enforce a fence that rejects the old owner's writes before replacement writes proceed. Every such test is judged against two recovery objectives. The recovery point objective (RPO) bounds acceptable lost work, and the recovery time objective (RTO) bounds the delay until useful work resumes.

The prompt-truncation bug from the opening example should never survive until runtime. A unit test should catch the tokenizer boundary, an integration replay should catch the batch shape and metadata path, and a fault-injection test should verify that the resulting alert blocks publication or rolls back to a known-good state for the injected case. @Tbl-software-faults-summary-ft organizes these gates by the recovery claim each one supports.

| **Reliability evidence**       | **Invariant exercised**                                                            | **Decision enabled**                                      |
|:-------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| **Boundary unit test**         | Tokenizer limits, tensor shapes, masks, and step metadata remain valid             | Reject the change before distributed execution            |
| **Deterministic replay**       | A recorded batch produces equivalent state on known-good hardware                  | Separate input or software defects from suspect hardware  |
| **Checkpoint restore drill**   | A committed manifest restores every shard and resumes at its named step            | Accept the generation as satisfying the recovery contract |
| **Membership fault injection** | A killed or partitioned worker loses ownership and cannot write with a stale epoch | Validate lease expiry, fencing, and communicator rebuild  |
| **Corruption injection**       | A changed shard, reduced buffer, or checkpoint fails the intended verifier         | Block the optimizer step or roll back before propagation  |
| **Dependency rollback test**   | A versioned runtime and artifact set can return to the last known-good combination | Authorize automated rollback instead of manual repair     |

: **Reliability Evidence and Recovery Decisions**: Tests earn operational value when each one establishes an invariant and authorizes a specific rejection, rollback, isolation, or restore decision. {#tbl-software-faults-summary-ft}

These safeguards matter only when each gate targets a concrete corruption path. A test that checks only whether the tokenizer runs is too weak; it must assert that system prompts, labels, masks, and sequence-length metadata survive preprocessing with the intended semantics. Integration replay then follows one recorded batch through loading, sharding, collation, and model input construction. Fault injection tests whether the detector fires before the protected commit and whether recovery satisfies the named RPO and RTO for the injected fault. A passing case supports that tested contract, not complete coverage of every possible corruption. Restore drills, stale-epoch rejection, and corrupted-shard rejection therefore provide evidence that generic build success cannot supply.

Several rows of @tbl-software-faults-summary-ft claim more than a passing test. They claim that a detector fires and a recovery path holds when something breaks, and a claim of that kind can be checked only by breaking something on purpose.

## Fault Injection Tools and Frameworks {#sec-ft-fault-injection-tools-frameworks}

An injected failure is useful evidence only when it resembles the production failure the system must survive. A multi-node training cluster that claims to tolerate network partitions should have that connection severed in a staging environment so engineers can observe what the orchestration layer does. Fault injection\index{Fault injection!testing discipline}\index{Fault injection!tools and frameworks} is the engineering discipline of deliberately perturbing a system to empirically verify that robustness mechanisms work before production traffic discovers the gap. Fault-injection tools for tensors and accelerators cover bit flips, corrupted tensor values, and accelerator-oriented failures [@chen2020tensorfi; @tsai2021; @grafe2023], while network partitions, latency injection, dependency termination, and API-response faults belong to chaos and distributed-systems testing practice [@basiri2016].

### Fault and error models {#sec-ft-fault-error-models}

A fault-injection experiment must specify duration, location, granularity, and propagation path. Its fault model\index{Fault model!abstraction} describes the originating disturbance, such as a transient single-bit upset or a permanent multi-bit defect. Its error model\index{Error model!propagation} describes the resulting corrupted state or computation. Results for transient single-bit faults do not establish resilience to permanent multi-bit defects [@sangchoolie2017].

The injection level determines which propagation paths the experiment includes. A register-level bit flip in a simulator such as gem5 [@binkert2011] can expose effects that a mutation of a PyTorch weight tensor omits. Conversely, hardware may mask an injected fault before software observes it. Location and propagation therefore matter when comparing results across fault models [@sangchoolie2017; @papadimitriou2021].

This divergence highlights the multi-tier filtering formalized by error masking [@mohanram2003]. The flowchart in @fig-error-masking-ft traces how a physical soft error traverses two successive screening diamonds—asking first whether corrupted data is read, and second whether it produces incorrect output or a crash—before escalating to an observable failure. A hardware disturbance that hits an unused functional unit, is overwritten prior to use, or lands in dynamically dead instructions is silently absorbed within the microarchitecture or runtime [@ko2021]. Because tensor-level mutations inject perturbations downstream of these architectural filters, their empirical error rates must be evaluated at that higher abstraction level.

::: {#fig-error-masking-ft fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Error masking**: Follow a soft error from the top. It becomes a failure only if the corrupted data is read and then also produces incorrect output; at each No branch it is masked, first by microarchitectural effects (unused components, overwritten values, squashed speculative instructions) and then by software effects (dead instructions, logical and compare operations, uninfluential branches). Because software-level fault injection sees only the second filter, it can misestimate a system's true resilience to transient errors." fig-alt="Flowchart starting at a soft error. A decision diamond asks whether corrupted data is read; No leads to masked in the microarchitecture. Yes leads to a second diamond asking whether output is incorrect or the system crashes; No leads to masked in software, Yes leads to failure. A shaded panel lists microarchitecture-level and software-level masking causes."}

These masking effects determine which abstraction level an experiment should target.

### Fault injection methods {#sec-ft-fault-injection-methods}

Fault injection methods trade realism against experimental scale. Hardware-based injection, through field-programmable gate array (FPGA) emulation or accelerated particle-beam exposure of a running accelerator [@velazco2010], supplies the calibration point because its faults pass through the same circuit-level masking as production faults. Software-based injection\index{Fault injection!software-based} is the scalable counterpart. Tools such as PyTorchFI\index{PyTorchFI!fault injection} [@mahmoud2020] perturb weights, activations, and gradients directly, covering many model states quickly without special hardware, and have shown that single bit-level faults can produce severe misclassifications, including "phantom" objects in detection models. The cost is an abstraction gap\index{Fault injection!abstraction gap}: a software tool that mutates a tensor skips the hardware masking that would have absorbed many of the same disturbances. Frameworks such as Fidelity\index{Fidelity!fault injection framework} [@he2020fidelity] narrow that gap by mapping how faults in registers, memory hierarchies, and numerical units become software-visible errors, so that injected faults resemble what physical hardware would produce.

::: {#exmp-fault-tolerance-software-fault-injection-limits .callout-example title="Software fault injection limits"}

**Scenario**: An engineering team validates a distributed training pipeline using software fault injection, concluding that tensor bit-flips always corrupt model gradient updates.

**Diagnosis**: Hardware-calibrated experiments reveal that software injection bypasses low-level hardware masking effects (such as ECC memory correction and gate-level masking) that prevent many register-level bit-flips from ever mutating software variables.

**Systems lesson**: In this experiment, bypassing hardware masking overstates the effect of the modeled physical faults. Tensor mutation still tests the software response to corrupted values; estimating production vulnerability additionally requires a calibrated model of which physical faults reach those values. The result must be interpreted at the injection level actually tested.

:::

For fleet recovery, the most valuable experiments inject faults at the level where recovery decisions are made. Killing a rank in the middle of a collective, partitioning a node from the rendezvous service, delaying a heartbeat past its timeout, and corrupting one checkpoint shard each exercise one row of @tbl-software-faults-summary-ft. Running these experiments continuously in staging, and in controlled form in production, keeps rarely executed recovery code from decaying between real incidents [@basiri2016]. A detection mechanism can identify corrupted or missing state, but only a recovery mechanism can replace it. Fault persistence determines whether to retry, quarantine, or replace a component, and checkpointing supplies the known-good training state from which any of those paths can resume.

## Checkpointing and Progress Preservation {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-restart-fundamentals-0ac2}

When a top-of-rack switch dies two weeks into the training run of a 175-billion-parameter model, the cluster loses 64 GPUs instantly. The system cannot simply restart from scratch; the sunk cost of weeks of compute is too high. The failure analysis in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-analysis-scale-6b4b established that large-scale training systems will experience such failures frequently, requiring robust mechanisms to preserve and resume progress.

Training fault tolerance has three obligations: preserve state, detect and classify failures, and resume or resize the job. Checkpointing supplies the first obligation. The sections that follow then build the rest of the recovery model: detection supplies evidence for a recovery decision, recovery procedures restore a consistent process group, and elastic recovery determines whether the job can continue with a changed worker set.

Two recovery objectives, introduced with the reliability evidence of @sec-ft-software-fault-detection-prevention, turn those obligations into a contract. The RPO bounds acceptable lost progress, so checkpoint age and replication lag must fit within it; the RTO bounds detection, resource replacement, restore, and warmup.
