Survivor-preserving warm restarts require specialized application and runtime support for dynamic membership changes without leaking CUDA memory, corrupting shared state, or deadlocking during communicator reconstruction. PyTorch's elastic framework (TorchElastic) does not preserve worker processes across membership changes: it stops the surviving workers and starts a new worker group. DeepSpeed's documented recovery path is checkpoint-centered rather than a survivor-preserving warm restart. A deployment that implements a warm-restart fast path still needs cold restart as a safety net. @Tbl-cold-vs-warm-restart contrasts the two strategies:

| **Aspect**                  | **Cold Restart**                 | **Warm Restart**                       |
|:----------------------------|:---------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|
| **Recovery time**           | 4--10 minutes (full reload)      | 30--90 seconds (single node reload)    |
| **State guarantee**         | Clean: all state from checkpoint | Assumes surviving state is valid       |
| **Implementation**          | Simple: kill all, reload all     | Complex: dynamic membership management |
| **Failure during recovery** | Retry cold restart               | Fall back to cold restart              |
| **Best for**                | Correlated failures, SDC events  | Single-node failures, GPU errors       |

: **Cold vs. Warm Restart Trade-Offs**: Cold restart kills every process and reloads from disk; warm restart preserves surviving workers and replaces only the failed node. Warm restart cuts recovery from minutes to seconds for the typical single-node failure but introduces software complexity around dynamic membership management. Mature deployments can run warm restart as the fast path and cold restart as the safety net. {#tbl-cold-vs-warm-restart}

### Recovery automation pipeline {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-recovery-automation-pipeline}

At the scale of 10,000+ GPUs, failures occur multiple times per day, so a human cannot handle each one. Recovery must be an autonomous control loop managed by the cluster's control plane. Published reports from large training fleets describe multi-stage automation that classifies failures and selects the minimum viable remediation [@dubey2024llama; @kokolis2025; @zu2024tpuv4].

The pipeline operates in four ordered stages:

1.  Health monitoring daemon\index{Recovery automation!health monitoring daemon}: Continuously scrapes GPU telemetry (ECC error counters, temperature, fan speed, NVLink status) alongside application metrics like training loss and step throughput, often from a sidecar container.
2.  Failure classifier\index{Recovery automation!failure classifier}: Determines whether a signal indicates a fatal error (for example, NVIDIA Xid error 48: double-bit ECC error\index{ECC error!uncorrectable}), a transient stall (for example, temporary network congestion), or a performance degradation (for example, thermal throttling).
3.  Action selector\index{Recovery automation!action selector}: Chooses a response consistent with the affected state and communication group. A hang may require a group restart rather than a local container restart; a confirmed hardware fault can require draining and replacement. A partition can justify a bounded wait, but replacement must fence the old ownership before accepting new writes.
4.  Validation stage\index{Recovery automation!validation stage}: Runs a recorded "canary batch" or validation workload under the expected numerical tolerance. Unexpected loss or gradient behavior triggers investigation of restored state and execution configuration, with fallback to an earlier validated snapshot when the new state cannot be trusted.

This automation shortens mean time to recovery from the tens of minutes that a page-diagnose-repair cycle takes when a human is in the loop to minutes for the common failure types. The Llama 3 team reports that automated tooling handled nearly all of the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_interruptions_str` interruptions in its `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_days_str`-day snapshot [@dubey2024llama]. The classification stage is critical. Treating every failure as a cold restart wastes compute on transient issues, while treating a hardware failure as transient allows corrupted computation to continue.

### Stragglers versus fail-stop failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distinguishing-stragglers-failures-285d}

::: {#dfn-fault-tolerance-straggler .callout-definition title="Straggler"}

***Straggler***\index{Straggler!definition} is a worker in a distributed training job that processes tasks significantly slower than its peers, creating a synchronization bottleneck.

1.  **Significance**: In a bulk synchronous parallel system, cluster throughput is bounded by the speed of the slowest rank. A single 10 percent performance drop on one node can reduce the effective compute capacity of thousands of nodes by 10 percent.
2.  **Distinction**: The synchronization models of @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-synchronization-models-396f treat a straggler as a throughput problem; fault tolerance must also separate slow progress from a stopped participant. A straggler can produce correct results while delaying its peers. Slowness alone establishes neither incorrect values nor a failed process.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that stragglers are caused only by "bad hardware." In reality, they are often caused by system jitter\index{Straggler!system jitter cause} from background OS processes, network congestion, or thermal throttling that varies across the data center floor.

:::

In synchronous training, a straggler sets the pace of the entire cluster, because AllReduce cannot complete until every rank has submitted its gradients.

For the simplified no-overlap straggler model, the step time becomes:
$$ T_{\text{step,straggler}}(N) = \max(T_{\text{rank}_0}, T_{\text{rank}_1}, \dots, T_{\text{rank}_{N-1}}) + \CommunicationTime $$

Stragglers arise from "gray failures\index{Gray failure!silent degradation}\index{Gray failure!straggler cause}\index{Straggler!gray failure cause}" that may not trigger explicit errors: thermal throttling reduces clock speed, degrading interconnect cables increase communication latency, OS background processes (memory scrubbing, log rotation) consume CPU cycles, and data loading from a congested network filesystem introduces variable I/O delays. A slow worker can continue meeting a liveness timeout while reducing training throughput, or become slow enough to trigger the same timeout as a failed worker. Progress measurements are therefore needed alongside liveness checks.

The challenge is distinguishing stragglers from failures. Stragglers should trigger *mitigation* (redistribute work, replace the slow node). Failures should trigger *recovery* (checkpoint-restart). Aggressive timeouts treat stragglers as failures, causing unnecessary job restarts that waste more compute than the straggler itself. Conservative timeouts waste compute waiting for stragglers that will never speed up.

Straggler mitigation strategies\index{Straggler!mitigation strategies}\index{Straggler mitigation|see{Straggler}} change either the work assignment or the execution resources. Dynamic load balancing\index{Straggler!dynamic load balancing} moves work away from slow workers while preserving the intended update, whereas bounded staleness\index{Straggler!bounded staleness} allows delayed gradients under an algorithm that tolerates them; its convergence cost depends on the workload and delay bound. Backup workers\index{Straggler!backup worker} replicate selected tasks and accept one result per logical contribution, trading extra GPU cycles for a shorter wait without double-counting gradients. At the infrastructure boundary, proactive replacement\index{Straggler!proactive replacement} uses hardware telemetry to identify suspect components and replace them when the expected benefit exceeds migration and recovery costs.

A simple cost calculation shows why a severe straggler may be cheaper to replace than tolerate.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lego-straggler-tax
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_usd

class StragglerTax:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    normal_step_s = 1.0
    throttle_factor = 0.50  # straggler runs at 50% speed
    gpu_cost_per_hour = Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.GpuTrainingUtilityScenarioPerHour.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    straggler_step_s = normal_step_s / throttle_factor
    healthy_gpus = n_gpus - 1
    effective_speed = 1 / straggler_step_s
    straggler_frac_pct = 1 / n_gpus * 100
    throughput_loss_pct = (1 - normal_step_s / straggler_step_s) * 100
    wasted_cost_per_hour = n_gpus * gpu_cost_per_hour * (1 - normal_step_s / straggler_step_s)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(straggler_step_s > normal_step_s, "Straggler must be slower")
    check(abs(throughput_loss_pct - 50.0) < 0.01, f"Expected 50% throughput loss, got {throughput_loss_pct}")
    check(abs(wasted_cost_per_hour - 1536.0) < 0.1, f"Expected $1536/hr wasted cost, got {wasted_cost_per_hour}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0)
    normal_step_str = fmt(normal_step_s, precision=0, commas=False)
    throttle_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(throttle_factor * 100) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    straggler_step_str = fmt(straggler_step_s, precision=0, commas=False)
    healthy_gpus_str = fmt(healthy_gpus, precision=0)
    effective_speed_str = fmt(effective_speed, precision=1, commas=False)
    straggler_frac_str = fmt_percent(straggler_frac_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    throughput_loss_str = fmt_int(throughput_loss_pct, commas=False)
    gpu_cost_str = fmt_usd(gpu_cost_per_hour, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
    wasted_cost_str = fmt_usd(wasted_cost_per_hour, precision=0, per="hour")
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_fault_tolerance_margin_003.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A red square source node with five arrows fanning out to five identical blue nodes."}

*A single straggler idles every healthy accelerator.*
:::

:::: {#nbk-fault-tolerance-straggler-tax .callout-notebook title="The straggler tax"}

Consider a `{python} StragglerTax.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster where a normal training iteration takes `{python} StragglerTax.normal_step_str` second. A single GPU enters a thermally throttled state, clocking down to `{python} StragglerTax.throttle_pct_str` speed, and now takes `{python} StragglerTax.straggler_step_str` seconds to complete its computation.

Because AllReduce cannot complete until every rank has submitted its gradients, the other `{python} StragglerTax.healthy_gpus_str` healthy GPUs sit idle waiting for the straggler.

```{=latex}
\tcbbreak
```

**Impact**:

- Normal step time: `{python} StragglerTax.normal_step_str` second
- Straggler step time: `{python} StragglerTax.straggler_step_str` seconds
- Effective cluster speed: 1 step/`{python} StragglerTax.straggler_step_str`s = `{python} StragglerTax.effective_speed_str` steps/sec

A single failing device (`{python} StragglerTax.straggler_frac_str` of the hardware) has reduced the throughput of the entire cluster by `{python} StragglerTax.throughput_loss_str` percent. At `{python} StragglerTax.gpu_cost_str`, this straggler wastes `{python} StragglerTax.wasted_cost_str` in idle compute.

**Systems insight**: Replacement is worthwhile only when the expected time saved exceeds recovery and replay costs. If the slowdown is expected to persist for the next $K$ useful updates, whose step times are $T_{\text{slow}}$ on the degraded allocation and $T_{\text{healthy}}$ after replacement, the simplified break-even condition is $K(T_{\text{slow}}-T_{\text{healthy}}) > T_{\text{restart}} + T_{\text{replay}}$. The right side includes waiting for capacity and restoring state. A short-lived slowdown may clear before replacement pays off; false-positive detection and uncertain persistence also affect the decision. MTBF describes failure recurrence, not how long this slowdown will last.

::::

Replacing a slow node while maintaining the original GPU count requires available capacity. An $N+1$ redundancy model reserves a hot spare for the isolation and promotion stages of @fig-sdc-controller, reducing allocation delay. Promotion still requires compatible resources, valid state, and communication-group reconstruction; an idle device alone does not guarantee recovery within seconds. A cold spare adds startup work, while a job without a reserved spare depends on the scheduler finding capacity or on repair. The hot spare buys shorter waiting time with devices that sit idle while the fleet is healthy. Fixed-size checkpoint-restart recovery restores the original resource count. Elastic recovery relaxes that requirement by allowing the job to continue with fewer workers when the remaining allocation can support it.

::: {#chk-fault-tolerance-detection-vs-recovery .callout-checkpoint title="Tuning detection and recovery"}

- [ ] **Timeout tuning**: given the heartbeat timeout rule $\HandoverTimeout = H + k\sigma_d$, explain what failure mode is traded away when $k$ is lowered from 5 to 3, and which failure mode worsens.
- [ ] **Warm vs. cold restart**: choose a warm restart or a cold restart for a single GPU failure in a 1,000-GPU job with surviving state intact, and identify two conditions that push recovery back toward the cold path.
- [ ] **Hot spare cost**: explain why a hot spare cuts recovery latency relative to detect-then-restart, including the standing cost the cluster pays to keep that spare available.
- [ ] **Straggler decision**: determine what governs whether to wait out a slowed node or kill it and recover onto healthy hardware.

:::

## Elastic Recovery {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-elastic-training-4f87}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: elastic-recovery-node-loss
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ELASTIC RECOVERY NODE LOSS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-elastic-training-4f87 opener.
# │
# │ Goal: Size the survivors when the Archetype A reference job loses one node.
# │ Show: 1,024-GPU job, 8-GPU node, 1,016 surviving GPUs.
# │ How:  Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference system: total minus one node.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_percent

class ElasticNodeLoss:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    job_gpus = Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference.system.total_accelerators
    gpus_per_node = Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference.system.node.accelerators_per_node

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    survivors = job_gpus - gpus_per_node

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(survivors == 1016, "prose quotes 1,016 surviving GPUs")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    job_gpus_str = fmt(job_gpus, precision=0)
    gpus_per_node_str = fmt(gpus_per_node, precision=0)
    survivors_str = fmt(survivors, precision=0)
    retained_pct_str = fmt_percent(survivors / job_gpus, precision=1, style="prose")
```

Suppose a `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.job_gpus_str`-GPU training job loses an `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.gpus_per_node_str`-GPU node to a hardware fault, but the cluster has no spare nodes available. A fixed-size recovery policy leaves the remaining `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.survivors_str` GPUs waiting until replacement capacity becomes available or the allocation is released. Elastic recovery allows the job to resize and continue with less compute, provided its state and parallel decomposition fit the smaller allocation.

::: {#dfn-fault-tolerance-elastic-training .callout-definition title="Elastic training"}

***Elastic training***\index{Elastic Training!definition}\index{Training!elastic} is the capability of a distributed training job to adjust its worker count across membership changes, potentially through a coordinated worker-group restart.

1.  **Significance**: It converts a permanent capacity loss into a temporary interruption followed by reduced throughput. A pure data-parallel `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.job_gpus_str`-GPU job that loses `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.gpus_per_node_str` GPUs retains `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.retained_pct_str` of its device count and may resume if the remaining devices can hold the state. Tensor- and pipeline-parallel jobs additionally need a feasible partition and compatible group sizes; retained device count does not guarantee the same fraction of throughput. The recovery policy must either preserve the effective batch size through additional accumulation or validate the optimization changes caused by a smaller batch.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike fixed-size checkpoint-restart recovery, which waits for replacement hardware to restore the original allocation, elastic recovery can restart or resume with a different worker count. The optimization loop may pause while membership, ranks, and state are re-established.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that elasticity is "automatic." In reality, recovery requires coordinated adaptation: the training framework, the data loader, and the orchestrator must all synchronize their state to ensure that no data samples are lost or double-counted during the resize.

:::

@Fig-elastic-flow charts this dynamic lifecycle through three sequential phases: execution begins with a balanced four-node AllReduce ring at full throughput (Phase 1), pauses at a rendezvous barrier to reload the last consistent checkpoint when Node 3 drops out (Phase 2), and dynamically contracts into a three-node topology that redistributes data shards (+33 percent per worker) to resume productive training at 75 percent throughput (Phase 3).

::: {#fig-elastic-flow fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Elastic training recovery**: Read the three phases top to bottom. Unlike static training, which aborts on failure, elastic training pauses when a node fails, reloads the last consistent checkpoint, re-forms the ring over the $N-1$ survivors, and redistributes the failed node's data shards among them. The job resumes at reduced throughput (75 percent here, assuming an unchanged per-worker rate), turning a hard failure into a temporary slowdown." fig-alt="Three stacked phases along a downward time arrow. Phase 1: four nodes in a ring, all healthy, at 100 percent throughput. Phase 2: node 3 is outlined in red and labeled failed, its ring link is broken, a checkpoint is loaded, and the remaining ranks wait at a rendezvous barrier. Phase 3: three renumbered nodes form a new ring, each with a one-third larger data shard, at 75 percent throughput."}

### Recovery adaptation mechanisms {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-elastic-training-mechanisms-49b1}

By contracting communication groups across surviving workers, elastic recovery converts what would otherwise be catastrophic job terminations into bounded capacity adjustments. As the transition from Phase 1 to Phase 3 in @fig-elastic-flow illustrates, shedding a lost node reduces active ring width rather than idling the entire cluster pending hardware replacement. The worker group may restart while the framework re-establishes membership, ranks, and state under the smaller resource allocation. When a failure reduces the worker count, the recovery path must adapt several training components before productive work resumes. Each adaptation addresses a specific consistency requirement that, if violated, would corrupt the model or waste computation.

Batch size adjustment is the first concern: with fewer workers, each worker must process more samples to maintain the global batch size, or the global batch size must be reduced. Reducing global batch size during recovery may require learning rate adjustment to preserve convergence properties.

Changing the global batch size changes the optimization regime as well as the amount of work per step. The linear scaling rule of @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-learning-rate-scaling-rules-fa26 multiplies the learning rate by the same factor $k$ as the batch size [@goyal2017accurate], but its validation with warmup for growing batches does not establish a universal recovery rule. The square-root alternative in @eq-lr-scaling illustrates another candidate policy for a changed worker count:

$$ \eta_{\text{new}} = \eta_{\text{base}} \times \sqrt{\frac{N_{\text{new}}}{N_{\text{base}}}} $$ {#eq-lr-scaling}

where $N$ represents the number of data-parallel workers, with per-worker microbatch size and accumulation count held fixed so global batch size scales with $N$. For a shrink, the square-root rule reduces the learning rate less than linear scaling does; that arithmetic does not establish which policy is more stable. Either policy requires validation for the optimizer, schedule, and workload. Preserving the global batch instead can avoid introducing this change in optimization regime.

Gradient accumulation offers that alternative: each surviving worker processes additional micro-batches before synchronization to maintain the original effective batch size. If worker count drops by half, doubling the accumulation steps preserves the number of examples per update and can retain the existing learning-rate schedule. Each worker then performs twice as much micro-batch computation per update, although communication and overlap determine the wall-time increase. Equal batch size does not imply bitwise-identical updates or identical behavior from operations that depend on micro-batch statistics.

Data loader redistribution must agree with the recovered training step and new membership. When workers are lost, the loader reassigns the remaining logical input stream so that the resize itself neither omits samples nor counts them twice in an update. Replaying work discarded by checkpoint rollback is expected; duplicating contributions within the resumed stream is a different error. The saved data position and sampling state distinguish those cases.

State resharding adds further complexity when using sharded model parallelism (ZeRO/FSDP), because the loss of a worker can remove the only live copy of its state shard. A surviving replica can supply that shard; otherwise recovery must reconstruct it from sufficient retained information or reload a complete checkpoint generation. Only then can the system redistribute valid state across the surviving workers. Changing shard ownership alone cannot recover missing values.

#### Spot instance preemption as a failure class {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-spot-instance-arbitrage-68ad}

Hardware faults are not the only event that removes workers from a running job. Cloud providers often price preemptible ("spot") instances below on-demand capacity, with the caveat that they can be reclaimed with little warning. Once workers vanish, recovery faces the same missing-state and membership problems as a hardware failure. An advance notice, when available, can allow a coordinated save or drain before departure and therefore changes the recovery opportunity.

Both fixed-size and elastic jobs can recover from preemption using checkpoints, but a fixed-size job must regain its required allocation before restarting. An elastic job can instead resume at reduced scale if enough capacity remains and the training invariants survive the resize. Recovery still pays for detection, state restoration, and group reconstruction; repeated reclamations can erase the apparent price advantage. In a scenario where spot capacity costs \$0.60/hour instead of \$3.00/hour, the savings can outweigh the lost work and resizing delays; @sec-fleet-orchestration-spot-instances develops the full spot-versus-on-demand cost model.

Spot capacity makes worker departure frequent; federated training makes it the default.

::: {#lhs-fault-tolerance-archetype-c-federated-mobilenet-client-dropout .callout-lighthouse title="Archetype C (Federated MobileNet): Dropout as the normal case"}

Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) makes worker departure an expected part of training. Its phone-class clients train while charging, idle, and connected. A round can tolerate some departures, but it still needs enough compatible updates before its deadline; otherwise the coordinator abandons the round [@mcmahan2017communication; @bonawitz2019towards]. Model-version checks prevent updates from an obsolete round from entering the current aggregate, while aggregation weights account for the examples contributed under the chosen learning algorithm. Version checks and weighting do not remove participation bias. Recovery must preserve the coordinator state needed to continue that algorithm, including the model, round position, and any persistent optimizer or sampling state, rather than assuming weights alone suffice. @Sec-edge-intelligence-client-scheduling-f675 develops the round design, including deadlines, participation requirements, and the bias that arises when some kinds of devices report less often than others.

:::

#### Framework support for elastic recovery {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-framework-support-elastic-training-8b75}

The framework question is which resize invariants it can enforce automatically: group membership, shard ownership, data coverage, and batch math. The recovery adaptation mechanisms (batch size adjustment, learning rate recalibration, data loader redistribution, state resharding) must be implemented by the training framework, and frameworks differ in how much of this recovery logic they automate after a failure.

PyTorch Elastic\index{PyTorch Elastic!worker failure detection} (TorchElastic) uses agents to monitor workers and a rendezvous mechanism to establish group membership [@pytorchElasticDocs; @pytorchRendezvousDocs]. On a failure or membership change, TorchElastic stops all surviving workers, forms a new worker group, and starts its workers with new `RANK` and `WORLD_SIZE` assignments. It handles rank reassignment and communication-group reconstruction after restart, but leaves batch size, learning rate, and checkpoint semantics to user code.

DeepSpeed [@rasley2020] provides ZeRO-based distributed training and checkpointing building blocks for large models [@deepspeedCheckpointingDocs]. Its recovery model is checkpoint-based: after a failure, the job reloads from the last durable checkpoint, and Universal Checkpointing addresses portability across some changes in parallelism and topology [@deepspeedUniversalCheckpointingDocs]. The elastic behavior still depends on the surrounding launcher and resource manager rather than being made transparent by the framework alone.

Ray Train, built on Ray's actor model, provides a checkpoint-oriented recovery path for worker failure and node preemption. Ray can restart a worker group after a failure and resume from the latest available checkpoint, while the training function remains responsible for saving and loading sufficient state [@rayTrainFaultToleranceDocs].

Horovod Elastic builds on Horovod's data parallel training system [@sergeev2018horovod] with a documented elastic state API for worker additions and removals [@horovodElasticDocs]. When the worker group changes, Horovod can reset ranks and reconstruct communication, while the training script remains responsible for convergence-sensitive choices such as learning-rate or batch-size policy.

The elastic training framework support summarized in @tbl-elastic-training-comparison compares the recovery automation and state management approaches across these frameworks.

| **Framework**       | **Failure Detection** | **Automatic Recovery** | **State Resharding** | **Cluster Integration** |
|:--------------------|:---------------------:|:----------------------:|:--------------------:|:-----------------------:|
| **PyTorch Elastic** |   Rendezvous timeout  |          Yes           |        Manual        |        Kubernetes       |
| **DeepSpeed**       |        External       |    Checkpoint-based    | Deployment-dependent |   External schedulers   |
| **Ray Train**       |   Actor supervision   | Checkpoint retry path  |  Checkpoint reload   |       Ray Cluster       |
| **Horovod Elastic** |    Driver heartbeat   |          Yes           |        Manual        |    Slurm, Kubernetes    |

: **Elastic Recovery Framework Comparison**: Frameworks differ in how they detect worker failures and how much of the recovery sequence (group reconstruction, state redistribution, batch size adjustment) they automate. {#tbl-elastic-training-comparison}

While these frameworks automate the mechanics of recovery, deciding exactly which model state must be preserved and resharded remains a workload-specific engineering choice.

### Model-specific training fault tolerance {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-modelspecific-training-fault-tolerance-4b70}

The checkpoint and recovery strategies developed in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-restart-fundamentals-0ac2 and @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-detection-recovery-0f54 require adaptation because workloads lose different kinds of state when they fail. The design question is therefore not simply how often to checkpoint, but which state variable would make a restart mathematically or economically wrong. For recommendation workloads, incremental checkpointing\index{Checkpointing!incremental}\index{Incremental checkpointing|see{Checkpointing}}, tiered checkpointing, and embedding versioning can reduce the cost of preserving fresh state. Incremental storage can still reconstruct an exact generation from a base and its required deltas; accepting stale or approximate state is a separate choice. @Tbl-training-recovery-state-invariants turns the workload differences into a compact recovery map.

| **Workload**   | **State at Risk**                                                                                  | **Checkpoint Implication**                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|:---------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| LLM training   | Optimizer state, curriculum position, document position, long-context schedule                     | Preserve the FP32 optimizer state where precision matters, shard writes with ZeRO/FSDP, move serialization off the critical path, and include the data-schedule position so the optimization trajectory resumes correctly. |
| Recommendation | Embedding freshness, feature-store version                                                         | Favor freshness over full-state exactness with incremental checkpointing, tiered checkpointing, and embedding versioning.                                                                                                  |
| Vision         | Augmentation seeds, shuffling order, batch-normalization statistics, progressive-resizing schedule | Capture the stochastic and normalization state that controls the input stream; weights alone are not enough to reproduce the training trajectory.                                                                          |
| Scientific ML  | Simulator state, search frontier, explored configurations, validation seeds                        | Treat the model, simulator, search process, and random state as one consistency unit so recovery does not duplicate exploration or invalidate comparisons.                                                                 |

: **Training Recovery State Invariants**: Workloads require different checkpoint contents because they make different state variables quality-bearing. The correct recovery policy starts from the state that would make a restart wrong, then chooses sharding, incrementality, or domain-state capture accordingly. {#tbl-training-recovery-state-invariants}

The common pattern is that recovery correctness is broader than weight restoration. LLMs can reload weights but resume with the wrong curriculum position; recommendation models can reload dense parameters but serve stale embeddings; vision models can reload weights but alter augmentation or normalization state; and scientific models can reload a neural network while losing the simulator state that made the data meaningful.

Elasticity and checkpointing provide the necessary resilience for long-running batch training jobs, but the operational calculus changes completely once the model is deployed to users. The challenge shifts from protecting *weeks of batch computation* to protecting *milliseconds of real-time latency*.

## Serving Fault Tolerance {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-serving-fault-tolerance-5375}

When a user asks a voice assistant to turn off the lights, they will not tolerate a five-minute pause while the inference server reloads from a checkpoint. Serving models presents a fundamentally different challenge: users expect millisecond-level responsiveness even when backend GPUs crash.

A serving replica is a runnable copy of the model that can accept requests; the routing layer chooses a replica, and a readiness check determines whether that replica can serve successfully. Replicas may share external state stores or keep request state in accelerator memory, so replacing compute does not necessarily replace the state a request needs. Serving fault tolerance asks how those mechanisms behave when replicas, GPUs, or state stores fail under live latency budgets. The focus here is narrower than a complete serving architecture: each mechanism is treated as a reliability boundary for real-time inference.

### Stateless vs. stateful serving {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-stateless-vs-stateful-serving-0a60}

The first serving decision is where request state lives, because that choice determines whether failover is a retry or a state-reconstruction problem. A stateless model worker retains no required per-session state between requests. It obtains the necessary context from the request or an external state store, so another ready worker can process the same request. A stateful application can therefore use stateless model workers, although its external store remains a reliability dependency.

The stateless pattern appears when the input itself carries all context: an image classifier processes one image, an object detector processes one frame, a single-turn text classifier processes one snippet, and an embedding service maps one input to one vector. Fault tolerance can then focus on replica health and request routing. Redundant replicas\index{Replication!redundant replicas} serve requests in parallel, load balancing\index{Load balancing!serving fault tolerance} sends traffic only to healthy replicas, health checks\index{Health check!serving failover} remove failed replicas from rotation, and automatic replacement starts a new replica when capacity falls. When a replica fails, in-flight requests to that replica can be retried elsewhere, because no quality-bearing session state has been lost.

The simplicity of stateless serving makes it the simpler architecture when the application permits it. However, many ML applications inherently require state across requests. Consider a chatbot: a single-turn question-answering system can operate statelessly, processing each question independently. A conversational assistant must preserve its history somewhere, but the model worker can still be stateless if each request carries the complete history or reads it from a durable external store. Worker-local state creates a stronger dependency when later requests rely on information available only at the selected replica.

Stateful serving appears when later work depends on retained session state. For a transformer, the key-value (KV) cache stores attention keys and values computed for earlier tokens so the worker can reuse them while generating subsequent tokens. This cache is derived state: if the authoritative token history and compatible model version remain available, a replacement can recompute it by processing that history again. Losing the history itself is a different failure because cache reconstruction no longer has its required input. Streaming speech recognition similarly maintains context from previous audio, recommendation sessions accumulate user context, and interactive editing maintains document state across edits. The fault-tolerance consequence is that failure loses quality-bearing state, not just serving capacity. KV cache loss requires reprocessing previous turns, session context loss forces users to repeat previous interactions, and accumulated user state loss degrades quality when context is unavailable. The mitigation choice follows the size, update rate, and quality value of that state: session affinity routes a session to the same replica, state checkpointing periodically saves session state, state replication maintains a standby copy, and graceful degradation keeps the service available at reduced quality if state cannot be recovered.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How the KV cache grows with sequence length and concurrency until it fills accelerator memory is developed in @sec-inference-scale-kv-cache-wall.
:::

@Tbl-stateless-stateful-comparison contrasts stateless and stateful serving fault tolerance, showing how the fundamental difference manifests in every aspect of design, from request routing to recovery complexity.

| **Aspect**               |      **Stateless Serving**       |             **Stateful Serving**            |
|:-------------------------|:--------------------------------:|:-------------------------------------------:|
| **Request routing**      |           Any replica            |            Session-affine replica           |
| **Failure impact**       |     Retry on another replica     |             Potential state loss            |
| **Recovery complexity**  |     Restart and load weights     |      Reload state + reconstruct context     |
| **Redundancy approach**  |      Active-active replicas      |          Replicated state + standby         |
| **Work after detection** | Route or retry to a ready worker | Recover required state, then route or retry |

: **Stateless vs. Stateful Serving Fault Tolerance**: State recovery adds work after failure detection. End-to-end failover also includes probe timeouts, routing, replacement readiness, and request retry; neither worker category implies a fixed latency. {#tbl-stateless-stateful-comparison}

Regardless of whether the serving architecture is stateless or stateful, maintaining availability under these constraints requires deploying redundant capacity.

### Redundancy and replication {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-redundancy-replication-2239}

Redundancy buys availability only when replica placement and spare capacity match the failure domain being defended against. Multiple copies of serving capability let the system continue operating when individual replicas fail.

#### Availability calculations {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-availability-calculations-ef0a}

For a single replica with availability $A_{\text{single}}$ (probability of being operational at any given time), @eq-availability-redundancy quantifies how multiple independent replicas achieve higher system availability:

$$ A_{\text{system}} = 1 - (1 - A_{\text{single}})^k $$ {#eq-availability-redundancy}

where $k$ is the number of replicas. For a service whose single replica is available 99 percent of the time, redundancy compounds as follows.

For a single replica, $A_{\text{single}} = 99\%$ corresponds to 3.65 days of downtime per year. Adding independent replicas changes the tail of the failure distribution quickly: two replicas give $A = 1 - (0.01)^2 = 99.99\%$, or 52.6 minutes of downtime per year, and three replicas give $A = 1 - (0.01)^3 = 99.9999\%$, or 31.5 seconds. The math is powerful, but it assumes independent failures and enough capacity on any surviving replica to meet the service target; shared power, shared networking, and shared software bugs reduce actual availability below these theoretical values.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_fault_tolerance_margin_004.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Time ladder showing annual downtime dropping from 3.65 days with one replica to 52.6 minutes with two and 31.5 seconds with three."}

*Redundancy turns days of downtime into seconds.*
:::

#### Replication strategies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-replication-strategies-aaa2}

The availability equation says how much redundancy can help; the replication topology determines how that redundancy behaves under normal execution and sudden hardware loss. @Fig-serving-redundancy contrasts two fundamental serving designs: active-active replication (left panel) splits ingress traffic evenly across three live replicas (one-third each) to maximize compute utilization, requiring spare headroom so surviving instances can absorb load if a replica drops; active-passive replication (right panel) funnels all traffic to a designated primary while maintaining a pre-warmed standby whose weights remain loaded in accelerator memory, ensuring rapid failover at the expense of an idle device.

::: {#fig-serving-redundancy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Serving redundancy strategies**: Active-active (left) splits traffic across three replicas, each carrying about one-third, which uses every device but requires enough headroom for the survivors to absorb a failed replica's share. Active-passive (right) sends all traffic to one primary and keeps a warm standby with weights already loaded, which simplifies failover at the cost of capacity that serves nothing while the primary is healthy." fig-alt="Two panels divided by a dashed line. Left, active-active: a load balancer splits requests along three arrows labeled one third to replicas 1, 2, and 3; text below reads survivors must absorb a lost replica load. Right, active-passive: a load balancer sends an arrow labeled all traffic to a primary and a dashed arrow labeled on failure to a dashed warm standby box; text below reads standby holds loaded weights but serves nothing."}
![](images/svg/serving-redundancy.svg)

:::

Geographic replication extends the same choice across regions. It protects against data-center or regional network failures, but requests routed to distant regions pay additional latency, and the active-active headroom problem reappears at regional scale. When a region fails, the surviving regions must absorb its traffic and, for stateful services, rebuild its sessions, so each region either carries spare capacity sized for the largest region it may absorb or accepts degraded latency during the failover. Traffic returns to a recovered region gradually, because its caches and warm replicas start empty and an abrupt shift back would overload it and trigger the same failover again. Multi-tier designs combine several replication policies at once: edge caches replicate for latency, regional serving clusters replicate for availability, and a global primary or coordination layer preserves consistency and freshness.

#### Replica placement and failure domains {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-replica-placement-failure-domains-73a7}

Effective redundancy requires placing replicas in independent failure domains. Different machines tolerate individual machine failures; different racks tolerate rack-level failures from power or top-of-rack switch issues; different availability zones tolerate data-center-section failures; and different regions tolerate entire data-center failures. The independence level should match the availability requirement and cost constraint: regional replication is expensive because it duplicates compute and network capacity, but it is necessary when regional failure must not become user-visible downtime.

Placement only creates the possibility of recovery. The serving system still needs a control loop that notices the failure, removes the affected replica from traffic, and preserves enough state that the user-visible service continues with bounded degradation.

### Failover mechanisms {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failover-mechanisms-5ddd}

When a replica fails, traffic must be redirected to healthy replicas, and the speed and reliability of that redirection determine how much of the failure users see. The mechanism decomposes into two questions: how the system decides that a replica can no longer serve, and what happens to stateful sessions already attached to it.

#### Health checking {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-health-checking-a604}

Health checks\index{Health check!liveness vs. readiness}\index{Health check!inference correctness probe} decide when traffic should move, so they must evaluate liveness, readiness, and inference correctness. A liveness check confirms that the process responds and triggers a restart when it does not. A readiness check confirms that the replica can serve: its weights are loaded, its accelerator is initialized, warmup has completed, and dependencies such as feature stores are reachable. An inference check runs a known input through the model and compares the output with the expected result, catching the silent failure in which the process is healthy but its answers are wrong. The load balancer acts on these signals.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ What each probe must test on an accelerator replica, from process liveness to a fixed-prompt inference check, is developed in @sec-inference-scale-health-checking-failover-070e.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: health-check-detection-budget
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HEALTH CHECK DETECTION BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-health-checking-a604
# │          failover-budget paragraph immediately below.
# │
# │ Goal: Show how probe interval, timeout, and failure threshold bound the time
# │       a crashed replica keeps receiving traffic.
# │ Show: 5 s interval, 2 s timeout, threshold 3 -> removal 12-17 s after crash.
# │ How:  Earliest removal = (threshold - 1) x interval + timeout (crash just
# │       before a probe); latest = threshold x interval + timeout (crash just
# │       after a successful probe). Probe settings are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_range, fmt_time

class HealthCheckDetection:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    interval_s = 5  # probe interval (scenario setting)
    timeout_s = 2  # per-probe timeout (scenario setting)
    fail_threshold = 3  # consecutive missed probes before removal
    success_threshold = 2  # consecutive clean probes before readmission

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    detect_min_s = (fail_threshold - 1) * interval_s + timeout_s
    detect_max_s = fail_threshold * interval_s + timeout_s

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(detect_min_s == 12, f"Expected 12 s earliest removal, got {detect_min_s}")
    check(detect_max_s == 17, f"Expected 17 s latest removal, got {detect_max_s}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    interval_str = fmt_time(interval_s, second, precision=0, commas=False)
    timeout_str = fmt_time(timeout_s, second, precision=0, commas=False)
    fail_threshold_str = fmt_int(fail_threshold)
    success_threshold_str = fmt_int(success_threshold)
    detect_range_str = fmt_range(detect_min_s, detect_max_s, unit=second, precision=0)
```

The probe parameters\index{Health check!trade-offs and thresholds} set the failover budget. With a `{python} HealthCheckDetection.interval_str` check interval, a `{python} HealthCheckDetection.timeout_str` timeout, and a failure threshold of `{python} HealthCheckDetection.fail_threshold_str` missed probes, a crashed replica leaves rotation `{python} HealthCheckDetection.detect_range_str` after it fails, depending on where the crash falls between probes. Every request routed to it in that window fails or waits for a client retry. Shortening the interval or lowering the threshold speeds failover but raises the false-positive rate, marking healthy replicas unhealthy during transient stalls and removing capacity exactly when load is high. A success threshold of `{python} HealthCheckDetection.success_threshold_str` clean probes applies the same caution in reverse, holding a recovered replica out of rotation until it has proved stable.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\Needspace{24\baselineskip}
:::

#### Session affinity and stateful failover {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-session-affinity-stateful-failover-27b2}

For stateful serving, session affinity\index{Session affinity!stateful failover} routes all requests within a session to the same replica. Load balancers maintain session-to-replica mapping through sticky sessions implemented with cookies, headers, or IP hashing. Affinity preserves locality but supplies no replacement copy when that replica fails. Checkpointing saves session state periodically, replication copies it to a standby, and external systems such as Redis or Memcached move it outside the model worker. The external store still needs its own availability and durability contract. Accepting state loss is valid only when the service can reconstruct derived state from retained history or explicitly begin a reduced-context session.

The choice depends on state size, update frequency, and the quality impact of state loss; @tbl-stateful-failover summarizes the trade-offs across the four common approaches:

| **Approach**                | **Recovery Latency** | **Consistency** | **Operational Complexity** |
|:----------------------------|:--------------------:|:---------------:|:--------------------------:|
| **State loss**              |         Fast         |       None      |            Low             |
| **Checkpointing**           |        Medium        |     Eventual    |           Medium           |
| **Synchronous replication** |         Fast         |      Strong     |            High            |
| **Distributed state**       |         Fast         |   Configurable  |           Medium           |

: **Stateful Failover Approaches**: Recovery latency, consistency, and operational complexity distinguish four approaches to session-state failover. Checkpoint recovery may lose updates after the saved snapshot. Distributed storage can provide different consistency contracts, and synchronous replication provides its promised guarantee only under the specified acknowledgment and fault model. {#tbl-stateful-failover}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
{{< pagebreak >}}
:::

### Model-specific serving fault tolerance {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-modelspecific-serving-fault-tolerance-3245}

Model-specific serving differences follow from what state is expensive to lose and how quickly the user needs a response. The policy question is therefore a state-loss budget: which state can be rebuilt, which state must be replicated, and which state may be degraded temporarily without violating the product contract. @Tbl-serving-recovery-state-invariants maps that question across the three common regimes.

| **Serving workload** | **State expensive to lose**                    | **Fault-tolerance policy**                                                                                  | **Degradation path**                                                   |
|:---------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| LLM conversation     | KV cache, conversation context, prefix state   | Replicate or checkpoint high-value session state; regenerate only when the latency budget allows.           | Rebuild from transcript, reuse cached prefixes, or ask for retry.      |
| Recommendation       | Fresh user features, item features, embeddings | Replicate feature stores, cache hot features, and monitor freshness as a reliability signal.                | Serve stale or default features with measured quality loss.            |
| Vision service       | Preprocessing state, device health, edge input | Retry stateless requests on healthy replicas and fail closed on preprocessing or accelerator-health faults. | Use a smaller local model, defer prediction, or return low confidence. |

: **Serving Recovery State Invariants**: Serving fault tolerance starts from the state whose loss changes user-visible quality. LLMs protect live context, recommendation systems protect feature freshness, and vision services protect preprocessing and device correctness. {#tbl-serving-recovery-state-invariants}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-cache-live-state
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KV-CACHE LIVE STATE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: [^fn-kv-cache-resilience] below (serving fault tolerance).
# │
# │ Goal: Size one full-context conversation's KV cache for a Llama-family 70B
# │       model, with grouped-query attention and with one KV head per query head.
# │ Show: 80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128K context, 128-dim heads; ~43 GB vs ~344 GB.
# │ How:  Models.Language.Llama3_70B.get_kv_cache_size at its context_length,
# │       BF16 (2 bytes); counterfactual via calc_kv_cache_size with .heads.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim.physics.memory import calc_kv_cache_size
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_text

class KvCacheLiveState:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    m = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    kv_bytes = BYTES_FP16  # BF16 and FP16 are both 2 bytes per element

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    head_dim = m.hidden_dim // m.heads
    kv_gqa = m.get_kv_cache_size(seq_len=m.context_length, batch_size=1, precision=kv_bytes)
    kv_mha = calc_kv_cache_size(
        n_layers=m.layers, n_heads=m.heads, head_dim=head_dim, seq_len=m.context_length, batch_size=1, bytes_per_elem=kv_bytes
    )
    ratio = (kv_mha / kv_gqa).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(40 < kv_gqa.to(GB).magnitude < 45, "footnote quotes about 43 GB per conversation")
    check(abs(ratio - m.heads / m.kv_heads) < 1e-9, "MHA/GQA ratio must equal heads/kv_heads")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    layers_str = fmt(m.layers, precision=0)
    kv_heads_str = fmt(m.kv_heads, precision=0)
    heads_str = fmt(m.heads, precision=0)
    context_k_str = fmt_text(fmt_int(m.context_length // 1024), "K")
    head_dim_str = fmt(head_dim, precision=0)
    kv_gqa_str = fmt_memory(round(kv_gqa.to(GB).magnitude) * GB, unit=GB, precision=0)
    kv_mha_str = fmt_memory(round(kv_mha.to(GB).magnitude) * GB, unit=GB, precision=0)
```

The KV cache[^fn-kv-cache-resilience] can be substantial (gigabytes for long contexts across attention layers). Losing it requires recomputing attention state from the retained token history, which can take seconds to minutes; previously delivered text need not be generated again. During an in-flight response, recovery must also know which output tokens the client has already received so a retry does not silently duplicate or replace part of the response.

[^fn-kv-cache-resilience]: [offset=-34mm] **KV Cache**\index{KV Cache!serving fault tolerance}: Stores key and value projections for all previous tokens across all attention layers, scaling as $2 \times \NumberOfLayers \times \NumberOfKeyvalueHeadsKv \times S \times \AttentionHeadDimension \times \ElementStorageSize$. For a Llama-family 70B model with `{python} KvCacheLiveState.layers_str` layers, `{python} KvCacheLiveState.kv_heads_str` key-value heads, `{python} KvCacheLiveState.context_k_str` context, `{python} KvCacheLiveState.head_dim_str`-dimension heads, and BF16 storage, the KV cache is about `{python} KvCacheLiveState.kv_gqa_str` per conversation; using `{python} KvCacheLiveState.heads_str` independent key-value heads would be about `{python} KvCacheLiveState.kv_mha_str`. Losing this derived state requires replaying retained tokens to rebuild their attention state, rather than generating the conversation again. Reconstruction can exceed serving latency service level agreements (SLAs) even when a replacement replica is already available.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/fault_tolerance_kv_live_state_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Memory ladder comparing a 64-head KV cache at 344 GB with a grouped-query KV cache at 43 GB, with the 8x gap marked as a ratio annotation."}

*Even with grouped-query attention, one long conversation holds tens of GB of live state.*
:::

LLM serving choices trade KV-cache recovery latency against memory and storage overhead. The simplest strategy is to accept regeneration cost by rebuilding KV cache from conversation history after failure, but this can turn a long conversation into a multi-second or multi-minute restart. KV-cache checkpointing saves live state periodically and bounds the amount of regeneration, while KV-cache replication keeps a standby copy for fast failover at the cost of extra memory. Prefix caching\index{KV Cache!prefix caching}, also offered as prompt caching\index{KV Cache!prompt caching}, reuses state for common system prompts and shared context. A compatible cached prefix can reduce reconstruction work if it survives the failure and remains accessible to the replacement worker. Cache reuse alone does not establish a failover guarantee or preserve the session-specific history.

Recommendation serving protects freshness rather than conversational continuity. Recommendations depend on user and item features from feature stores, so feature-store unavailability can either degrade ranking quality or block recommendations entirely. The serving decision is the staleness budget: replicated feature stores keep recent features available across zones, local caches cover hot features, fallback to stale features accepts measured quality loss, and default features let the service return a lower-quality result when lookup fails. Real-time features such as recent user actions make freshness monitoring part of fault tolerance, because a pipeline that keeps serving old features is available operationally but wrong semantically. Large embedding tables may also sit behind dedicated embedding services, which need their own replication and failover plan.

Vision serving is usually closer to the stateless end of the spectrum because each image or frame can be retried on another replica. That simplicity changes where the checks belong. Thermal throttling threatens latency, while uncorrected memory errors threaten numerical validity; health policy must distinguish those consequences. Preprocessing checks must also prevent invalid resize, crop, color conversion, or normalization from producing apparently valid predictions. At the edge, disconnection can require a validated smaller local model, delayed nonurgent work, or abstention when the available computation cannot meet the prediction contract.

When redundancy cannot preserve full service, the remaining choice depends on the application contract. A validated reduced-capability response can preserve useful availability; if no such response is acceptable, the system must reject or defer the work. Graceful degradation makes the permitted reduction explicit before failure occurs.

## Graceful Degradation {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-graceful-degradation-9122}

During a major regional network outage, an e-commerce site suddenly loses access to its heavy, GPU-accelerated recommendation cluster. Rather than showing users empty pages or crashing, the site instantly switches to serving precomputed, generic popular items. The serving fault tolerance mechanisms developed in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-serving-fault-tolerance-5375 aim to maintain full service, but graceful degradation dictates what happens when those defenses are overwhelmed.

::: {#dfn-fault-tolerance-graceful-degradation .callout-definition title="Graceful degradation"}

***Graceful degradation***\index{Graceful Degradation!definition} is a fault tolerance strategy in which a system responds to resource exhaustion or component failure by deliberately reducing service quality (falling back to a smaller model, serving cached results, or returning partial outputs) rather than failing completely, maintaining measurable availability at reduced capability.

1.  **Significance**: Graceful degradation converts total outage risk into a controlled quality reduction. A recommendation system can fall back from a large ranker to a collaborative-filtering model on GPU failure, maintaining request availability with a quality penalty that must be measured for that workload. The engineering calculation includes both the requests served and the utility lost during fallback.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike complete system failure (where the service returns errors to all requests), graceful degradation provides a managed transition through a predefined capability hierarchy in which each fallback level has known accuracy, latency, and resource characteristics that allow the system to continue satisfying SLOs at reduced quality.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that degradation is automatic in well-designed systems. Graceful degradation requires explicit preengineering: fallback models must be preloaded or precomputed, switchover logic must detect the failure condition and trigger the transition without human intervention, and each degradation level must have been validated to actually satisfy its reduced SLO before it is needed in production.

:::

### Degradation dimensions {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-degradation-dimensions-4b25}

A degradation plan must name which service property will be sacrificed before an incident begins. @Tbl-graceful-degradation-dimensions summarizes the main levers. The table is a pre-incident design checklist, not an outage-time brainstorming aid: each sacrificed property needs a measured quality budget, an activation condition, and a recovery path before the failure occurs.

| **Dimension**        | **What the System Sacrifices**    | **Typical Fallback**                                                                           |
|:---------------------|:----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Quality              | Model accuracy or ranking quality | Use a simpler model, such as a collaborative-filtering fallback for a multi-tower recommender. |
| Latency              | Response speed                    | Batch more requests together to preserve throughput and model quality under high load.         |
| Coverage             | Result completeness               | Return top-10 search results instead of top-100.                                               |
| Freshness            | Recency of computed results       | Serve cached or stale candidates, such as hour-old news recommendations during an outage.      |
| Feature completeness | Input richness                    | Use content features when user history or real-time context is unavailable.                    |

: **Graceful Degradation Dimensions**: Degradation plans choose which service property can be reduced while still returning a useful answer. Naming the dimension in advance prevents the system from treating every failure as a binary serve-or-crash decision. {#tbl-graceful-degradation-dimensions}

These dimensions are not interchangeable. A search product may sacrifice coverage by returning fewer results while keeping freshness intact; a recommender may sacrifice freshness by serving cached candidates while preserving latency; and an interactive assistant may sacrifice quality by using a smaller model while keeping the session alive. The correct fallback is therefore workload-specific. It follows the property whose temporary loss least harms the application and whose recovery path can be validated before the incident.

### Graceful degradation strategies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-graceful-degradation-strategies-e85e}

The dimensions in @tbl-graceful-degradation-dimensions become operational only when the service binds each sacrificed property to a specific fallback mechanism. The strategy ladder starts with model fallback when the primary inference path is too expensive or unavailable, then moves to feature fallback when input quality degrades, and finally to load shedding when demand exceeds capacity and the system must preserve the highest-value requests first.

#### Model fallback {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-model-fallback-bc6e}

Model fallback turns quality into an explicit availability lever by maintaining multiple model versions with different resource requirements. The primary model\index{Graceful degradation!primary model} provides full capability at the highest resource cost, a secondary model\index{Graceful degradation!secondary model} reduces capability and resource demand, a tertiary model\index{Graceful degradation!tertiary model} preserves minimal capability, and a static fallback\index{Graceful degradation!static fallback} serves precomputed defaults with no inference at all. When the primary path is unavailable or overloaded, the policy descends only as far as resource pressure requires, then returns upward after the primary path is healthy again.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: model-fallback-cascade
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MODEL FALLBACK CASCADE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-model-fallback-bc6e prose below.
# │
# │ Goal: Pin the three named vision models' sizes and ImageNet top-1 accuracy.
# │ Show: ViT-Large 307M / 88%; EfficientNet-B4 19M / 83%; MobileNetV3-Large 5.4M / 75%.
# │ How:  Models.Vision.*.parameters; Literature.Benchmarks.*ImageNetTop1.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature, Models
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_percent

class ModelFallbackCascade:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    vit_params_m = Models.Vision.ViT_Large.parameters.to(param).magnitude / 1e6
    effnet_params_m = Models.Vision.EfficientNetB4.parameters.to(param).magnitude / 1e6
    mobilenet_params_m = Models.Vision.MobileNetV3_Large.parameters.to(param).magnitude / 1e6
    vit_top1 = float(Literature.Benchmarks.ViTLargeImageNetTop1)
    effnet_top1 = float(Literature.Benchmarks.EfficientNetB4ImageNetTop1)
    mobilenet_top1 = float(Literature.Benchmarks.MobileNetV3LargeImageNetTop1)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    # (no derived values; each rung is a named registry entity)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(vit_params_m > effnet_params_m > mobilenet_params_m, "each fallback rung must be smaller")
    check(vit_top1 > effnet_top1 > mobilenet_top1, "each fallback rung must trade accuracy for cost")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    vit_params_str = fmt(vit_params_m, precision=0)
    effnet_params_str = fmt(effnet_params_m, precision=0)
    mobilenet_params_str = fmt(mobilenet_params_m, precision=1)
    vit_top1_str = fmt_percent(round(vit_top1 * 100) / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
    effnet_top1_str = fmt_percent(round(effnet_top1 * 100) / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
    mobilenet_top1_str = fmt_percent(round(mobilenet_top1 * 100) / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
```

An image classification cascade makes the trade-off concrete. The primary path might run a ViT-Large model with `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.vit_params_str` million parameters and `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.vit_top1_str` ImageNet top-1 accuracy, fall back to EfficientNet-B4 with `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.effnet_params_str` million parameters and `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.effnet_top1_str` accuracy under pressure, then fall back again to MobileNet-V3-Large with `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.mobilenet_params_str` million parameters and `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.mobilenet_top1_str` accuracy when only minimal classification remains affordable. If even that path cannot meet the SLO, the service can return cached labels, a coarse category, or "classification unavailable" rather than blocking the request indefinitely. For that ladder to be real rather than aspirational, the production system must keep multiple models deployed, route requests to the appropriate level, monitor fallback frequency, and measure the quality impact of each level.

Recommendation and ranking systems use the same pattern when a complex deep learning model falls back to a top-n popularity list, a linear ranker, or a cached response during primary serving failures. Complex models often fight for the last mile of accuracy while simple heuristics provide the bulk of the utility, so the fallback path must be monitored as a first-class quality signal rather than treated as a silent failover. Otherwise the product appears healthy while quality is silently traded for availability.

#### Feature fallback {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-feature-fallback-0730}

Feature fallback controls how much input quality the model may lose before the request must be blocked. When feature retrieval fails, validated population-level defaults or cached values can substitute for missing user or item features. The model must have been trained or evaluated with those missing-feature semantics; an average embedding or a vector from another encoder is not automatically a compatible input. Approximate features are useful only when their representation and measured prediction quality satisfy the fallback contract.

The key design step is prioritizing features by their measured contribution to prediction quality. @Tbl-feature-degradation-tiers illustrates a four-level policy in which critical features block the request, important features use defaults, useful features use cached values, and optional features can be omitted. Its quality-loss ranges are example policy budgets, not transferable properties of those feature categories; deployment requires measurements showing that each permitted fallback meets its budget.

| **Tier**      |      **Example Features**     | **Missing Action** |  **Quality Impact**  |
|:--------------|:-----------------------------:|:------------------:|:--------------------:|
| **Critical**  |        User ID, Item ID       |   Block request    |     Cannot serve     |
| **Important** | User history, Item attributes |    Use defaults    | 5--10% quality loss  |
| **Useful**    |       Real-time context       |     Use cached     |  2--5% quality loss  |
| **Optional**  |       Secondary signals       |        Omit        | $< 2\%$ quality loss |

: **Graceful Feature Degradation Tiers**: Features classified by importance to prediction quality, with the corresponding response when each tier is unavailable. Critical features block the request entirely; lower tiers allow the system to fall back to defaults, cached values, or omission with bounded quality impact. The tiers convert a binary "feature available or not" question into a four-step degradation ladder. {#tbl-feature-degradation-tiers}

When feature degradation alone is insufficient to maintain system stability under extreme load, the serving infrastructure must begin actively dropping requests.

#### Load shedding {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-load-shedding-8476}

Load shedding protects the system by sacrificing selected requests before overload spreads to every request. Random shedding is the simplest policy: drop a fraction of incoming requests and preserve enough capacity for the rest. Its weakness is that it treats all requests as equally valuable. Priority-based shedding turns quality-of-service degradation into an explicit policy by serving premium users before free users, revenue-generating requests before analytics requests, and interactive traffic before background batch work. The system is still degrading, but it is degrading according to a predeclared service contract rather than whichever queue happens to fill first.

Admission control\index{Graceful degradation!admission control} applies the same idea at system entry points. It rejects requests that would exceed capacity rather than accepting work that will degrade every request already in the system. Circuit breakers\index{Circuit breaker!serving resilience} extend the same protection to individual dependencies by failing fast when a model replica, feature store, or supporting service is unhealthy, so that one failing dependency cannot exhaust connection pools across the fleet; @sec-inference-scale-circuit-breakers-backpressure-e61c develops their states and the backpressure signals that accompany them.

#### Graceful degradation implementation {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-graceful-degradation-implementation-1aa5}

Implementation begins by turning the degradation ladder into a control loop. Tail-latency percentiles reveal delayed responses, dependency-specific error rates locate failed calls, resource utilization exposes pressure, and growing queues indicate a mismatch between arrivals and completions. These signals support entry and exit conditions for each degradation level. A trigger can justify load shedding before diagnosis is complete, but the signal alone does not establish the underlying cause.

Degradation triggers\index{Graceful degradation!triggers} define conditions that activate degradation. @Lst-degradation-triggers illustrates three common trigger conditions that progressively activate fallback mechanisms based on latency, error rate, and feature store health.

::: {#lst-degradation-triggers lst-cap="**Progressive Degradation Triggers**: Conditions that activate graceful degradation based on tail latency, error rate, and feature store health. Each trigger activates a different fallback mechanism appropriate to the detected problem."}

```{.python}
# Monitor tail latency for user-facing impact
if p99_latency > threshold:
    activate_model_fallback()  # Switch to faster, simpler model

# Track error rates to detect downstream failures
if error_rate > threshold:
    activate_circuit_breaker()  # Fail fast, prevent cascade

# Feature store slowdowns degrade recommendation quality
if feature_store_latency > threshold:
    activate_feature_fallback()  # Use cached/default features
```

:::

Degradation should increase progressively as conditions worsen rather than switch at one cliff. The system can raise the fallback percentage gradually as load increases, then require sustained improvement before traffic returns to higher-capability paths. Hysteresis prevents oscillation between primary and fallback modes when the service hovers near a threshold.

### Degradation monitoring and alerting {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-degradation-monitoring-alerting-87c2}

Because graceful degradation trades quality for availability, monitoring must make that trade visible rather than letting the system appear healthy while serving lower-fidelity results. The monitoring surface must expose how much service quality has been traded away. @Tbl-degradation-monitoring-action-map turns that surface into an action map: fallback share reveals how often model quality was reduced, default-feature share reveals input-quality loss, drop rate reveals capacity protection, and the primary-vs-fallback quality gap reveals whether the degraded path remains acceptable. Its escalation thresholds illustrate one policy; the service's permitted degradation duration and quality loss must determine the deployed thresholds.

| **Signal**                      | **Quality trade exposed**                       | **Escalation rule**                                                              | **Postincident question**                              |
|:--------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| Fallback-model request share    | Model capability reduced to preserve serving    | Sustained activation beyond 5 minutes becomes a warning.                         | Did the fallback preserve enough user value?           |
| Default-feature request share   | Input richness reduced because dependencies lag | Severe degradation affecting over 50% of requests becomes critical.              | Which feature dependency needs replication or caching? |
| Load-shed request rate          | Coverage reduced to protect the service         | Any growth after the circuit breaker opens triggers capacity investigation.      | Was admission control early enough to prevent cascade? |
| Primary-vs-fallback quality gap | Product quality lost during the incident        | Degradation beyond 1 hour escalates even when availability metrics look healthy. | Is the fallback path still a valid product experience? |

: **Degradation Monitoring Action Map**: Graceful degradation is safe only when the quality trade is observable. Each signal ties a degraded serving mode to the escalation and postincident question that prevent silent quality loss. {#tbl-degradation-monitoring-action-map}

After the event, postincident analysis should identify the root cause, evaluate fallback effectiveness, measure user and business impact, and define improvements that prevent recurrence. Implementing these fallback mechanisms safely requires deep visibility into the system's runtime state. When a complex recommendation pipeline begins degrading, operators must rapidly determine which microservice is failing, and that diagnosis depends on distributed debugging and observability.

## Distributed Debugging and Observability {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distributed-debugging-observability-1a7f}

At 2:00 AM, latency on the flagship generative API spikes from 200 ms to 5 seconds, but CPU, memory, and network metrics all look perfectly normal.
