The latency breach can justify immediate mitigation under a predefined policy; choosing a targeted repair requires locating the stalled work across hundreds of microservices. Distributed debugging and observability provide the diagnostic capability required to locate these invisible bottlenecks.

### Diagnostic challenges in distributed ML systems {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distributed-ml-systems-hard-debug-8d8a}

Distributed ML debugging is hard because the evidence needed for recovery is split across timing, state, scale, and model behavior. Distributed systems exhibit nondeterministic behavior from multiple sources. Network timing variations change execution order, thread scheduling differences alter race conditions, GPU kernel execution order varies across runs, and floating-point operation ordering changes results. A bug that manifests on one execution may not reproduce on subsequent executions. These "Heisenbugs"[^fn-heisenbug-ml-concurrency] appear to disappear when observed.

[^fn-heisenbug-ml-concurrency]: **Heisenbug**\index{Heisenbug!distributed debugging}: A pun on Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, popularized in @gray1986computers's analysis of why production systems fail. Instrumentation perturbs timing, so observing the bug changes it. In distributed ML training, inserting gradient logging alters collective timing and can mask the very race that caused the silent corruption.

Partial failures turn that nondeterminism into a recovery problem. A single machine can also suffer partial failures, but distribution adds independently progressing workers and communication paths: one component can stop while others continue, leaving peers uncertain whether it has failed or become unreachable. Scale then removes manual inspection as a viable debugging method: with thousands of components, automated tools must filter massive telemetry streams and identify the few signals that explain the incident. ML systems add model behavior to the same diagnostic problem because silent accuracy degradation produces wrong results without errors, numerical issues like NaN and infinity propagate through computation, data-dependent bugs manifest only for specific inputs, and learning causes expected behavior changes that can resemble bugs.

### Observability pillars {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-observability-pillars-0e45}

Observability supports both immediate mitigation and investigation of the cause. Suppose a recommendation service suddenly violates its latency SLO while the model replicas still report healthy GPU utilization. Metrics establish the timing and scope of the symptom, traces show which service span consumes the request budget, and logs record events inside that service. @Fig-observability-three-pillars connects these streams to operational decisions. A single signal can justify an action, such as shedding load when a queue exceeds its budget. Joining request and trace context with model versions, deployment tags, and time windows strengthens the diagnosis when several causes could explain the same symptom. Correlated evidence narrows those possibilities; it does not by itself prove the physical or software cause.

::: {#fig-observability-three-pillars fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The three pillars of observability**: Diagnosis of fleet failures requires correlating three signal types. Metrics reveal *when* and *where* a problem occurs (for example, GPU utilization drops). Logs provide the *what* through event context (for example, an out-of-memory exception). Traces provide the *why* by linking events across the distributed lifecycle (for example, identifying the request that triggered the memory spike). The signals become actionable only once they are joined on shared identifiers, which is what lets an operator choose a recovery action." fig-alt="Three boxes labeled metrics, logs, and traces, each with its role and an example: GPU utilization drops, an out-of-memory exception, and the request behind the spike. Arrows lead from all three into a box reading correlate on shared identifiers, listing request, trace, model version, feature version, and deployment, which leads to a recovery action box: shed load, restart replica, roll back, or degrade gracefully."}
![](images/svg/observability-three-pillars.svg)

:::

Metrics are the first evidence because they compress fleet behavior into time series that can trigger action. In ML fleets, useful metrics span infrastructure signals such as CPU and GPU utilization, memory allocation, network bandwidth, and storage I/O; application signals such as request rate, latency percentiles, error counts, queue depths, and cache hit rates; and ML-specific signals such as inference latency by model, batch utilization, feature retrieval latency, feature freshness, and prediction distributions for drift detection. A metric stream becomes fault-tolerance infrastructure only when an alert maps to a recovery decision. High p99 latency may trigger load shedding, a falling cache hit rate may trigger fallback features, and a sudden prediction-distribution shift may block a rollout before it corrupts user-facing decisions.

Logs provide the event context that a metric intentionally discards. Structured logging\index{Structured logging!JSON format} uses formats such as JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) with consistent fields, so incident tooling can search by service, request, model version, GPU, feature store, or trace identifier. @Lst-structured-log-entry shows a GPU memory allocation failure that records both the local failure context and the trace identifiers needed to connect the event to distributed metrics and spans.

::: {#lst-structured-log-entry lst-cap="**Structured JSON Log Entry**: A structured log entry for a GPU memory allocation failure, including trace and span identifiers for correlation with distributed traces and resource metrics for diagnosis."}

```{.json}
{
  "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:23:45.123Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "inference-server",
  "trace_id": "abc123",
  "span_id": "def456",
  "message": "GPU memory allocation failed",
  "gpu_id": 3,
  "requested_bytes": 4294967296,
  "available_bytes": 2147483648
}
```

:::

For fault tolerance, the important logging property is consistent correlation rather than the particular backend. Log levels should map incidents to escalation consistently across components, but the recovery system depends more on whether operators can query events by the same request, trace, model version, feature version, and deployment identifiers that appear in metrics and spans. Log aggregation is therefore useful because it preserves the join between local failure context and fleet-wide symptoms.

Traces show where latency or failure propagated across distributed components. A trace\index{Distributed tracing!trace} is the end-to-end journey of a request, a span\index{Distributed tracing!span} is one operation within that journey, and context propagation\index{Distributed tracing!context propagation} carries the trace identity across service boundaries. A trace through an ML inference pipeline illustrates how these spans compose:

```text
Trace: user-request-12345
|-- Span: api-gateway (5 ms)
|   `-- Span: auth-service (2 ms)
|-- Span: feature-service (15 ms)
|   |-- Span: user-feature-lookup (8 ms)
|   `-- Span: item-feature-lookup (12 ms)
|-- Span: inference-service (45 ms)
|   |-- Span: preprocessing (3 ms)
|   |-- Span: model-inference (40 ms)
|   `-- Span: postprocessing (2 ms)
`-- Span: response-formatting (1 ms)
Total: 66 ms
```

OpenTelemetry provides a standard API for distributed tracing\index{Distributed tracing!observability}. Backend systems like Jaeger, Zipkin, or cloud tracing services store and visualize traces. The durable requirement is not the particular tracing backend; it is preserving enough context to answer whether the fault lives in request routing, feature retrieval, model execution, postprocessing, or a dependency outside the model service.

### ML-specific debugging {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-mlspecific-debugging-27d5}

Operational signals are not enough when a computation is numerically valid but wrong for the model. ML systems also require specialized debugging capabilities.

#### Numerical debugging {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-numerical-debugging-ee2a}

Numerical debugging targets failures where tensors remain valid objects but contain invalid values. NaN detection\index{Numerical debugging!NaN detection}[^fn-nan-gradient-propagation] exposes values that can propagate through later arithmetic without a process crash. @Lst-nan-detection shows a minimal diagnostic check; the caller must act on the result to prevent publication of the affected output.

[^fn-nan-gradient-propagation]: **NaN propagation**\index{NaN propagation!training corruption}: Many IEEE 754 arithmetic operations propagate a NaN operand, so an invalid gradient can contaminate dependent updates without stopping the process. The affected scope depends on the computation's data dependencies. Zero divided by zero and the logarithm of a negative real value produce NaNs; division of a nonzero finite value by zero or floating-point overflow can instead produce infinity, which may cause a later invalid operation. Checking only for a process crash therefore misses numerical failures.

::: {#lst-nan-detection lst-cap="**NaN Detection**: This check flags NaN output for diagnosis. The caller must block publication or choose a fallback; a logged request identifier refers to an input retained by the application for replay."}

```{.python}
# Check tensor for NaN values
# (propagate from any corrupted computation)
if torch.isnan(output).any():
    log.error("NaN detected in output", request_id=request_id)
    # Caller must retain a replayable input reference and block or replace this output
```

:::

During training, gradient statistics make numerical faults visible before they corrupt the whole run. Gradient norm detects explosion or vanishing, gradient distribution detects anomalies, and layer-wise gradients identify problematic layers.

Mixed-precision training[^fn-mixedprecision-fault-tolerance] can introduce numerical issues. A dynamic loss scaler reduces its scale after detecting nonfinite gradients, indicating overflow or another invalid operation rather than proving underflow. Gradient magnitudes, skipped updates, and comparison with a higher-precision replay help distinguish range problems from other causes; ordinary FP16 rounding differences are not themselves faults.

[^fn-mixedprecision-fault-tolerance]: **Mixed-precision numerical issues**\index{Mixed-precision training!numerical issues}\index{Mixed-precision training!numerical fault tolerance}: FP16's positive finite range starts near $6 \times 10^{-8}$ with subnormals and ends at 65,504; FP32's positive normal range spans approximately $1.2 \times 10^{-38}$ to $3.4 \times 10^{38}$, with subnormals below it. Scaling loss before backpropagation and unscaling gradients afterward reduces underflow risk, while dynamic scaling can skip nonfinite updates and lower the scale. BF16 reduces range pressure relative to FP16 at the cost of lower significand precision, without eliminating overflow or invalid operations.

#### Data debugging and validation {#sec-fault-tolerance-data-debugging-validation}

Data bugs surface as valid-looking but wrong inputs, so debugging must verify semantic correctness at each pipeline boundary in addition to numerical validity. Validation checks expected format, shape, value ranges, required fields, and encoding before data reaches the model, catching malformed examples while the failure is still local to the input path.

Once the input passes those static checks, the system needs evidence about behavior over time. Distribution monitors track feature drift, null-rate changes, and outliers as they emerge, while transformation instrumentation logs intermediate shapes and statistics so teams can compare each stage against known-good data. Together, these signals separate a corrupted input path from a numerical failure inside the model.

#### Straggler detection and analysis {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-straggler-detection-analysis-6925}

Straggler diagnosis asks which component is slow enough to become a failure-equivalent bottleneck. A slow serving replica delays requests routed to it and can trigger retries under load; its effect on the service's tail percentile depends on its traffic share and the routing policy. A request that waits for several required parallel branches is instead bounded by the last required completion. Operation-level timing\index{Straggler!timing instrumentation} instrumentation measures time for each operation, enabling latency attribution across pipeline stages. @Lst-timing-instrumentation wraps operations in context managers that emit per-span timing metrics, making it straightforward to compare performance across replicas.

::: {#lst-timing-instrumentation lst-cap="**Operation-Level Timing**: Context manager instrumentation attributes latency to individual pipeline stages, enabling straggler detection by comparing the same span across replicas."}

```{.python}
# Wrap operations in timing context managers for latency attribution
with timer("feature_lookup"):
    features = feature_store.lookup(
        ids
    )  # Often the latency bottleneck
with timer("model_inference"):
    predictions = model(features)  # Host submission time for asynchronous GPU work
```

:::

For asynchronous GPU execution, the host span above measures submission time, not completed device work. Use device events around the relevant stream and wait for event completion before reporting GPU elapsed time. Compare like-for-like component timing across replicas using percentile analysis. p50 shows typical performance, while p99 shows tail latency. Comparing p99 across replicas identifies workers whose slow path has become a fleet-wide bottleneck.

The diagnosis must then separate the root causes that produce the same slow-worker symptom. Hardware issues include thermal throttling and memory errors, data skew means some inputs are slower to process, resource contention occurs when other processes consume resources, and network issues create slow connections to data stores.

### Common failure patterns {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-common-failure-patterns-3306}

Combining these observability streams helps detect recurring optimization pathologies. @Fig-training-failure-signatures contrasts an idealized healthy loss trend with gradient explosion, premature plateaus, and NaN divergence. Real stochastic training need not decrease monotonically, so a transient rise alone does not establish failure. The useful diagnostic compares the observed change with expected variation and corroborating signals.

#### Training failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-training-failures-bc3a}

A training-loss signature is useful because it narrows the hypotheses that recovery must test. The trajectories in @fig-training-failure-signatures illustrate symptoms, including nonfinite values that need not crash the process. @Tbl-training-failure-response-map pairs spike, plateau, and divergence patterns, plus the silent hang a loss curve cannot show, with a candidate cause and a first response. That pairing guides investigation without treating the curve as a unique diagnosis.

::: {#fig-training-failure-signatures fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Training failure signatures**: Common patterns of model loss over time that indicate underlying system or algorithmic failures. (A) Normal training. (B) Gradient explosion. (C) Loss plateau. (D) NaN divergence. Identifying these signatures automatically is essential for rapid recovery in autonomous training pipelines." fig-alt="Plot showing four loss curves: (A) Normal Training with smooth descent, (B) Gradient Explosion with a sudden spike, (C) Loss Plateau where learning stalls, and (D) NaN Divergence with erratic oscillation collapsing to NaN."}
```{python}
#| echo: false
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style
import numpy as np

book_style.set_book_style()
COLORS = book_style.COLORS

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(8.6, 6.4))

steps = np.linspace(0, 100, 200)
np.random.seed(42)

# PANEL A: Normal Training
ax = axes[0, 0]
noise = np.random.normal(0, 0.02, len(steps))
loss_a = 2.4 * np.exp(-0.035 * steps) + 0.35 + noise
ax.plot(steps, loss_a, color=COLORS['GreenLine'], linewidth=2.0)
ax.set_title('(A) NORMAL TRAINING\nSmooth monotonic descent with batch variance', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['GreenLine'], pad=6)

ax.annotate(
    'Start',
    xy=(steps[0], loss_a[0]),
    xytext=(16, 2.7),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS['GreenLine'], lw=1.1),
    fontsize=7.2,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['GreenLine'],
)
ax.annotate(
    'Converged',
    xy=(steps[-1], loss_a[-1]),
    xytext=(68, 0.9),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS['GreenLine'], lw=1.1),
    fontsize=7.2,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['GreenLine'],
)

ax.text(
    50,
    0.15,
    'Signature: stable descent, bounded gradient variance',
    ha='center',
    va='center',
    fontsize=7.0,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['GreenLine'],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', fc=COLORS['GreenL'], ec=COLORS['GreenLine'], lw=0.8),
)

ax.set_xlim(-2, 102)
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 3.1)
ax.set_ylabel('Loss', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.set_xlabel('Steps', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', color=COLORS['grid'], linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.6)

# PANEL B: Gradient Explosion
ax = axes[0, 1]
loss_b = 2.4 * np.exp(-0.035 * steps) + 0.35 + np.random.normal(0, 0.02, len(steps))
spike_idx = 90
loss_b[spike_idx : spike_idx + 15] += np.linspace(0, 1.7, 15)
loss_b[spike_idx + 15 : spike_idx + 35] = np.linspace(loss_b[spike_idx + 14], 1.1, 20)
ax.plot(steps, loss_b, color=COLORS['RedLine'], linewidth=2.0)
ax.set_title(
    '(B) GRADIENT EXPLOSION\nSudden catastrophic spike exceeding loss bounds', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['RedLine'], pad=6
)

spike_step = steps[spike_idx + 14]
spike_val = loss_b[spike_idx + 14]
ax.annotate(
    'Spike',
    xy=(spike_step, spike_val),
    xytext=(spike_step - 18, 2.7),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS['RedLine'], lw=1.1),
    fontsize=7.2,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
)

ax.text(
    50,
    0.15,
    r'Signature: loss spike, gradient norm $\geq 100\times$ baseline',
    ha='center',
    va='center',
    fontsize=7.0,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', fc=COLORS['RedL'], ec=COLORS['RedLine'], lw=0.8),
)

ax.set_xlim(-2, 102)
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 3.1)
ax.set_ylabel('Loss', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.set_xlabel('Steps', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', color=COLORS['grid'], linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.6)

# PANEL C: Loss Plateau
ax = axes[1, 0]
loss_c = np.copy(loss_a)
plateau_idx = 40
loss_c[plateau_idx:] = loss_c[plateau_idx] + np.random.normal(0, 0.015, len(steps) - plateau_idx)
ax.plot(steps, loss_c, color=COLORS['OrangeLine'], linewidth=2.0)
ax.set_title(
    '(C) LOSS PLATEAU\nLearning stalls prematurely; zero meaningful descent', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['OrangeLine'], pad=6
)

ax.annotate(
    'Plateau Region',
    xy=(70, loss_c[plateau_idx]),
    xytext=(70, 2.2),
    ha='center',
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS['OrangeLine'], lw=1.1),
    fontsize=7.2,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['OrangeLine'],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.25', fc=COLORS['OrangeL'], ec=COLORS['OrangeLine'], lw=0.8),
)

ax.text(
    50,
    0.15,
    'Signature: vanishing gradient norm, optimizer stagnation',
    ha='center',
    va='center',
    fontsize=7.0,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['OrangeLine'],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', fc=COLORS['OrangeL'], ec=COLORS['OrangeLine'], lw=0.8),
)

ax.set_xlim(-2, 102)
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 3.1)
ax.set_ylabel('Loss', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.set_xlabel('Steps', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', color=COLORS['grid'], linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.6)

# PANEL D: NaN Divergence
ax = axes[1, 1]
nan_steps = steps[:140]
osc = np.sin(nan_steps * 0.4) * np.exp(0.022 * nan_steps) * 0.22
loss_d = 1.9 * np.exp(-0.02 * nan_steps) + 0.65 + osc
loss_d = np.clip(loss_d, 0.50, 2.95)
loss_d[-1] = 2.85
ax.plot(nan_steps, loss_d, color=COLORS['RedLine'], linewidth=2.0)
ax.set_title(
    '(D) NAN DIVERGENCE\nErratic numerical oscillation collapsing to Inf / NaN', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['RedLine'], pad=6
)

# NaN Halt box at crash point
ax.scatter([nan_steps[-1]], [loss_d[-1]], color=COLORS['RedLine'], edgecolor='white', linewidth=1.5, s=60, zorder=6)
ax.text(
    82,
    2.1,
    'NaN Halt\n(Crash)',
    ha='center',
    va='center',
    fontsize=7.5,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.35', fc=COLORS['RedL'], ec=COLORS['RedLine'], lw=1.0),
)
ax.annotate('', xy=(nan_steps[-1], loss_d[-1]), xytext=(82, 2.3), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS['RedLine'], lw=1.1))

ax.text(
    50,
    0.15,
    'Signature: numerical overflow, IEEE-754 exception trap',
    ha='center',
    va='center',
    fontsize=7.0,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', fc=COLORS['RedL'], ec=COLORS['RedLine'], lw=0.8),
)

ax.set_xlim(-2, 102)
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 3.1)
ax.set_ylabel('Loss', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.set_xlabel('Steps', fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', color=COLORS['grid'], linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.6)

plt.tight_layout()
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.36, wspace=0.28)
plt.show()
plt.close()
```
:::

| **Signature**              | **Likely Interpretation**                                                         | **Recovery Response**                                                                                |
|:---------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Spike followed by recovery | Transient input or numerical anomaly; the curve alone does not identify the cause | Preserve the suspect batch and step evidence, then replay before deciding whether to continue.       |
| Spike followed by plateau  | Optimizer instability, corrupted state, or a persistent data-path defect          | Pause, replay from a known-good checkpoint, and compare input, optimizer, and worker evidence.       |
| Gradual divergence         | Data drift, numerical instability, corrupted state, or worker desynchronization   | Compare per-rank telemetry and evaluation evidence; isolate hardware only when replay implicates it. |
| Hang without an error      | Collective deadlock or crashed worker blocking synchronization                    | Use timeout detection and restart or reconstruct the worker group.                                   |

: **Training Failure Response Map**: Training-loss curves are operational evidence only when they lead to different recovery actions. The response map ties each signature to the failure class most likely to explain it and to the first action operators should take. {#tbl-training-failure-response-map}

These diagnostic responses protect long-running batch workloads, but identifying failures in real-time user-facing systems demands an entirely different latency budget.

#### Serving failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-serving-failures-3322}

Serving failures require the same symptom-to-action mapping under much tighter latency constraints. @Tbl-serving-failure-response-map separates the common symptoms by what they reveal and what the serving system must do first.

| **Symptom**                | **Likely Interpretation**                                                               | **Immediate Response**                                                                         |
|:---------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Latency spikes             | Resource contention, garbage collection, cold caches, or model reloads                  | Check placement and capacity; repeated spikes usually mean the problem is no longer transient. |
| Rising error rates         | Dependency failure, data-format change, or model bug                                    | Investigate immediately because errors compound across dependent services.                     |
| Silent quality degradation | Model drift, feature degradation, or data-pipeline fault                                | Use quality monitoring beyond standard operational metrics.                                    |
| Cascade failure            | Timeout exhaustion, resource depletion, or error propagation from one failing component | Trip circuit breakers and preserve isolation boundaries before the failure spreads.            |

: **Serving Failure Response Map**: Serving incidents must be classified quickly because every diagnosis competes with a user-facing latency budget. The table ties each symptom to the first operational response rather than treating all serving failures as generic errors. {#tbl-serving-failure-response-map}

Cascade failures are particularly insidious because the root cause is obscured by the symptoms it generates. A concrete diagnosis shows how the three observability pillars work together to trace a cascade back to its origin.

::: {#exmp-fault-tolerance-diagnosing-cascade-failure .callout-example title="Diagnosing a cascade failure"}

**Scenario**: A recommendation system experiences sudden latency spikes.

**Diagnosis**: The three observability pillars narrow the failure path. Metrics\index{Metric!observability} reveal the symptom: p99 latency jumped from 45 ms to 800 ms at 14:32, with error rate increasing from 0.1 percent to 15 percent. Traces\index{Trace!observability} locate the delay in the feature-service span, which consumes 700 ms instead of the normal 12 ms, while model inference remains at 40 ms. Logs\index{Log!observability} show repeated connection timeouts to the user embedding cache at 14:31, followed by requests bypassing the cache and reaching the embedding database directly. That evidence identifies cache unavailability and increased downstream demand; it does not yet distinguish a failed cache process from a network or resource problem.

**Systems lesson**: Cache unavailability can transfer enough demand to overwhelm the embedding database. A circuit breaker and a validated default-embedding path can limit that cascade while diagnosis continues. The fallback must also respect the quality budget and avoid sending the rejected demand to another saturated dependency.

:::

Correlating metrics, logs, and traces allows operators to isolate failures and trigger automated remediations before an entire cluster is compromised. How these observability pipelines and fault tolerance strategies operate in practice, however, is best understood through real deployments. Production clusters running frontier models and global services illustrate how organizations translate theoretical reliability models into operational systems.

## Case Studies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-case-studies-927f}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: opt175b-case-study
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPT-175B CASE STUDY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Case-studies opener and
# │          @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-largescale-llm-training-fault-tolerance-f4aa.
# │
# │ Goal: Pin the OPT-175B run's reported cluster size, restart counts, host
# │       churn, and sustained throughput to Literature.TrainingRuns.
# │ Show: 992 GPUs; at least 35 manual and ~70 automatic restarts; >100 hosts;
# │       147 TFLOP/s per A100, about 47 percent of A100 dense FP16 peak.
# │ How:  Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175B*; fraction = 147 / A100 peak_flops.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware, Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_percent

class Opt175BCaseStudy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    gpus = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BGpus)
    manual_restarts = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BManualRestarts)
    auto_restarts = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BAutomaticRestarts)
    hosts_cycled = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BHostsCycled)
    tflops_per_gpu = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BTflopsPerGpu)
    a100_peak_tflops = Hardware.Cloud.A100.compute.peak_flops.to(TFLOPs / second).magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    peak_fraction = tflops_per_gpu / a100_peak_tflops

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(0.45 < peak_fraction < 0.50, "prose says 'near 50 percent of FP16 peak'")
    check(manual_restarts < auto_restarts, "paper: more automatic than manual restarts")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    gpus_str = fmt(gpus, precision=0)
    manual_restarts_str = fmt(manual_restarts, precision=0)
    auto_restarts_str = fmt(auto_restarts, precision=0)
    hosts_cycled_str = fmt(hosts_cycled, precision=0)
    tflops_per_gpu_str = fmt(tflops_per_gpu, precision=0)
    peak_fraction_str = fmt_percent(round(peak_fraction * 100) / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
```

Published production systems make the chapter's scale lesson concrete, with failure detection, state preservation, and observability reappearing as checkpoint tax, topology reconfiguration, chaos testing, and elastic recovery. Public operational reports from Meta, Google, Netflix, and Microsoft reveal how organizations navigate these trade-offs when operating at fleet scale. Treat the operational numbers as reported magnitudes that reveal the design pressure, not as universal constants. Meta's Open Pre-trained Transformer (OPT-175B) training run on a `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.gpus_str`-GPU cluster provides the first example, a run that had to absorb dozens of hardware failures without aborting.

### Large-scale LLM training at Meta {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-largescale-llm-training-fault-tolerance-f4aa}

The training of the Open Pre-trained Transformer (OPT-175B) at Meta provides a documented study of failure during a large deep-learning job [@zhang2022opt]. Over two months on `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.gpus_str` NVIDIA A100 GPUs, the team reported at least `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.manual_restarts_str` manual restarts and estimated `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.auto_restarts_str` or more automatic restarts due to hardware failures, alongside the cycling of more than `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.hosts_cycled_str` hosts [@zhang2022opt; @opt2022logbook]. Numerical instability created a separate recovery problem. These counts establish repeated interruption, but cycling hosts and restarting jobs are different events; their totals do not directly measure one common MTBF. The recovery design had to preserve progress while distinguishing failed execution resources from suspect optimization state.

During the OPT run, the team monitored progress through train-log freshness checks. The public logbook records a 15-minute modified-file threshold, later relaxed to one hour, as part of restart monitoring [@opt2022logbook]. For a hang that raised no error, this threshold contributed to $T_{\text{detect}}$; polling and response delays could extend the wait before restart. The logbook illustrates the trade-off of @eq-timeout-calculation in operational form, since relaxing the threshold reduced sensitivity to delayed logs while allowing longer idle windows.

Recovery procedures also had to account for loss spikes associated with numerical instability. Unlike a fail-stop event, this symptom made recent model state suspect without identifying a failed device. The team combined rollback to an earlier checkpoint with a lower learning rate to recover from divergence [@opt2022logbook]. The paper separately reports approximately `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.tflops_per_gpu_str` TFLOP/s per A100 (about `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.peak_fraction_str` of dense FP16 peak) [@zhang2022opt]; that execution-rate metric alone does not establish end-to-end useful throughput after interruptions and replay. The enduring lesson is the distinction between recovery paths. A failed device calls for replacement and restoration of valid state, while numerical divergence can require an older checkpoint and a changed optimization policy. Retaining checkpoint history makes that second path possible.

### Google TPU pod resilience {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-google-tpu-pod-resilience}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tpuv4-pod-cubes
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TPUv4 POD CUBES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-google-tpu-pod-resilience.
# │
# │ Goal: Derive the pod's cube count from the registry pod size.
# │ Show: 4,096 chips as 64 cubes of 64 chips; one chip = 1/4096 of capacity.
# │ How:  Systems.Pods.TPUv4_4096.chips / cube size (4x4x4, architectural constant).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_math

class TpuV4PodCubes:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    pod_chips = Systems.Pods.TPUv4_4096.chips
    cube_chips = 4 * 4 * 4  # 4x4x4 cube, the OCS-switched building block [@zu2024tpuv4]

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    n_cubes = pod_chips // cube_chips

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(n_cubes * cube_chips == pod_chips, "pod must be a whole number of cubes")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    pod_chips_str = fmt(pod_chips, precision=0)
    n_cubes_str = fmt(n_cubes, precision=0)
    cube_chips_str = fmt(cube_chips, precision=0)
    chip_share_math = fmt_math(rf"1/{pod_chips}")
```

Google's TPUv4 supercomputer combines configurable topology with recovery software. A pod contains `{python} TpuV4PodCubes.pod_chips_str` chips organized as `{python} TpuV4PodCubes.n_cubes_str` cubes of `{python} TpuV4PodCubes.cube_chips_str` chips, each arranged in a $4{\times}4{\times}4$ 3D mesh [@zu2024tpuv4]. Losing one chip removes `{python} TpuV4PodCubes.chip_share_math`th of pod capacity, but can interrupt an entire job that requires that participant. The recovery unit therefore exceeds the failed device.

The OCS fabric assembles healthy cubes into job-sized slices. Software components including `libtpunet` and `healthd` support topology setup and health monitoring. Machine outages can require reallocation to spare cubes; supported OCS outage patterns instead admit fault-tolerant routes around unavailable links. Replacement and routing therefore address different fault classes.

The study reports 99.98 percent system availability, with hardware outages affecting approximately 1 percent of training jobs [@zu2024tpuv4]. Daily failure rates were 0.08 percent of TPU machines, 0.005 percent of ICI cables, and 0.04 percent of OCS units. These are deployment measurements, not guarantees of uninterrupted job throughput. The architectural lesson is to match each failure boundary to a feasible replacement or routing mechanism.

### Netflix chaos engineering for serving dependencies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-netflix-chaos-engineering}

While training resilience focuses on long-running batch jobs, Netflix's published work on Chaos Engineering\index{Chaos engineering!serving resilience} [@basiri2016] provides the serving-side contrast. The premise is simple but operationally demanding. Because production systems have many interacting dependencies, teams should validate steady-state behavior by deliberately injecting failures instead of waiting for real incidents to discover whether fallbacks work.

For ML serving, the same discipline applies to feature stores, model-serving dependencies, caches, and fallback paths. A model endpoint can be healthy while a feature service is slow, stale, or unavailable; if the system lacks a tested fallback, a local dependency problem can become user-visible latency or degraded recommendations. Chaos tests make those assumptions executable by injecting latency, terminating dependencies, or forcing fallback paths in controlled conditions.

The recovery procedure for these injected faults centers on fallback hierarchies. If the primary deep learning model fails or times out, the serving system can switch to a lighter model, cached response, or simple popularity-based default. The systems lesson is that resilience in ML serving is not a static property but a continuous practice of active verification. A fallback path that is never exercised is documentation, not fault tolerance.

### Microsoft DeepSpeed fault tolerance {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-deepspeed-fault-tolerance}

Microsoft's DeepSpeed\index{DeepSpeed!checkpointing fault tolerance} illustrates the boundary between a training framework and the recovery control plane. Its ZeRO-based training and checkpointing primitives partition large-model state across workers [@rasley2020; @deepspeedCheckpointingDocs; @rajbhandari2020]. Losing a worker can strand its shard, so framework support must be paired with durable checkpoints and an orchestrator that restores a valid worker group.

This checkpoint-centered path does not imply in-memory repair\index{Checkpointing!in-memory replication}. Universal Checkpointing supports selected parallelism and topology changes [@deepspeedUniversalCheckpointingDocs], but the launcher chooses the replacement allocation and the training script preserves data coverage, batch size, and optimizer invariants. The end-to-end guarantee belongs to that combination, rather than to the framework alone.

Across these production case studies, three architectural patterns recur. First, detection speed\index{Fault tolerance!detection speed} belongs in the recovery budget. Meta's log-freshness threshold and Google's health monitors determine when recovery can begin, while Netflix's chaos experiments test detection and fallback for selected dependency failures. Checkpoint age and replication lag separately govern recoverable state. Second, the atomic unit of failure\index{Failure domain!atomic unit of failure} shapes the architecture. Google combines cube replacement with fault-tolerant routing, DeepSpeed-based jobs restore parameter shards from durable checkpoints, and Netflix validates service-dependency fallbacks. Third, fault tolerance is a spectrum\index{Fault tolerance!spectrum} rather than a switch. Exact state recovery trades normal-operation overhead against lost work and recovery time; graceful degradation additionally trades service capability against continued availability. Those distinct trade-offs help identify the misconceptions that follow.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-fallacies-pitfalls-74b8}

An infrastructure team might spend weeks hardening their storage layer against disk failures, only to have their entire training run destroyed by a subtle software bug in their PyTorch distributed backend. Fault tolerance for distributed ML systems involves counterintuitive mathematics and subtle trade-offs where conventional data center wisdom often fails.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Hardware failures are the main concern.*

This intuition comes from traditional systems where disk failures, power outages, and network partitions dominate. In ML systems, hardware failures are only one part of a broader incident mix.

Long-lived, stateful ML jobs expose failure paths that hardware redundancy cannot cover. A malformed checkpoint path can make recovery impossible, a mismatched collective library can hang all ranks, an undersized shared-memory limit can crash data loaders, and a stale feature schema can silently corrupt training. Their relative frequency depends on the deployment, but even an infrequent software or configuration fault can destroy the same multi-day job that hardware redundancy was meant to protect.

Investing heavily in hardware redundancy while neglecting software robustness (input validation, gradual rollouts, configuration management) leaves many important failure modes unaddressed. The most reliable ML systems treat software bugs as inevitable and design defensively.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Setting checkpoint interval by intuition.*

Organizations commonly set checkpoint intervals based on "feels right": "every hour seems reasonable" or "every 1,000 steps." The Young-Daly formula reveals these intuitions are often wrong. For the 1,000-GPU cluster of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling, whose GPU-only MTBF is 50 hours, with a checkpoint write time of 5 minutes:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: young-daly-intuition-fallacy
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ YOUNG-DALY INTUITION FALLACY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-fallacies-pitfalls-74b8
# │          ("Setting checkpoint interval by intuition") — the display equation
# │          and the slower-storage follow-up sentence.
# │
# │ Goal: Reproduce the two Young-Daly optimal intervals from a hypothetical
# │       1,000-GPU cluster at the chapter's own MTBF so the "intuition is
# │ Show: tau_opt = sqrt(2 * T_write * MTBF) for a 5-minute and a 15-minute write.
# │ How:  Work in minutes; tau = sqrt(2 * write_min * mtbf_min); round to whole
# │       minutes for display.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.core.units import minute
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_display_math, fmt_int, fmt_time

class YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    # The 1,000-GPU row of the chapter's cluster-MTBF table, plus two write times.
    cluster_gpus = ClusterMtbfScaling.sizes[3]  # the 1,000-GPU row of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling (scenario sweep)
    mtbf_min = round(float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours) / cluster_gpus * 60)  # cluster MTBF, minutes
    write_fast_min = 5  # checkpoint write time, fast storage
    write_slow_min = 15  # checkpoint write time, slower storage / larger model

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    arg_fast = 2 * write_fast_min * mtbf_min
    tau_fast_min = math.sqrt(arg_fast)
    tau_slow_min = math.sqrt(2 * write_slow_min * mtbf_min)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(165 < tau_fast_min < 180, "5-minute write at 50 h MTBF should give a ~173-minute interval")
    check(tau_slow_min > tau_fast_min, "slower storage must lengthen the optimal interval")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    tau_opt_fast_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"T^\ast_{{\text{{ckpt}}}} = \sqrt{{2 \times {write_fast_min} \times {mtbf_min}}} = "
        rf"\sqrt{{{arg_fast}}} \approx {fmt_int(round(tau_fast_min))} \text{{ minutes}}"
    )
    tau_opt_slow_min_str = fmt_time(round(tau_slow_min) * minute, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
```

`{python} YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy.tau_opt_fast_eq_math`

The intuitive "every hour" checkpoints nearly three times more often than the expected-waste optimum. It reduces potential lost work, but the added write overhead outweighs that benefit under this model. A tighter RPO can still justify the shorter interval. If checkpoint time increases to 15 minutes (larger model, slower storage), the optimal interval stretches to `{python} YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy.tau_opt_slow_min_str`, further still from the "every 15 minutes" that some teams adopt to "stay safe." The decision must balance expected waste with the recovery contract rather than treat either interval as universally correct.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *If each GPU is 99.99 percent reliable, a 10,000-GPU cluster is also 99.99 percent reliable.*

Reliability does not compose by averaging; it compounds by multiplication. For $N$ serial components each with availability $A$, and assuming their failures are independent, the aggregate availability is $A^N$. The 9s-of-reliability calculation (notebook \ref{nbk-fault-tolerance-9s-reliability}) applied that rule to `{python} NinesReliability.n_gpus_str` GPUs at `{python} NinesReliability.availability_str` availability and found every GPU simultaneously up only `{python} NinesReliability.cluster_pct_str` of the time, so the cluster spends most of its life with at least one device down. Individual component reliability is necessary but nowhere near sufficient at fleet scale. System-level fault tolerance (checkpointing, elastic recovery, redundancy across failure domains) must be designed explicitly, not assumed to emerge from per-component MTTF.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Using MTBF calculations as if failures were independent.*

The reliability equation $\MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}} = \MeanTimeToFailure_{\text{component}}/N$ assumes component failures are statistically independent. In production, however, failures correlate across common physical and operational dependencies. A shared power domain\index{Correlated failure!shared power domain} can fail an entire rack when an uninterruptible power supply faults, a shared top-of-rack switch\index{Correlated failure!shared switch} isolates all attached accelerators, shared software\index{Correlated failure!shared software} bugs triggered by specific inputs crash all replicas simultaneously, and cooling failures induce clustered thermal throttling\index{Correlated failure!thermal correlation} across adjacent chassis.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: correlated-failure-pitfall
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CORRELATED FAILURE PITFALL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Pitfall "Using MTBF calculations as if failures were independent."
# │
# │ Goal: Show how a correlated hazard 10x the independent rate collapses MTBF.
# │ Show: 1,000 GPUs x 50,000-hour MTBF -> 50 h; adding a 10x hazard -> ~5 h.
# │ How:  MTBF = MTTF / N; combined rate = (1 + 10) x independent rate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_time

class CorrelatedFailurePitfall:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    cluster_gpus = ClusterMtbfScaling.sizes[3]  # the 1,000-GPU row of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling (scenario sweep)
    hazard_multiple = 10  # scenario assumption: correlated hazard 10x the independent rate

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    independent_mtbf_h = gpu_mttf_h / cluster_gpus
    effective_mtbf_h = 1 / ((1 + hazard_multiple) / independent_mtbf_h)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(4.0 < effective_mtbf_h < 5.0, "prose says the effective incident MTBF drops to 'about 5 hours'")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    cluster_gpus_str = fmt(cluster_gpus, precision=0)
    gpu_mttf_attr_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word", attributive=True)
    independent_mtbf_str = fmt_time(independent_mtbf_h, "hour", precision=0, style="word")
    effective_mtbf_str = fmt_time(round(effective_mtbf_h), "hour", precision=0, style="word")
```

Correlated failures change two quantities that the simple MTBF equation hides: incident frequency and blast radius. A cluster with `{python} CorrelatedFailurePitfall.cluster_gpus_str` independent GPUs each with `{python} CorrelatedFailurePitfall.gpu_mttf_attr_str` MTBF has a first-GPU-failure MTBF of `{python} CorrelatedFailurePitfall.independent_mtbf_str`. If a shared power, cooling, or software hazard adds an incident rate 10 times larger than that independent first-failure rate, the effective incident MTBF drops to about `{python} CorrelatedFailurePitfall.effective_mtbf_str`. Separately, a correlated incident may take out 10 GPUs at once, increasing recovery cost even if the independent GPU failure rate itself has not changed. Reliability engineering must identify and mitigate correlation through diversity: different power feeds, different network paths, different software versions in canary deployments.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Component MTTF values predict individual failure timing.*

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Fallacy — component MTTF values predict individual failure timing.
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_math, fmt_time

class FleetReliabilityFallacyRates:
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    fleet_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    fleet_rate_per_h = fleet_gpus / gpu_mttf_h
    hours_between = 1 / fleet_rate_per_h

    check(abs(hours_between * fleet_rate_per_h - 1) < 1e-9, "interval must be reciprocal of fleet rate")

    _fleet_tex = fmt(fleet_gpus, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _mttf_tex = fmt(gpu_mttf_h, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    fleet_gpus_str = fmt_count(fleet_gpus, label="GPU")
    fleet_rate_eq_math = fmt_math(f"{_fleet_tex}/{_mttf_tex} = {fmt(fleet_rate_per_h, precision=1, commas=False)}")
    hours_between_str = fmt_time(hours_between, "hour", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
```

Engineers read a GPU MTTF of `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.gpu_mttf_str` and plan around a five-year replacement cadence per device. MTTF is a population mean, not a lifetime assigned to each component. A GPU with MTTF `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.gpu_mttf_str` might fail at 200 hours or last 100,000 hours. Under the chapter's independent constant-rate model, a fleet of `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.fleet_gpus_str` has an aggregate rate of approximately `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.fleet_rate_eq_math` failures per hour, or roughly one failure every `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.hours_between_str`. This planning model helps size recovery capacity and spare pools. It does not make device-health monitoring pointless: temperature, error history, and recurring anomalies provide condition-specific evidence that the population mean alone lacks.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Ignoring restart overhead in checkpoint planning.*

The Young-Daly formula accounts for checkpoint save time, but practitioners often overlook the substantial overhead incurred during restart. In shared clusters, job scheduling delays\index{Recovery procedure!job scheduling delay} to acquire replacement GPUs consume minutes before execution can even begin. Once allocated, distributed storage reads impose significant checkpoint loading latency, communication re-establishment requires NCCL ring topology reconstruction, and warmup time\index{Warmup!recovery overhead} delays progress further while initializing kernels, refilling data pipelines, populating caches, and aligning optimizer schedules and model statistics with restored state.

Total restart time can be 3--5$\times$ checkpoint save time. A 5-minute checkpoint write and a 20-minute restart are separate costs: the write is paid when saving, while the restart is paid after failure, in addition to lost work since the last completed checkpoint. That recovery term should be included in the expected waste and recovery-SLO budget; it should not be added to $\CheckpointWriteTime$ as though it were paid at every checkpoint unless a specific recovery-aware checkpoint model derives that dependency.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Every failure should be handled as a full restart.*

Engineers often treat all failures as "node crashed, restart from checkpoint," but different failure modes require different responses. Transient stalls such as network congestion can permit a bounded wait or safe retry when state and the communication group remain valid; a brief fault can still require recovery if it corrupts state or leaves the group unusable. Permanent device loss requires replacement or a feasible resize, together with restoration of the missing state. Silent corruption requires a trusted recovery point, which may precede the latest checkpoint and therefore motivates checkpoint history retention. Persistent resource exhaustion (OOM, memory fragmentation) needs reconfiguration before restart; otherwise the job can crash again immediately. As @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-taxonomy-e78c details, misdiagnosing failure type wastes compute: restarting for a harmless stall discards useful work, while continuing from corrupted state can contaminate later updates.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Assuming checkpoints are consistent without validating state.*

Modern frameworks checkpoint transparently, creating the illusion of automatic consistency. In practice, distributed checkpoints require cross-node coordination that can fail subtly across multiple dimensions. Rank desynchronization\index{Checkpoint consistency!rank desynchronization} occurs when workers record different training steps, such as rank 0 snapshotting iteration 1000 while rank 1 captures iteration 1001. Similarly, transient storage failures can cause partial writes\index{Checkpoint consistency!partial writes} that leave behind truncated shards, sharded optimizer state lag\index{Optimizer!state lag} leaves optimizer states misaligned with model weights when captured asynchronously, and in-flight gradients\index{Checkpoint consistency!in-flight gradients} from incomplete AllReduce operations can produce ambiguous reduction boundaries.

Production systems must implement checkpoint validation: verify all shards exist, verify iteration numbers match, verify optimizer state matches model state. Organizations that discover corrupted checkpoints during recovery from a failure have no recourse except restarting from an earlier (potentially much earlier) checkpoint.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Fault tolerance can be tested only when failures happen.*

Fault tolerance mechanisms are code paths that execute rarely during normal operation. Like disaster-recovery systems that go unvalidated until an outage strikes, unexercised recovery logic steadily accumulates bugs. Checkpoint restoration procedures fail because training never previously crashed to exercise them, fallback models remain unverified because the primary never went offline, and circuit-breaker thresholds quietly drift out of calibration against evolved traffic patterns.

Chaos engineering (intentionally injecting failures) replaces an assumption of correctness with evidence for the fault models and recovery paths exercised. Organizations that kill selected GPUs during controlled training tests, inject network partitions, and fail primary models can discover broken recovery paths before a production incident. Coverage still depends on injection location, duration, load, and failure combinations; passing one campaign does not establish resilience to every failure.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Using elastic training as a substitute for checkpointing.*

Elastic training adjusts parallelism degree when workers fail, but resizing still requires a consistent recovery state. Reducing the active worker count requires redistributing model shards, optimizer states, and data assignments, often through checkpoint reload. Below some minimum viable size, training becomes infeasible because the model no longer fits or the batch policy cannot be maintained; the job must wait for sufficient capacity before restoring. If a failure was caused by a software bug triggered by specific data, the bug persists in remaining workers. Elastic training is complementary to checkpointing, not a replacement. Resizing alone does not justify a lower checkpoint frequency: the recovery contract, failure rate, and checkpoint cost still determine that choice.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Overhead budgets are fixed fractions of training time.*

Reference tables that show "pipeline bubble: 10 percent, checkpoint overhead: 5 percent, failure recovery: 3 percent" are easy to read as physical laws and pass through as line items in capacity plans. They are engineering targets, not constants. Pipeline bubble overhead depends on the number of microbatches and the interleaved schedule; elastic recovery can reduce waiting for replacement capacity while still restarting workers and restoring state; checkpoint overhead is a function of model size, storage bandwidth, and whether checkpointing is synchronous or asynchronous. Treating these numbers as fixed percentages leads to passive acceptance of avoidable inefficiency. The Young-Daly formula already shows that checkpoint cadence is a decision; the same is true of every other overhead listed in the reference tables.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Adding GPUs without accounting for communication and recovery overhead.*

Capacity plans typically account for Amdahl's Law and AllReduce overhead but treat reliability as a fixed background condition. At extreme scale, each additional GPU increases the aggregate failure rate, which inflates the expected recovery and replay time per job. There exists a cluster size beyond which the time lost to failures and recovery exceeds the time saved by additional parallelism, and wall-clock training time increases rather than decreasing with $N$. This is the reliability version of diminishing returns and it applies on top of the Amdahl ceiling. The two effects must be modeled together. Starting from a single-node useful-compute rate, scaling efficiency accounts for distributed execution losses; a further retained-progress fraction can account for recovery and replay excluded from that measurement. Measured distributed model FLOPs utilization (MFU) already includes scaling losses over its measurement window, so multiplying it by scaling efficiency again counts those losses twice. Whole-run useful goodput must count only retained progress and include recovery time in the denominator; its reliability penalty generally grows with $N$ under the independent-failure model.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Silent data corruption is negligible because hardware has ECC.*

GPUs and memory systems include extensive error correction\index{ECC!end-to-end limitation} (ECC, CRC, parity), creating the intuition that silent data corruption is negligible. Large-scale CPU SDC and memory-error studies show that silent corruptions and memory faults still occur at fleet scale and can escape ordinary error reporting [@dixit2021silent; @sridharan2015]. For a 10,000-GPU cluster, even rare per-device corruption events become operationally relevant because the system continuously executes enormous volumes of memory and arithmetic operations. ECC and link CRCs remain necessary layers, but they protect stored and transmitted bits rather than arithmetic, so they are not an end-to-end correctness proof for a training run. Silent corruption can produce loss spikes, gradient NaNs, or failed convergence, but none of those symptoms identifies hardware as the cause. End-to-end validation therefore combines checksums on data and checkpoint shards, cross-rank digests for agreement, redundant computation or replay where the risk justifies its cost, and statistical monitoring for model-level anomalies. The evidence must distinguish a bad batch, numerical instability, synchronization error, and corrupted hardware before the system drains a device or rolls back state.

:::

Recognizing these fallacies prevents engineers from optimizing for the wrong failure modes. The core principles required to build resilient machine learning fleets follow from the quantitative reasoning developed throughout this chapter.

## Summary {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-summary-48b0}

Fault tolerance turns the statistical expectation of hardware failure into a manageable operational routine. Individual component reliability compounds across thousands of devices, driving system-level MTBF from years down to hours. At fleet scale, systems must bound lost work and recovery delay through recovery that is automatic, fast, and minimally disruptive to training or serving.

Checkpointing provides the foundational mechanism for preserving training progress across failures. Synchronous checkpointing offers simplicity but imposes I/O overhead that scales with model size, while asynchronous approaches overlap durable writes with computation after consistent capture. The Young-Daly formula, $\OptimalCheckpointIntervalCkpt = \sqrt{2 \times \CheckpointWriteTime \times \MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}}}$, minimizes saving-and-rework waste under its first-order assumptions, while RPO and RTO constrain acceptable lost work and recovery delay. Immutable shards and a manifest published last identify a committed generation; valid capture and validation determine whether it is safe to restore. During membership change, resource-enforced fencing rejects stale writes. Idempotency, inherited deadlines, and retry budgets bound the additional traffic generated by recovery. Elastic training can then resume with a changed worker set when the training algorithm preserves its data, batch-size, and optimizer invariants.

Serving fault tolerance presents a different recovery budget from training. Training can tolerate minutes of recovery when the restored state satisfies its optimization contract, while interactive serving must preserve responsiveness and authoritative session history. Stateless model workers use replica redundancy and routing; stateful workers additionally need a policy for recovering session state. LLM KV caches can be reconstructed from retained history when latency permits, or replicated when reconstruction would exceed the request budget. Graceful degradation supplies a validated fallback when full service cannot be restored in time. Meta's OPT-175B run reported at least `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.manual_restarts_str` manual and an estimated `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.auto_restarts_str` or more automatic restarts due to hardware failures, alongside a separate need to recover from training instability. Netflix's dependency experiments illustrate the serving counterpart: recovery must be exercised against the faults the service expects to tolerate.

Recovery depends on evidence about both the failure and the state being restored. A loss spike can originate in hardware, data, numerical behavior, or synchronization. Suspect state can justify a pause or rollback while investigation continues; attributing the cause to a device requires corroborating telemetry, replay, or integrity evidence. Restore drills and fault injection then test whether the selected response actually preserves valid state and meets its recovery budget. Passing those tests establishes evidence for the exercised fault model, rather than a guarantee against every failure.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Failure is normal operation"}

* **Scale makes failure routine**: A 10,000-GPU cluster\index{Failure!inevitability at scale} encounters hardware failures every few hours under the chapter's component-rate assumptions; software must treat failure as a normal state.
* **Symptoms require evidence before recovery**: A loss spike or slow rank does not identify its cause. Correlate telemetry with replay or integrity checks, then use restore drills and fault injection to test the selected response against its stated fault model.
* **Checkpointing is the baseline**: Synchronous writes pause training; asynchronous writes can overlap storage I/O with computation, but require staging memory and a consistent, durably committed snapshot before recovery can use it.
* **Recovery is a contract**: RPO bounds lost progress, RTO bounds recovery delay, MTTR combines with MTBF to determine steady-state availability, a manifest identifies committed state, and fencing prevents an expired worker epoch from writing after replacement.
* **Checkpoint cadence balances two costs**: Under the first-order assumptions, $\OptimalCheckpointIntervalCkpt = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \MeanTimeBetweenFailures_{\text{system}}}$ balances checkpoint write overhead against expected rework; for the 175B running example on a `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster it lands near `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.tau_opt_min_str`. The selected interval must also meet limits on lost progress; recovery delay needs its own budget.
* **Elasticity enables persistence**: Designing training jobs to be "elastic"\index{Elastic training!resilience} (rebuilding communication groups and rebalancing data shards as traced in @fig-elastic-flow) can reduce waiting for replacement capacity. The runtime must preserve valid state and data coverage, and either preserve batch size or validate the changed optimization policy. Checkpoint cadence still determines how much work must be replayed.
* **Serving recovery follows the state budget**: Preserve authoritative history, then choose reconstruction, checkpointing, or replication for derived state according to the latency contract (@tbl-stateful-failover). A ready replacement provides useful service only when it can also recover the context the request needs.
* **Degradation is a designed mode**: When recovery cannot finish inside the latency budget, a fallback validated in advance (a smaller model, cached results, default features, or shed low-priority load) keeps the service useful, provided monitoring exposes how much quality was traded away.

:::

Fault tolerance makes the coordination tax a deliberate part of the execution budget. @Sec-appdx-c3-taxonomy-case-3 works a complete coordination-bound diagnosis, attributing a large run's lost wall time to checkpoints, failures, pipeline bubbles, and scheduling. In the Fleet Law (@eq-fleet-law), checkpoint pauses, detection timeouts, and restarts all land in the synchronization term $T_{\text{sync}}$. The chapter's mechanisms spend Coordination ($C_3$) so that a failure does not erase completed Compute, and asynchronous checkpointing and warm restart earn their complexity by moving part of that synchronization cost into $\OverlappedTime$ or shrinking it outright. The useful comparison is between time spent preserving and validating state during normal operation and time lost reconstructing trustworthy execution after a failure. A cheaper recovery mechanism is valuable only when it still meets the workload's limits on lost progress, response delay, and degraded quality.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From resilience to resource management"}

Keeping the fleet running despite inevitable hardware failures requires three layers: checkpointing preserves progress, elasticity absorbs node losses, and redundancy protects stateful serving sessions. A fault-tolerant cluster still needs orchestration, however, to decide which jobs run where, when to preempt, and how to share resources fairly among competing workloads.
